Controlled replay shows that correct user-target binding is more consequential than additional proposal detail alone, while a multi-turn extension reveals that provider objectives can remain influential even without final authorization by reshaping how the agent responds to user constraints and resistance. These findings expose a broader trust boundary: capabilities designed to serve the user can be redirected toward objectives originating outside the user-agent relationship.

title: Readable Before Actionable: Causal Tracing of Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Indirect prompt injection causes LLM agents to follow commands embedded in external data. A probe may distinguish instructions from data without identifying a state edit that changes the next action. We study this gap through counterfactual role probes, component-wise activation patching, and separate interventions on AgentDojo trajectories. Role decoding survives changes in content and format. In controlled Qwen tests, it precedes strong tool-choice effects from patches along an independently estimated role direction. On AgentDojo, directions estimated from hijacked and resisted training trajectories reduce attack success at pre-action and injected-span positions, but have little effect at random positions. In longer Qwen trajectories, single-position edits become less effective at later layers; span-wide and repeated edits reduce attack success on the same evaluation set. Removing the learned channel subspace preserves role decoding, yet effective intervention directions transfer poorly across the tested channels. These findings distinguish a readable role signal from an effective behavioral intervention: depth matters in controlled tool choice, while position and context also matter in attack trajectories.

title: An Exploration of Attacks on AI Agent Systems
abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.

title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.

title: Prompt-Injection Probes Learn the Conversation, Not Just the Injection
abstract: Linear probes on a model's hidden states are used as cheap monitors for indirect prompt injection: they screen the tool outputs an agent reads and send suspicious ones to a slower second check, so every false alarm has a cost. But a probe learns whatever separates its training examples. The standard evaluation of injection probes can be passed without the model: conversation position and text lengths alone reach 0.91-0.98 AUROC. When each attack is compared with the same conversation without the injection, or with harmless text formatted like an injection, standard probes flag most of these harmless cases. We add such cases to the training data as matched negatives. Across six open models, in applications seen during training and at the default threshold, changing only the training data cuts false alarms on injection-free conversations from 41-80% to 4-27%, and on harmless look-alikes from 92-98% to 3-16%. With a threshold set on normal traffic, our probe still catches a median 95% of the attacks that fooled the agent (91% without our data). In new applications, false alarms stay low, but detection depends on the model and on how the threshold is set. The same data also helps a text-only filter.

title: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
abstract: LLMs over external data face a per-instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety-utility frontier and forcing a choice between over-refusal and over-compliance. We argue the missing capability is \textbf{per-instruction credit attribution} and formalize it as External-Data Instruction Classification, an identify-classify-act decision over each embedded directive. We propose \textbf{EDIC}, a decomposed reward framework for per-instruction compliance. A scene-grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful-rejection by up to 7.7\% and Arena-Hard-Auto utility by 12.5\% on Qwen3-4B. The code repository is hosted at https://github.com/yingyingxia666/EDIC.

title: SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
abstract: Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM-driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built-in isolation. We argue that restoring SOP is neither sufficient (a same-origin public sink can leak private data) nor necessary (legitimate tasks require authorized cross-origin flows) for protecting the security of users. We propose SPIDES, which instead enforces information-flow control by gating primitive browser actions such as typing, clicking and navigating on labels propagated from element-level HTML confidentiality and integrity annotations. Untrusted and confidential content is masked from the agent's context, while policies block unauthorized flows, providing security guarantees against both prompt injection and data exfiltration that hold independently of the model driving the agent. To evaluate SPIDES and baseline defenses under a common threat model, we build MicroNet, a closed ecosystem of 28 interlinked websites with element-level ground-truth labels and paired benign/adversarial tasks. SPIDES achieves 0% attack success rate by design while retaining high task completion rate and autonomy. Our findings demonstrate that information-flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state-of-the-art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SPIDES.

title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space
abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large-language-model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. In this Systematization of Knowledge, we present PIAtlas, a taxonomy organized instead around how the injected instruction is constructed to subvert the underlying model. Its six classes, one per subversion mechanism, form the roots of a hierarchy of techniques and sub-techniques that researchers can use to describe attacks consistently and design more systematic evaluations. We derive the taxonomy from how LLMs are trained, prompted, and influenced by human-like framing, and compare it with historical attack data. To ground this comparison, we release PICorpus, to our knowledge the largest license-clean collection of public prompt-injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to PIAtlas under a human-verified protocol. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine several techniques drawn from only a few mechanisms. It also reveals gaps that existing labels obscure: widely used agent benchmarks test only part of the attack space, and adaptive attackers favor mechanisms that curated benchmarks underrepresent. PIAtlas thus provides a common foundation for understanding this attack space, improving benchmark coverage, and guiding red teaming and defenses.

title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a "BREAKING" tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.

title: KNOX: Hardware-assisted Regulatory Sandbox for Generative Models
abstract: Regulations require companies to run AI models in a regulatory sandbox, an isolated environment that enables monitoring model behavior by regulators, prior to deployment. But, they do not spell out the technical mechanisms to design such a sandbox. Ideally, a regulatory sandbox should show (i) compliance (checks against regulations, and deviations from intended behavior, i.e., unauthorized tool and system calls); (ii) confidentiality (protects model weights from regulators); (iii) attestability (produces tamper-resistant evidence of model behavior for monitoring); and (iv) scalability (evidence is verifiable by multiple regulators). Several prior works (information-flow control, prompt-injection defenses, control-flow integrity, and traditional sandboxing) address specific compliance aspects but lack confidentiality, attestability, and scalability. TEEs meet some of these requirements, but simply running models inside a TEE is insufficient as we need compliance mechanisms. We present KNOX, the first regulatory sandbox, built by running AI workloads inside TEEs. We demonstrate KNOX using agentic workloads. For compliance, we derive an attested policy manifest (with the applicable regulations, the expected tool calls, and the permitted system calls) for a given user prompt. Before an executor performs an action, an attested reference monitor compares it against the attested policy manifest and allows it only if it matches. Every action and verdict is recorded in an attested execution graph, enabling regulators to verify the model's execution and its compliance. We show that KNOX meets all requirements, and can check for compliance with regulations and deviations from intended behavior (e.g., due to prompt injection); and incurs low overhead (<1%).

title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.

title: Attention-based Classification for Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which adversarial instructions are embedded in external data processed by a language model, pose a significant threat to the integrity of deployed LLM agents. Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) is a recently proposed white-box detection method that identifies prompt injection attacks by monitoring how a model's attention is distributed between user task tokens and data tokens, claiming dataset-agnostic detection via a scalar focus score threshold. In this paper, we provide the first evaluation of Attention Tracker in a realistic agentic IPI setting using the AgentDojo benchmark, finding that the dataset agnosticism claim does not hold. We find that in agentic environments, long structured tool outputs subvert the fundamental assumptions Attention Tracker makes about attention that the method depends on and produces near-chance detection on AgentDojo across most model families. We propose AttnDA, an extension replacing the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over the per-head focus score vector, and evaluate both methods in a cross-dataset setting spanning four benchmarks. AttnDA improves detection performance across agentic and tool-integrated benchmarks, though transfer to AgentDojo remains challenging regardless of classifier choice. A covariance ablation further shows that removing inter-head correlation structure substantially contributes to performance, with complex covariance assumptions causing significant degradation on cross-domain data. These results indicate that the attentional distraction signal underlying focus-score-based detection does not transfer reliably to agentic environments, and that learned linear classifiers over head-level attention features offer improved detection performance, provided training data from the target deployment domain is available.

title: Protection Is Not One Event: A Survey of RAG Protection Research by Measured Endpoint
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems face security, privacy, and copyright risks including content leakage, source reconstruction, unauthorized access, data poisoning, and prompt injection. Yet RAG protection studies use incompatible evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models. We present a systematic survey and human-coded evidence map of 118 full-text-confirmed RAG defense papers, organized by measured endpoint rather than claimed goal or defense mechanism. Our seven-family taxonomy covers content disclosure, formal privacy proxies, access control and suppression, corpus-use detection, and pipeline integrity and attribution. Thirty-two annotators double-coded the papers kappa=0.867. The survey identifies three gaps. First, retrieval reranking and context rewriting each span five or six endpoint families, so mechanisms do not identify protection outcomes. Second, only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary endpoint; under the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% of records have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, and none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, most evaluations use general-purpose question-answering datasets and non-adaptive attacks rather than sensitive data and adaptive, multi-turn extraction. Our controlled RAG testbed shows that preventing verbatim copying does not prevent private-fact recovery: a normalized 8-gram guard reduces 20-token copying to 0.0%, but a three-query adaptive attacker recovers 48.3% of hidden facts on Qwen3-8B. We release the taxonomy, dataset, coding protocols, and testbed to enable comparable, claim-aligned RAG security evaluation.

title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.

title: AgentShield: Fortifying Web Applications Against AI Agents and Agentic Browsers
abstract: LLM-powered browser agents are transforming web automation by autonomously interacting with websites and executing complex workflows. However, the effectiveness of existing anti-bot defenses against these systems remains unclear. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of modern agentic browsers against widely deployed anti-bot mechanisms, characterizing their capabilities, limitations, and behavioral differences from humans. Our results show that many defenses designed for traditional automation struggle to reliably detect autonomous AI-driven agents. Accordingly, we introduce AgentShield, a behavioral fingerprinting framework that targets the Perception-Reasoning-Action (PRA) loop underlying agentic user clients. By leveraging dynamic web forms that progressively reveal content and capture fine-grained interaction telemetry, AgentShield exposes behavioral artifacts that enable differentiation between human users and autonomous agents. We further demonstrate Extinction-induced Policy Drift (EPD), a novel attack in which repeated obstruction of task completion causes agents to relax their safeguards and engage in unsafe behaviors. Finally, we present defensive prompt injection techniques that exploit agent-specific weaknesses to mitigate emerging forms of autonomous web abuse that rely on content extraction. Our results highlight both the shortcomings of current web defenses against agentic user clients and the feasibility of practical detection mechanisms tailored to this new generation of web automation.

title: The Long Con on the Web: Earn-then-Exploit Fraud Attacks against Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents increasingly operate with web access and high privileges, creating a new attack surface where web fraud can directly target autonomous agents. Existing studies mainly focus on malicious links, prompt injection, and interface deception, while content-level web fraud against agents and the amplification of attacks through agent trust remain underexplored. In this paper, we present EtE (Earn-then-Exploit), a web fraud attack framework against coding agents, in which a malicious website first provides multiple rounds of genuinely verifiable assistance to establish trust and then introduces task-related instructions that cross intended operational boundaries. To systematically evaluate its effectiveness, we construct 56 organizational environments (8 task contexts x 7 attack consequences) and evaluate three representative coding agents. EtE achieves an average scene-level attack success rate of 71.4%, including 85.7% on Codex-GPT-5.5, 67.9% on ZCode-GLM-5.3-Flash, and 60.7% on QwenCode-Qwen3.7-Plus, significantly outperforming all injection-based baselines. More importantly, our experiments reveal that coding agents exhibit trust-like behavioral reliance on previously helpful Web sources, and that such accumulated credibility significantly increases their susceptibility to subsequent malicious instructions. Based on this finding, we propose action-authorization separation (AAS), which prevents web content from directly authorizing privileged actions and reduces the attack success rate to 0% while preserving 100% task completion, outperforming all evaluated defense baselines.

title: The Devil is in the Context: Nine Dimensions of Prompt Injection Attacks
abstract: Prompt injection is usually discussed and evaluated as a single, homogeneous type of attack. However, vulnerabilities reported in real-world systems show that prompt injections vary widely. Moreover, the same instruction can be a prompt injection in one context and a legitimate request in another, depending on the user's intent and the system's policies. Ignoring this variation leaves gaps in how defenses are evaluated, and can give a false sense of security against real-world attacks. We identify nine dimensions along which prompt injection attacks differ. Together, they form a taxonomy that describes the injected instruction itself, its relation to the user's task, and how it manifests in the target system. Each dimension affects which defenses can detect or prevent an attack. We first use the taxonomy to characterize six real-world prompt injection vulnerabilities, showing how much these attacks differ. We then apply it to nine prompt injection benchmarks and find that most cover only a small region of this space. Combining benchmarks helps, but 13% of pairwise category combinations remain untested, mostly among the less commonly represented categories. Finally, we show that the taxonomy supports automated annotation of benchmarks and targeted generation of new test cases to fill these gaps. The taxonomy is also useful beyond benchmarks. Defense authors can use it to state which types of prompt injection they evaluated against, and system operators can use it to identify which attacks apply to their system and choose defenses to match.

title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, the standard injection template (AgentDojo's important_instructions) never redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY. Across 12 AgentDojo cells, SPILLWAY leads tested defenses in mean under-attack utility and composite scores. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, mean attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker stays below one percent, and SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.

title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
abstract: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects. In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions. Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.

title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
abstract: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
abstract: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).

title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning
abstract: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.

title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

title: SEOYUN: Refusal-Inducing Exam Documents for AI-Glasses Pipelines
abstract: Camera-equipped glasses can convert an examination page into a query to a vision-language model (VLM). Device detection addresses possession; a complementary question is whether an examination document can reduce the usefulness of an unauthorized capture. We present SEOYUN, an application-specific framework for refusal-inducing exam documents, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions. We use reverse jailbreaking to describe the direction of the objective: inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal. Refusal induction and defensive visual prompt injection already have precedents; our contribution is a threat model, analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol for examination use. We distinguish refusal from correct-answer leakage, show why removing an added dummy option is not itself a reduction in the original answer space, and derive a sampling comparison under explicitly stated camera assumptions. The protocol separates digital, simulated, and physical inputs and requires held-out evaluation after subject-specific selection. A local CSAT candidate corpus and rendering harness have been prepared, but this version reports no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results. Accordingly, SEOYUN is a research framework, not a validated defense or a basis for allegations against individuals.

title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Prompt Injection, Exfiltration Paths, and Practical Defenses
venue: Lecture notes in networks and systems

title: MongoGuard: A Mongolian Prompt Injection Attack Detection Model Based on Contrastive Learning
InjectGuard-RAG: Lightweight Defence Against Indirect Prompt Injection in Retrieval-Augmented Small-LLM Agents
Prompt-based attacks and defenses in large language models: A systematic review of threat models, taxonomies, and evaluation practices
A Systematic Survey of Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses in LLM-Integrated Applications and Agentic Systems
venue: International Conference on Big Data and Information Analytics (BigDIA)
abstract: Prompt injection (PI), listed as LLM01:2025 by OWASP, converts a data-representation problem into an execution-control problem: untrusted content is processed alongside privileged instructions, while large language models lack a native instruction/data boundary. Unlike jailbreaking, which primarily targets content-safety policies, PI targets application control flow and can induce unauthorized tool calls, information disclosure, or persistent-state corruption. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) studies PI from a provenance and information-flow perspective. It contributes (1) a three-tier attack taxonomy organized by contamination vector, attacker capability, and persistence; (2) a critical comparison of four defense lines and their trust assumptions; and (3) a cross-benchmark reporting audit together with Safe Utility Ratio (SUR), a metric for exposing security gains obtained by sacrificing task utility. We formalize PI as low-integrity data influencing high-integrity control flow, separate this integrity failure from subsequent confidentiality leakage, and identify evidence gaps in adaptive and stateful-agent evaluation.

title: Hijacking Tool-Integrated LLM Agents via Indirect Prompt Injection: A Benchmark Scaffold and Threat Taxonomy
venue: International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI)
abstract: Tool-integrated large language model (LLM) agents compose privileged actions — file reads, email dispatch, shell invocation — from the reasoning traces of a probabilistic model. Because the same channel carries both task data and latent instruction, any adversary who can place text into the data pipeline gains a tool-call influence that is bounded only by the agent's authorization envelope. Indirect prompt injection exploits this conflation. The security properties of such agents are not yet well characterized in the open literature: reports exist, but reproducible infrastructure, statistically grounded protocols, and explicit threat decompositions remain scarce. This paper does not claim a novel attack. It contributes three artifacts that the prior reports lack: (i) a reproducible benchmark scaffold for indirect prompt injection against a LangChain-style ReAct agent, parameterized over model, tool set, and injection medium; (ii) a consolidated threat taxonomy that unifies the HTML-comment, Base64, and hidden-CSS vectors introduced by Greshake et al. [1] with a supervisor-reframing adaptive variant designed to defeat system-prompt defenses in the sense of Perez and Ribeiro [2]; and (iii) an evaluation protocol specifying trial counts, confidence intervals, position-sensitivity ablations, and detection-latency measurements that a downstream empirical study can execute against real Llama 3 8B and 70B endpoints [3]. The scaffold is designed to be composable with InjecAgent [4] and AgentDojo [5]. We explicitly decline to report attack-success rates in this paper: the full empirical pass against live model endpoints is the next release of the artifact. What we do provide is the apparatus, the power analysis, and the qualitative behavioral shape of representative ReAct traces collected during scaffold development, clearly labeled as such. The contribution is infrastructural, not declarative.

title: Entropy-Based Adaptive Isolation for Indirect Prompt Injection Defense in MCP-Integrated LLM Agents
venue: International Conference on Electronic Information Engineering and Computer Technology (EIECT)
abstract: Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables large-language-model agents to invoke external tools and fetch third-party data. However, maliciously contaminated tool-returned content can trigger indirect prompt injection, which manipulates agents to execute unintended actions. We evaluate EAI on the InjecAgent benchmark with strict stratified train-validation-test splitting to avoid information leakage. For the held-out test partition (421 indirect-injection samples and 27 benign samples, qwen-turbo), EAI achieves an ASR-valid of 13.68%, compared with 29.30% for static isolation and 36.87% under no-defense setting. On the test set, zero false-positive rate is achieved, where all benign payloads are assigned to the low-risk tier. The full corpus contains 2108 indirect-injection samples and 136 benign samples, which are disjointly divided into training, validation and test partitions. This paper proposes EAI(Entropy-Based Adaptive Isolation), a lightweight pluggable defense module. EAI computes weighted character-level information entropy, and further constructs a composite risk score fusing normalized content length and instruction-keyword density. According to risk levels, three-tier adaptive isolation templates are dynamically selected without additional LLM inference overhead. EAI can be seamlessly plugged into existing MCP agent pipelines to mitigate indirect prompt-injection threats.

title: Hybrid Constitutional Classifiers for Prompt Injection Defense
venue: IEEE International Conference on Electro Information Technology
abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid constitutional classifier system that combines a lightweight input classifier with a fine-tuned generative LLM to enhance security while maintaining efficiency. Our approach integrates a DeBERTa-based classifier for filtering adversarial prompts before they reach the model and a small LLM that performs response monitoring to prevent unsafe completions in real time. Through extensive benchmarking, we demonstrate that our hybrid approach effectively mitigates adversarial inputs while significantly reducing inference latency compared to large-scale models like LLaMA-2 13B. We further explore optimization techniques such as model quantization and knowledge distillation to improve system performance with minimal degradation in classification accuracy. Our results indicate that the hybrid system achieves detection accuracy of 96.97% for inputs and 78.79% for the outputs, maintaining robust safe filtering capabilities while offering 67% lower latency in overall compared to conventional large LLM classifiers. The deployment of a hybrid constitutional classifier system for real-time AI applications enhances LLM security by providing a scalable, high-performance defense against prompt injection attacks, enabling safer AI interactions in critical domains.

title: Prompt Injection and Tool-Result Poisoning Against MCP Tool-Use Agents in Privileged Infrastructure: A Threat Model, Defense Architecture, and Preliminary Empirical Evaluation
abstract: LLM agents connected to shells, cloud commandline interfaces, databases, and secrets managers via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) inherit the authority those tools carry. An adversary who can write to any resource the agent later reads can redirect that authority without touching the agent directly. This paper formalizes the threat: an adversary model for external indirect prompt injection and tool-result poisoning against MCP agents on privileged site reliability engineering (SRE) infrastructure, a STRIDE-based threat taxonomy organized by injection point, attacker goal, and stealth level, and four SRE attack scenarios spanning shell, cloud-CLI, database, and secrets access. Existing prompt-level, structured-query, and capability-based information-flow defenses each leave residual attack surface against free-form privileged tool output. Drawing on object-capability theory and least privilege, we propose a three-layer architecture: a capability broker scoping each tool invocation to a task-bound token, a runtime policy engine validating proposed operations against declared intent, and a provenance and taint tracker carrying origin metadata through the reasoning chain. The evaluation is preliminary – three openweight models, no per-layer ablation, and guardrail rules not designed independently of the evaluated corpus (Section VIII) – but within that scope a containerized SRE testbed across twelve attack scenarios shows compromise falling from 72.8% (262/360 trials) disabled to 0% (0/360) enabled, no false positives on a benign control, and a held-out check against new pretexts holding at 0/90.

title: Prompting for LLM Security and RAG: A Survey from Zero-Shot to Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) and Prompt-Injection Defenses
venue: IEEE International Conference on AI in Cybersecurity (ICAIC)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in security-sensitive workflows such as incident triage, code review, threat hunting, and retrieval-augmented assistants. In these settings, prompting is not only a performance tool but also a security control surface: LLMs may consume untrusted content (tickets, logs, web pages, retrieved documents) that can adversarially manipulate outputs via prompt injection. This paper presents a structured, practitioner-oriented survey that unifies (i) core prompting methods (zero-shot, few-shot), (ii) reasoning-structured prompting (chains/trees/graphs of thought), (iii) robustness methods (self-consistency), (iv) efficiency workflows (skeleton-of-thought), and (v) automatic prompt optimization (APO) and learned prompting (directional stimulus prompting). We additionally synthesize cybersecurity-specific research on prompt injection, indirect prompt injection benchmarks, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, coordinated Prompt–RAG attacks, and interface-level defenses (structured queries). We provide a taxonomy, summary tables, and a decision guide for selecting prompting strategies under accuracy– cost–security constraints.

title: Secure MCP-Based Tool-Augmented RAG for Industrial IoT Diagnostics Under Indirect Prompt Injection, Retrieval Poisoning, and Modality Outages
venue: International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
abstract: Industrial IoT diagnostics require integrating diverse evidence streams, such as telemetry, event logs, configuration snapshots, and operational knowledge bases, while adhering to safety and security requirements. Tool-augmented retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) facilitates this integration by merging retrieval processes with the regulated use of tools. In Operational Technology (OT) settings, two primary risks associated with deployment are: (i) indirect prompt injection through retrieved materials or tool outputs, which can disrupt the model context and result in behavior that contradicts established policies; and (ii) limited visibility caused by tool failures, gaps in telemetry, and delayed logging, which diminishes evidential support and raises the chances of producing unsubstantiated outputs. This paper examines a protocol-aligned architecture that integrates MCP-exposed tools within a defense-in-depth RAG pipeline. The approach employs hybrid retrieval and reranking, instruction-aware content filtering, typed least-privilege tool mediation with audit logging, evidence-bound generation with citation enforcement, and outage-aware abstention policies. An OT-oriented stress-test suite is defined based on prior RAG security evaluations, and utility, security, and degradation metrics are reported using a proprietary multi-site IIoT dataset. The findings indicate the importance of treating retrieval and tool interfaces as distinct security boundaries in industrial diagnostic assistants.

title: Enhancing the Robustness of Visual Language Models Against Prompt Injection Attacks
venue: International Conference on Innovations in Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Development (ICIETSD)
abstract: AI-powered browsers increasingly leverage vision-language models (VLMs) to analyze images displayed on webpages for context-aware assistance. However, these systems are vulnerable to adversarial text injection attacks embedded within images-as demonstrated by recent Brave browser exploits where low-contrast text overlays manipulated AI behavior while remaining imperceptible to users. Traditional text-based filters cannot address this threat since malicious instructions are embedded as image pixels, not webpage text. We propose ViT-Shield, a lightweight preprocessing defense that detects adversarial text overlays in images before VLM processing. Through knowledge distillation from a Vision Transformer teacher to a ResNet18 student, we achieve$\mathbf{9 6. 0 \%}$detection accuracy on 5,000 COCO images with synthetically generated attacks varying in font family, size, position, and contrast levels. Our student model requires only$\mathbf{1 1. 2 M}$parameters and processes images in$\mathbf{8 m s}$at$\mathbf{5 1 2} \times \mathbf{5 1 2}$resolution-enabling real-time scanning of webpage images within browser pipelines. The distilled model achieves$7.68 \times$compression while retaining 99.48 % of teacher performance, making deployment feasible in resource-constrained browser environments. ViT-Shield is the first practical defense against image-based prompt injection in AI browsers.

title: Constitutional Sanitization and Fine-Tuning for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM-Based Log Analysis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in log-analysis workflows to summarize operational logs, alerts, tickets, and other external records. Because these records are untrusted data, they may contain malicious instructions. This paper studies indirect prompt injection in a scoped LLM-based loganalysis task where the model must preserve forensic information while refusing instruction-like text embedded in logs. We evaluate Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct under No Defense, Delimiter-based Datamarking, Constitutional Sanitization, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-based supervised fine-tuning (SFT) conditions. Evaluation uses a frozen 1,000-row external validation set with 600 attacks and 400 benign logs, with source-lineage and near-duplicate checks against the original training and pilot data. On this set, Qwen SFT plus Sanitization reduces attack success rate (ASR) from 519/600 (86.50%) to 251/600 (41.83%), while Llama Sanitization reduces ASR from 329/600 (54.83%) to 59/600 (9.83%). These gains are not cost-free: Llama Sanitization blocks or refuses 97/400 benign logs, and its explanation BERTScore, a metric based on Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), is 0.6492 versus 0.8561 for No Defense. The results support a scoped defense strategy: sanitize untrusted log content, report security and utility together, and treat residual ASR and benign blocking as deployment-relevant trade-offs rather than claims of absolute security.

title: MAMORI: A Cross-Lingual Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-Using LLM Agents
venue: International Artificial Intelligence and Data Processing Symposium (IDAP)
abstract: Language-model agents that call tools can be hijacked through indirect prompt injection; an attacker hides instructions inside the data that agent later reads and follows. Almost all of the attacks, benchmarks and defenses for this problem have been built and tested in English, which leaves a basic question open. If a defense stops an English injection, does it still work when the same injection is written in another language? To find out, we built MAMORI (Multilingual Agent Measurement Of Robustness to Injection), an extension of the AgentDojo environment that rewrites one attack across six languages and three scripts and also produces code-switched and transliterated forms. MAMORI records how each payload was translated, so a drop in safety cannot be blamed on a bad translation. Evaluating GPT-4o-mini in two simulated environments, we find that the weakness is not a low-resource problem but an English one. High-resource German is compromised 97.5% of the time, as often as mid-resource Turkish, Korean, and Arabic at 100%, while English alone holds out at 35%. None of the four English-tuned defenses we tried, namely a neural detector, structured delimiting, prompt repetition and tool filtering have lowered attack success in any non-English language and several raise it. Knowing that the attacker picks the language, a single-language score is misleading. We therefore propose Adversarial Cross-Lingual Robustness (ACLR), the agent’s resistance in its weakest language and the Multilingual Safety Illusion (MSI), the gap between an English score and that worst case. On the undefended agent, an English-only test reports 65% security while ACLR is 0% and MSI is 0.65.

title: Assessing Defenses Against Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM Systems
venue: International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
abstract: Prompt injection poses a critical security and compliance risk for large language model (LLM)-integrated systems. This paper treats prompt injection as a system-level governance challenge and introduces a model-agnostic guardrail architecture that performs prompt-level risk assessment prior to LLM inference. As a core component, we develop a dedicated prompt injection detector trained using Adaptive Layer LoRA on an in-house annotated dataset. Experiments across Gemma and Qwen model families show that baseline prompted LLMs exhibit unstable precision-recall tradeoffs and elevated false positive rates, while increasing prompt complexity alone does not improve robustness. In contrast, LoRA fine-tuned models achieve deployment-grade performance, reaching up to 99.05% accuracy with substantially reduced false positives, false negatives, and attack success rates.

title: Weaponizing Words: Direct & Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM
abstract: As AI systems—particularly LLM applications—proliferate across products and workflows, security has not kept pace. Prompt injection is the failure mode most likely to turn well-intentioned LLM applications into unsafe systems [4]. This 75-minute, code-first tutorial focuses exclusively on the two forms that matter in practice: direct injection through trusted input channels and indirect injection via retrieved or linked content. Using two reproducible demos—EmailGPT (direct) and EchoLeak (indirect)—participants will reproduce end-to-end attacks that override system instructions, exfiltrate secrets, and trigger unauthorized actions, then harden the pipelines step by step. Labs run on free notebooks with small open models and mock tools; no API keys required. We distill why guardrails and “better prompts” alone are insufficient—instruction-following bias, collapsed trust boundaries, and tool autopilot—and build a deployable defense-in-depth stack: input canonicalization, instruction/data separation, untrusted-context labeling, structured I/O contracts, provenance and taint tracking, deny-by-default tool policies, and red-team regression tests. Attendees leave with working intuition, tested code, and a practical checklist they can drop into RAG flows, agents, and email assistants the same day.

title: Position: Agents Orchestrate, Policy Enforces — A Deterministic Tool-Use Control Pattern for Agentic Assistants over Sensitive EEG Data
abstract: Agents that use language models to call external tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are entering sensitive environments, such as assistants that take action based on the emotional state they infer using electroencephalography (EEG). Prompt injection, tool poisoning, and unauthorized tool invocation threaten such agents while they act on state derived from identity-bearing EEG data. The position of this paper is that tool-use security cannot rely on the model’s decision, because the channel that carries legitimate instructions also carries the attack. The agent should issue action requests, but leave authorization to a deterministic policy engine. Three trust boundaries with ordered controls, mapped to an MCP threat taxonomy, implement the approach. A feasibility suite of 57 test cases, 32 adversarial and 25 benign, exercises the implementation: with controls disabled every scripted adversarial call executes; with all controls enabled the engine denies all 32 and executes all 25 benign actions. Allow/deny lists and schema checks issue most first denials; output sanitization never decides a rejection, so poisoned output content at the tool-output boundary (B3) remains unevaluated. The result is deterministic denial of the covered malicious and malformed invocations without any claims about robustness. In a rule-blind preliminary trial across four language models, all 21 malicious calls that reached the engine were denied. That small, one-time trial is not a robustness benchmark. Robustness needs an adaptive adversary, independent benchmarks, comparisons with existing deterministic defenses, and evaluation of returned-content attacks.

title: DISARM: Taint-gated counterfactual auditing for efficient defense against indirect prompt injection
abstract: The integration of external tools and untrusted data has transformed large language models (LLMs) into autonomous agents, but also exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where adversarial instructions in external content can manipulate tool use and compromise system behavior. Existing defenses use input filtering, reasoning correction, or execution control, but often trade attack suppression against task utility or runtime cost. We propose DISARM , a training-free defense that mediates action commitment at the tool boundary between agent-internal planning and external tool execution. DISARM keeps ordinary steps on a lightweight fast path and invokes one additional planner run only for selected checkpoints after removing any detected suspicious spans. It compares the proposed and replayed actions by tool path and critical arguments, allowing consistent actions, using the replayed action when only critical arguments differ within an unchanged tool path, and blocking tool-path deviations. This selective single-replay policy jointly targets security, utility, and low latency. On AgentDojo with GPT-4o, DISARM reduces the four-attack average attack success rate (ASR) from 23.01% to 0.37% while increasing utility under attack (UA) from 63.69% to 73.63%. On benign tasks, its 4.29s latency is 9.44% above No Defense but 56.22% and 66.80% below MELON-Aug and IPIGUARD, respectively. Across five LLM backends, the largest observed suite-level average ASR is 1.56%. Complementary WASP and all-suite fixed-configuration adaptive evaluations further examine transfer and gate coverage: no successful attacker objective is observed in the evaluated Base64 and fragmentation cases, whereas semantic parameter pollution retains 1.11% ASR. These results support DISARM as a lightweight tool-boundary defense while exposing the boundary of cue-based gating.

title: Denominator Dilution: A Composability Failure of Ratio-Based Verifiers Under Indirect Prompt Injection in Clinical RAG Systems
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series
abstract: Retrieval-augmented clinical AI that drafts Brief Hospital Course (BHC) notes is vulnerable to hijacking by malicious instructions planted in the retrieved chart. We study indirect prompt injection against BHC generation on MIMIC-IV Note across three model families and a 3×3 attack catalog. The catalog crosses three content families, fabricated diagnoses, substituted drugs, and critical lab values, with three tiers, templated, naturalistic, and adaptive. We test a two-layer defense: a strict-grounding system prompt (Layer 1) and an ontology-grounded Evidence Verification Ratio (EVR) detector calibrated to a 5% false-positive rate (FPR) on clean defended notes (Layer 2). On Llama-3.1-8B, Layer 2 cuts attack success rate by 11.5 percentage points (pp) alone but only 8.5 pp when stacked on the length-changing Spotlighting baseline, a 3.0 pp composability loss. We name this failure denominator dilution, formalize it, and show that the mechanism is general in principle: any ratio-based factuality or hallucination share detector stacked behind a length-changing prompt defense is exposed to the same failure mode, though we demonstrate it empirically in a single setting. We close the gap with ABSOLUTE-K, a detector that thresholds the absolute count of unsupported clinical concepts rather than their ratio to total concepts. Because it never normalizes by a length-sensitive denominator, ABSOLUTE-K shrinks the gap to 0.5 pp and exceeds the unstacked Layer-2 baseline at the same calibrated FPR. Layer 2 runs CPU-only in milliseconds on a standard desktop PC; the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge takes seconds.

title: e2a: A Secure Agent-Native Email Gateway with Phishing and Prompt-Injection Defense
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations (EMNLP)
abstract: Email is becoming the universal interface for AI agents, but an ingested message contains untrusted, malicious data the agent may execute as instructions.The indirect prompt-injection failure underlies real-world incidents such as EchoLeak (M365 Copilot, CVE-2025-32711) and the Gemini-in-Gmail hidden-HTML hijack.We present e2a, a deployable, open-source authenticated-email gateway that gives an agent a verified email identity and exposes two agentagnostic defense hook points.The (G)ateway authenticates senders via SPF/DKIM/DMARC and parses MIME structure; the (L)LM-layer screens the normalized prompt for injection.On top of the gateway, we construct a benchmark that isolates email structure as the firstclass injection surface: one payload rendered across eight transport surfaces.We measure the per-surface evasion delta for open-source classifiers, three commercial security APIs, and frontier LLM judges.We find that structural hiding defeats detection.A naive text/plainfirst parse costs every detector substantial AUC, dropping most classifiers below chance, and even on the gateway's structure-aware view no non-LLM detector survives.A frontier LLM judge on the same view recovers most of the loss, and conditioning the threshold on crypto- graphic sender authentication (DMARC) lifts held-out recall further. No single layer suffices.e2a is live and open-source (Apache-2.

title: LogicInception: Discourse-Level Indirect Prompt Injection via Causal Chain Construction
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
abstract: Existing indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks commonly face a stealth-effectiveness tradeoff: features that make payloads effective can also make them detectable because attack intent is localized in a single payload.LogicInception moves IPI to discourselevel inference: attack logic is decomposed into register-matched declarative fragments distributed across tool outputs and linked by fabricated causal dependencies that the agent reconstructs through reasoning.To our knowledge, it is the first IPI framework to demonstrate successful unauthorized tool execution with no directive instruction anywhere in the injected content.No fragment contains a command or exploits instruction-following; the attack emerges from the agent's own inference.We observe an empirical capabilitysafety amplification pattern: discourse-level amplification correlates with task capability across the evaluated models.On 1,139 scenarios with 5 defenses, LogicInception achieves 42.9-48.8%ASR at 88% per-fragment stealth, while all baselines remain below 8% composite success.The three prompt-level defenses reduce baseline ASR by up to 72% but reduce LogicInception by less than 7%; we trace this asymmetry to three architectural factors that motivate discourse-level rather than contentlevel countermeasures.This defense asymmetry is larger for higher-utility models in our evaluation, suggesting a tension between reasoning capability and safety.

title: Staying on Task: Defending Against Prompt Injection via Task Consistency Checking
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in real-world applications process heterogeneous inputs, including system prompts, user requests, and external content, exposing them to prompt injection attacks.Existing defenses, including prompt-level safeguards, external filters, and source-aware instruction handling, remain brittle against diverse direct and indirect prompt injection attacks.We propose CBC (Consistency Before Complying), a task-consistency alignment framework to defend against taskredirection prompt-injection attacks.CBC characterizes task consistency through semantic conflicts along action, constraint, and domain dimensions, then uses structured reasoning to determine whether newly introduced instructions are consistent with the original task before acting on them.Using targeted synthetic supervision, we train CBC to reason about task consistency and further strengthen this capability through dual-objective online alignment while preserving task utility.Across three model families and a diverse set of direct and indirect prompt-injection benchmarks, CBC improves defense success rates by up to 13.2 percentage points over the strongest baseline while better preserving task utility under attack.Our code and models can be found at https: //github.com/XOTaichi/CBC-PI.git. SystemYou are a research assistant.

title: Securing the Tool Layer: A Threat Taxonomy and Runtime Defense Framework for Model Context Protocol Deployments
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has rapidly emerged as the dominant standard for connecting large language models to external tools, databases, and services.Yet this convenience introduces a fundamentally new attack surface that existing LLM safety measures fail to address: adversaries can now compromise AI agents not through the user prompt, but through the tools the agent trusts.We present SHIELDMCP, a runtime security framework grounded in two contributions.First, we introduce a structured threat taxonomy derived from analysis of 80+ attack techniques catalogued under the SAFE-MCP initiative within the Linux Foundation's OpenSSF, spanning 14 tactical categories adapted from the MITRE ATT&CK methodology.Second, we describe an interception architecture that performs realtime validation of MCP tool calls and responses, combining structural analysis with semantic intent verification to detect tool poisoning, indirect prompt injection through tool outputs, and supply chain manipulation.In red-team evaluation across five popular LLM backends, SHIELDMCP reduces attack success rates from 74% to under 9% for tool poisoning and from 47% to under 6% for indirect prompt injection via tool responses, while adding fewer than 120ms of median latency per tool call.We discuss deployment considerations, the tension between security and agent utility, and lessons applicable to any organization integrating MCP into production workflows.Our framework is categorized as an Emerging system intended for real-world deployment.

title: Attenuation, Not Amplification: Measuring Indirect Prompt Injection Propagation and Containment in Multi-Agent LLM Delegation Chains
abstract: Abstract Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems route work along chains of cooperating agents, which raises a basic security question: does an indirect prompt injection planted in external data grow, persist, or fade as it travels down the chain? We investigate this question in a controlled pipeline of executor, relay, coordinator, and validator agents governed by a canary-based safety policy — a secret access code and a forbidden phrase that must never be disclosed. The study crosses three open-weight instruction-tuned models (1.7–3.8B parameters), four depth levels (a single-agent baseline plus 2, 3, and 4 hops), three payload families (a naive override, a policy-formatted block, and an authority notice), and a delimiter-plus-sanitizer “zero-trust” defense, for a total of 2,520 pipeline runs (30 per condition). Contrary to our initial hypothesis of cascading amplification, payload propagation attenuated with depth: the propagation rate fell from 31.1% at two hops to 14.8% at three hops and 8.9% at four hops (odds ratio 0.45 per hop, 95% CI 0.35–0.57). Coordinator-level violations were rare across multi-agent chains (3.8%) relative to a single-agent baseline (75.6%), and a validator agent intercepted 91.3% of single-agent coordinator violations. The zero-trust defense reduced propagation and coordinator violations (odds ratios 4.2 and 5.0 in its favour), but end-to-end violation rates were already near floor (0.9% versus 0.7%), leaving no detectable end-to-end benefit. Effects were strongly model-dependent: the relay stage retained the payload in 64.7% of cases for Phi-3.5-mini but only 8.6% for Qwen2.5-3B. We conclude that per-hop payload retention, rather than chain depth itself, governs multi-agent injection risk, and we discuss why these small-model, summarization-style findings should not be extrapolated to self-replicating payloads or frontier models.

title: "PromptGame Dataset: Prompt Injection Attack Benchmark and Defense Evaluation Data"
abstract: "This dataset accompanies the paper \"Semantic Integrity Under Prompt Injection: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Equilibria in Adversarial Natural Language Processing Systems\" published in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security.The dataset contains: (1) A comprehensive benchmark of 50 prompt injection attack types across four categories\u2014direct injection (15 types from TensorTrust), RAG poisoning (12 types from PoisonedRAG), separator\/delimiter exploits (13 types from Li et al.), and cascading agent attacks (10 types from InjecAgent)\u2014with 150 concrete attack instances; (2) Evaluation results from experiments across four LLM architectures (GPT-4o, Claude 3, LLaMA-3-70B, Mistral-7B) testing three defense mechanisms (Semantic Prompt Binding, Adaptive Risk Assessment, Randomized Token Embedding Shuffling); (3) Metrics including Attack Success Rate, Semantic Fidelity, defense overhead, and equilibrium satisfaction rates (SRE, ISE, CRE); (4) System prompts used for evaluation across 10 applic"

title: Mitigating LLM Prompt Injection, Hallucination, and Security Risks using Semantically Encoded Compiler Stage Watermarks
Securing LLM Powered AI Browsers Against Prompt Injection: A Comprehensive Survey, Threat Taxonomy, and Defense Framework
ContrastShield: A Contrastive Fine-Tuning Approach for Robust Prompt Injection Detection in LLM Pipelines
Ariadne: Adaptive, Human-in-the-Loop Defense for AI Agents against Indirect Prompt Injection
GraphShield: A Graph-Structured Defense Framework for Prompt Injection in RAG and Multi-Agent LLM Systems
Adapting Whisper for Hindi-English Code-Switched ASR: Prompt Injection vs. LoRA Fine-Tuning
A Hybrid Prompt Injection Defense Framework Using Rule-Based and Learned Detection with Policy-Driven Sanitization
WORKFLOW CENTRIC ANALYSIS AND OPTIMIZATION OF INDIRECT PROMPT INJECTION ATTACKS AGAINST AGENTIC LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
abstract: Autonomous and tool-augmented language-model agents are becoming increasingly popular, but they remain vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI). IPI is attacker-controlled instructions embedded in untrusted content (e.g., web pages, tool outputs, documents, or interface metadata) that the agent reads or encounters while completing a user task. Previous works shows that IPI can override intended behavior, redirect goals, and induce sensitive information disclosure, through low-salience surfaces that may be more noticeable for agents than for human users. Existing IPI evaluations often emphasize single prompts, pages, or episodes, which risk understating risk in realistic multi-step agent workflow. This thesis studies IPI as a workflow level threat in stateful web operating tasks. In this context attacker effectiveness may depend on when malicious content is encountered, what surface is attacker controlled, and how the attack is adapted to a target agent and defense configuration.To support controlled end-to-end measurement, this thesis produces WEAVE (Workflow Exploitability and Agent Vulnerability Evaluation). WEAVE is an executable evaluation harness for web workflows with explicit injection hooks, tiered attacker capabilities, and objective payload-specific grading. Using WEAVE, this work shows that IPI success varies significantly across tasks and across workflow context. This work further evaluates attacks that optimize offline prompt-and-placement variants for a specific agent and defense configuration. It shows that offline optimization improves attack success in multiple workflows while yielding interpretable signals about influential attack components and forms of commonly successful attacks. Finally, this work demonstrates how attacker-side optimization signals can inform defender-side hardening. Using optimization guided defensive profiling to reduce attack success relative to a baseline hardened agent. Overall, the results motivate treating IPI as a system-level security problem spanning agent architecture, observation channels, workflow structure, attacker optimization, and defense design.

title: PROMPT INJECTION ATTACKS IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS VIA A COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS OF ATTACK VECTORS, DEFENSE MECHANISMS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
venue: Proceedings of the Institute of Applied Mathematics
abstract: We present an extended taxonomy of 7 attack vectors and formalize prompt injection as an adversarial optimization problem.Empirical evaluation on GPT-4 (0613), Claude 3 Opus, and Gemini 1.5 Pro using a curated dataset of 1,000 validated attack scenarios shows baseline safeguards provide ~58% ± 3.2% protection (42% ASR).State-ofthe-art single-layer defenses reach at most ~82% but with elevated false positives.Our main contribution is an integrated six-layer defense-in-depth framework (building on but extending prior techniques like spotlighting [15] and multi-model verification [16]), which reduces ASR to 3.2% ± 1.1% (p < 0.001 vs. baseline) with acceptable false-positive rates (~5.3%) and moderate latency.Ablation confirms architectural separation and multimodel verification as key contributors.We analyze five real-world incidents (2023-2025) and provide deployment guidelines.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: A Survey of Attack Methods, Root Causes, and Defense Strategies
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI applications across diverse domains.
