abstract: The rise of LLMs has introduced a new opportunity in software devolvement, task automation, searching for information, etc. One of the cases where we find LLMs play a major role in web application and that makes LLMs a perfect attack vector for threat actors to use direct or indirect prompt injection attack to extract sensitive information about other users or other info that are not intended to be accessible and in other situation threat actors could try to jailbreak the model. One of the solution to outcome these attacks is to place an input filter that inspects the imputed prompt by the user and an output filter that inspects the response of the LLMs. Previous work in the field of Red Teaming AI had shown a different method for building prompts that can bypass the LLMs security, thus jailbreak the model, but when the model begins leaking sensitive information output filters will detect that and that could lead to operation failure. So the way to obfuscate the whole conversation between the adversary and the LLM in order to bypass input and output filter remain under research.

title: Beyond Shared Embedding Spaces: Towards LLM Architectures with Explicit Authority Control for Prompt Security
venue: International Conference on Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AAIML)
abstract: Large Language Models are highly susceptible to prompt injection because their architecture fails to separate system instructions from untrusted user data. Current defenses offer only superficial mitigation by addressing symptoms, not the root cause. This paper proposes a fundamental architectural shift to enforce this separation through mechanisms like authority-aware attention and segregated processing pathways. We outline existing vulnerabilities and present an architectural roadmap towards next-generation LLMs with structurally enforced instruction integrity and inherent resilience against prompt injection.

title: A Systematic Review of Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: Trends, Taxonomy, Evaluation, Defenses, and Opportunities
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into various infrastructure and interactive applications. However, their inherent linguistic flexibility introduces security vulnerabilities, particularly through Prompt Injection (PI) attacks. This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the evolving landscape of PI attacks, including their development trends, classification schemes, evaluation methodologies, defense strategies, and areas for future research. We analyze the evolution of attacks from basic natural language overrides to complex multi-turn manipulations, indirect injections using structured formats such as JSON and XML, and tool-assisted exploits involving automated prompt generation and multi-modal inputs like images. PI attacks are categorized by the level of manipulation, including character, word, sentence, and semantic levels, and by adversarial intent, such as prompt leaking and harmful content generation. The study analyzes these techniques within different LLM architectures and application contexts, including machine translation and Chain of Thought reasoning. It also reviews common evaluation benchmarks, datasets, and metrics. Mitigation strategies examined include automated red teaming frameworks, input validation, content filtering, and alignment through training. It differentiates itself from previous works by conducting a systematic review specifically focused on immediate injection, organizing its attacks, defenses and research gaps. Finally, this review identifies major research challenges and suggests critical directions for improving LLM safety and robustness.

title: Execution-Aware Stage-Wise Evaluation Framework for Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM-Based Email Agents
abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks have emerged as a critical security threat to large language model (LLM)-based email agents. However, existing evaluation benchmarks largely rely on simulated environments that cannot verify whether an attack will actually succeed in practice, often determining attack success solely based on tool invocation, which leads to frequent misclassifications of attack outcomes. In this paper, we propose execution-aware stage-wise evaluation (EASE) as an automated framework that quantitatively assesses the vulnerability of email agents to IPI attacks in a realistic environment integrated with the Gmail application programming interface (API) and multiple LLM APIs. EASE automates the entire pipeline of delivering attack emails, triggering the LLM agent, and collecting tool invocation logs, and judges attack success by whether the delivered email actually fulfills the attacker’s intent, using tool invocation only as a proxy baseline. Additionally, EASE’s modular architecture allows new LLMs, defense prompts, and attack datasets to be plugged in or replaced independently, and a Streamlit-based web interface makes the framework accessible to non-developers. To validate EASE’s effectiveness, we conducted 15,336 experiments using 639 attack samples across six LLMs under four defense conditions. The results demonstrate that executing attacks in the live service reveals what proxy-based judgment misses: 13.9% of proxy-judged successes are actually failures when the execution outcome is verified. We also observe that the same defense prompt can paradoxically increase the attack success rate for certain LLMs, underscoring the need for execution-grounded evaluation tools such as EASE. EASE is released as an open-source package on GitHub so that email agent developers and security researchers can adopt it immediately.

title: TrustTrace: Provenance-Aware Tracing of Indirect Prompt Injection Propagation in LLM-Assisted Learning Workflows
abstract: Indirect prompt injection can persist through retrieval, generation, and revision after the visible payload disappears. Existing defenses primarily detect suspicious inputs or constrain immediate actions, but they provide less evidence about which source influenced which final-artifact span through a temporally valid route. This paper presents TrustTrace, a provenance-aware framework for source-to-artifact tracing in LLM-assisted learning workflows. TrustTrace constructs a heterogeneous temporal graph over sources, retrieved contexts, prompts, responses, revision operations, and artifact spans. A dual-flow encoder separates legitimate evidence transmission from unauthorized control transmission, while differentiable reachability supports source attribution, contaminated-span localization, activation-stage estimation, and complete-path recovery. A bounded counterfactual verifier performs fact-preserving neutralization, suffix replay, calibrated set-valued attribution, and abstention. The primary pipeline uses procedurally separated GPT-5.5 profiles; construct validity is therefore tested with independent human ratings, a Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct generation set, and an independent Qwen3 neutralization-and-judging stack. On the independently audited EduTrace-IPI subset, TrustTrace improves strict Complete-Path F1@3 from 0.631 to 0.684 over the architecture-matched terminal-supervision baseline and from 0.659 to 0.716 after disagreement-flagged workflows are excluded. Human ratings of 800 stratified artifact spans correlate with the continuous contamination score at Spearman $\rho =0.78$ , and an independent Qwen3 verifier preserves most of the primary result (Span-F1 0.731 and Complete-Path F1@3 0.671). On Qwen3-generated workflows, TrustTrace obtains Span-F1 0.681 and Complete-Path F1@3 0.598 without retraining. Binary detection gains remain comparatively small, and specialized guards remain stronger on selected native input- or action-level metrics. The evidence supports TrustTrace as a complementary forensic layer for calibrated span and path tracing rather than a replacement for preventive defenses.

title: PhishRoute: Cost-Aware Multi-Agent Gating for Phishing Email Detection
venue: IEEE World Conference on Applied Intelligence and Computing (AIC)
abstract: Published LLM-based phishing detectors route every inbound email through a frontier model, which is costly at enterprise scale and, less obviously, can be suboptimal: invoking an LLM on emails a cheap classifier already resolves confidently can add false positives rather than remove them. We present PhishRoute, a five-agent detector with a learned gating router that decides, per email, whether expensive LLM agents run at all. The cheap tier (URL heuristic, header authentication, 27-feature logistic regression, AUC 0.993) reaches F1=0.9780 at zero token cost on a sender-disjoint 4,131-email test set. The expensive tier (LLaMA 3.1-8B text agent; dual-corpus RAG over 8,085 legitimate / 7,819 phishing vectors) is invoked only when the router escalates. On an n=1,000 held-out sample, a gradient-boosting router (selected over logistic regression, decision trees, and an uncertainty-margin rule) matches always-invoking-the-LLM’s recall exactly (17 FN both) while improving precision (0.9857 vs. 0.9817) and cutting token cost 59.3% (917 vs. 2,254 tok/email); McNemar’s test finds zero cases where gating is wrong and always-LLM is right. This corrects an initial n=200 result whose apparent optimum did not survive a 5× -larger reevaluation – we report that correction transparently. We also report an adversarial-robustness probe (robust to HTML/URL obfuscation; vulnerable to LLM-generated phishing and prompt injection), calibration metrics, and a fine-tuned DistilBERT baseline that exceeds PhishRoute on raw F1 (0.9952) at the cost of requiring supervised fine-tuning. Temporal evaluation on 2023–2025 emails yields F1=0.9879 with no per-year degradation.

title: Evaluating LoRA Adaptation and Fine-Tuning for Multi-Class Adversarial Prompt Detection in Transformer Models
venue: IEEE International Conference on AI Engineering and Innovations (AIEI)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed the way we interact with AI, but their openness also makes them vulnerable to malicious prompt attacks. Two of the most common threats are jailbreak attacks, where users trick models into bypassing safety filters, and prompt injection attacks, where hidden instructions are inserted into otherwise normal text. Detecting these adversarial prompts is challenging because attacks evolve at a fast pace and appear benign at first sight. In this work, we explore how different supervised fine-tuning strategies affect the ability of transformer models to detect such types of attack. We compare LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning on Google’s Gemma2B, Microsoft’s Phi-2 and TinyLlama with full fine-tuning of smaller transformer models like BERT-base, mDeBERTa and DistilBERT. Our dataset takes examples from several widely used datasets, including JailBreakV-28K, TrustAIRLab’s In-the-Wild Jailbreak Prompts and deepset/prompt-injections, covering three categories: benign, prompt injection, and jailbreaking. We have found LoRA-tuned Gemma-2B, TinyLlama and Phi2 performs competitively with fully fine-tuned BERT models while training only at fractions (less than 1%) of parameters. This shows that LoRA fine-tuning can maintain strong detection performance while reducing the computational cost significantly in large models, making it a practical solution for improving the safety of language models while keeping the base model weights freezed and still usable for general tasks like generating explanations for the detection. Our findings suggest that efficient supervised fine-tuning techniques like LoRA can help build faster, efficient, and scalable defense systems against evolving jailbreak and prompt injection attacks.

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Step-Level Tool-Call Safety Evaluation in Industrial Control Systems
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Industrial Technology Applications (AIITA)
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to operate industrial systems through structured tool calls to Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems interfaces. However, unsafe tool-call behaviors—arising from reasoning errors, contextual prompt injection, or explicit malicious requests—can directly lead to physical damage and safety incidents. Despite recent progress in agent safety, standardized benchmarks for evaluating step-level tool-call safety in industrial environments remain lacking. In this work, we present a guardrail-oriented dataset and benchmark for industrial LLM agents. We propose a three-mode safety taxonomy that distinguishes benign, injected-benign, and malicious requests, capturing both explicit attacks and covert contextual manipulations that induce unsafe behaviors in otherwise legitimate tasks. Based on this taxonomy, we construct a step-level dataset using a fully automated multi-agent pipeline that (i) generates industrial environments and tasks, (ii) injects structured contextual manipulations, (iii) samples tool-call trajectories, and (iv) assigns deterministic safety labels grounded in PLC constraints and industrial safety specifications. We further design a challenging cross-domain benchmark spanning six industrial domains, including water treatment, semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceutical fermentation, oil refining, nuclear cooling, and food processing. The benchmark enforces domain-specific entity naming, realistic numeric values, and constraint mismatches where physical safety limits are stricter than PLC register bounds, enabling systematic evaluation of guardrail generalization under distribution shift. Experimental results show that strong instruction-tuned LLMs, while effective at handling explicitly malicious requests, struggle to detect unsafe behaviors induced by contextual prompt injection, revealing a critical blind spot in existing safety mechanisms. In contrast, a guardrail model fine-tuned on our dataset demonstrates substantially improved sensitivity to step-level safety violations, particularly in injected-benign scenarios, while maintaining robust performance against explicit attacks. These findings highlight the necessity of step-level supervision and the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark for developing reliable industrial agent guardrails. Our dataset and benchmark provide a standardized testbed for step-level tool-call safety in industrial LLM agents and establish a foundation for future research on safe and reliable autonomous industrial systems.

title: Prompt Injection Attack Detection with Machine Learning
venue: Innovations in Intelligent Systems and Applications Conference (ASYU)
abstract: The introduction of large language models into our lives has created a revolution, allowing artificial intelligence to be easily used and accessible by everyone. With this opportunity, large language models are now used in every step of our lives, from education to economy, agriculture to health, and are on their way to becoming a part of us. This widespread use of large language models attracts the attention of malicious people and brings with it security problems and concerns. Despite this rapid growth and expanding attack surface area, the precautions taken by model publishers are inadequate. This study focuses on the current inadequacy in the relevant field and presents a detection suggestion against 'Prompt Injection' attacks, one of the most commonly used attacks against large language models. Within this scope, 10 different models developed using various approaches were used to analyze the input text and classify whether or not it contained attacks. The tests showed that the most successful results were obtained with the BERT-based model, achieving 88 % accuracy and an F1 score of 87 %. The most important feature that distinguishes the study from existing studies is that, unlike existing detection models, it has the ability to detect in Turkish.

title: Safeguarding LLM-Applications: Specify or Train?
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on AI Engineering – Software Engineering for AI (CAIN)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful tools used in several applications such as conversational AI, and code generation. However, significant robustness concerns arise with LLMs in production, such as hallucinations, prompt injection attacks, harmful content generation, and challenges in maintaining accurate domain-specific content moderation. Guardrails aim to mitigate these challenges by aligning LLM outputs with desired behaviors without modifying the underlying models. Nvidia NeMo Guardrails, for instance, rely on specifying acceptable/unacceptable behaviours. However, it is challenging to predict and address potential issues of LLMs in advance to create these guardrails. Also, manual updates from software engineers are often required to maintain and refine these guardrails. We introduce LLM-Guards, specialised machine learning (ML) models trained to function as protective guards. Additionally, we present an automation pipeline for training and continual fine-tuning of these guards using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). We evaluated several small LLMs, including Llama-3, Mistral, and Gemma, as LLM-Guards for challenges such as moderation and detecting off-topic queries, and compared their performance against NeMo Guardrails. The proposed Llama-3 LLM-Guard outperformed NeMo Guardrails in detecting offtopic queries, achieving an accuracy of 98.7% compared to 81%. Furthermore, the LLM-Guard detected 97.86% of harmful queries” surpassing NeMo Guardrails by 19.86%.

title: A Prompt Injection Detection Model Addressing Over-Defense
venue: International Conference on Informatics and Information Technologies (CIIT)
abstract: Web applications that incorporate Large Language Models (LLMs) are at serious risk from prompt injection attacks, which let attackers to modify model behaviour by using maliciously designed inputs. While numerous detection and defense mechanisms have been proposed, existing approaches often suffer from over-defense, limited generalization, or impractical deployment assumptions. In this paper, we propose a hybrid prompt injection detection model based on contextual language modeling aided by DeBERTa, semantic similarity analysis by Sentence BERT (SBERT), and feature engineering after examining prompt injection attack detection techniques. In the investigation and evaluation of this model on a set of 571 prompts with various attack vectors, the model resolves the issue of over-defense with a balance of precision and recall of 96.88% and 93.94% respectively, thereby rejecting the threat of false positives. This suggests the importance of each of the techniques and the significance of feature engineering.

title: ShadowPlay: Engineering Defenses Against Role-Based Prompt Injection and Dependency Hallucination in LLM-Powered Development
venue: International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized software development by providing intelligent code generation and assistance capabilities. However, their integration into development workflows introduces critical security vulnerabilities that traditional cybersecurity measures fail to address. This paper presents ShadowPlay, a novel multi-layered defense framework specifically engineered to detect and mitigate two emerging threat vectors: role-based prompt injection attacks and dependency hallucination vulnerabilities. Our approach combines formal verification techniques with Machine Learning (ML)-based behavioral analysis to create a comprehensive security solution. The framework employs four integrated components: a semantic prompt analysis engine, a real-time dependency verification system, a behavioral monitoring module, and a response validation layer. Through extensive evaluation on over 20,000 attack scenarios across diverse threat categories, ShadowPlay demonstrates superior performance with 95.1% overall accuracy, 97.2% precision, and only 1.8% false positive rate, while maintaining an average response latency of 127 milliseconds. Our contributions include the first formal mathematical model for these attack vectors, a production-ready defense architecture, and comprehensive empirical validation demonstrating significant improvements over existing approaches.

title: A Hybrid LLM Firewall for Direct Prompt Injection and Instruction Smuggling Defense
venue: International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI)
abstract: We present a Hybrid Large Language Model (LLM) firewall that integrates policy-based safeguards, a DeBERTa-v3 semantic classifier, and response verification into a unified defense against direct prompt injection and instruction smuggling. The firewall inspects each prompt before it reaches the target LLM, either rejecting it or allowing it to proceed through a two-stage screening pipeline. In the first stage, a policy-based filter detects prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts using rule- and keyword-driven checks, complemented by outbound filtering to mitigate leakage in generated responses. Prompts that pass this stage are then evaluated by our DeBERTa-v3-based model, which classifies requests based on inferred intent to capture smuggling attempts that may evade keyword triggers while maintaining intent-aware analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach improves instruction smuggling detection over policy-only and model-only baselines, while maintaining low false-positive rates through intent-aware classification.

title: A Structural Decomposition of Prompt Injection Threats Targeting Large Language Models
venue: International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used for text generation, summarization, and question answering. Their growing integration into applications and third-party services introduces new security risks. Among these, prompt injection is especially concerning: adversaries manipulate model behavior by embedding malicious instructions in user inputs or external data. This paper presents a structured decomposition of such attacks. We propose a three-dimensional taxonomy based on attack vector, mode of operation, and adversarial goal. Using this framework, we classify known attack patterns, including direct prompt manipulation, third-party channel exploitation, data poisoning, and human-assisted strategies. We also review defenses such as input sanitization, role-based access control, monitoring, and instruction-data separation. The taxonomy provides a foundation for systematic analysis and comparison of prompt injection vulnerabilities, supporting more robust defensive architectures.

title: Fine-Tuning Multimodal Vision-Language Models for Brain CT Diagnosis via a Triple-Branch Framework
venue: International Conference on Digital Image Processing and Computer Applications (DIPCA)
abstract: Medical image analysis, particularly for brain CT scans, requires advanced techniques to improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Existing multimodal models often struggle with the complexities of domain-specific medical images and their associated reports. This article presents TriMedTune, a novel triple-branch framework designed to fine-tune multimodal models for brain CT diagnosis. The proposed framework consists of three core components: Hierarchical Visual Prompt Injection (HVPI), Diagnostic Alignment for Terminology Accuracy (DATA), and Medical Knowledge Distillation with Uncertainty Regularization (MKD-UR). These modules enhance the model’s ability to process and interpret medical images by improving visual context understanding, aligning diagnostic terminology, and ensuring robust performance through knowledge distillation and uncertainty modeling. The framework utilizes efficient training strategies, including LoRA-based fine-tuning, dynamic prompt sampling, and mixed-precision optimization. Experimental evaluations show that TriMedTune outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple performance metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in medical image diagnosis and report generation.

title: RIPE-II: Retrieval In-Place Poisoning Evaluation with Indirect Injections
venue: International Conference on Dependable Systems & Networks/Proceedings
abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have enhanced the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by effectively addressing challenges such as hallucinations and generating irrelevant responses. However, integrating the RAG technique into LLMs introduces privacy risks and potential data leakage issues from the retrieval pipeline. Indirect Prompt Injections (IPIs) occur when hidden instructions inside retrieved documents slip into a model’s context as trusted evidence, exploiting weak guardrails in RAG systems and leading to unauthorized data leaks, ambiguous outcomes, and policy overrides. Existing defenses rely on brittle delimiter heuristics or limited retriever adjustments, leaving RAG systems vulnerable to adversarial directives blended seamlessly into retrieved content.In this paper, we present RIPE-II, a corpus-level benchmark that evaluates IPIs under a realistic content-poisoning threat model. RIPE-II constructs delimiter-free, position-aware poisoned corpora across multiple domains and includes both textual and visual injections. Our design explicitly models mid-document placement, chunking, truncation, and cross-component propagation, reflecting how enterprise RAG systems ingest and process content. We introduce a two-stage evaluation framework that separates retrieval exposure from generation-time compliance and distinguishes embedding-based similarity from semantic override using a calibrated LLM-based judge. Across biomedical, financial, scientific, open-domain question answering, including multi-hop reasoning and web passage retrieval settings, we find that poisoned documents can reach the final model context in up to 97% of queries and rank first in up to 94% of cases, showing that retriever and reranker choices substantially shape RAG security exposure. We further show that cosine-based attack scoring can underreport semantic compromise by more than 5×, demonstrating that lexical or embedding similarity alone is insufficient for evaluating indirect prompt injection risk.

title: SCD-Net: A Deep Semantic Contrastive Defense Network Against Prompt Injection in Power Grid LLMs
venue: International Conference on Electronic Information, Computer and Aerospace Remote Sensing (EICARS)
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into power grid Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems introduces unprecedented operational efficiencies but exposes critical infrastructure to stealthy prompt injection attacks. Conventional defenses, such as statistical gateways and general-domain perplexity filters, suffer from severe domain mismatches when applied to specialized industrial contexts, resulting in an irreconcilable trade-off between system usability and security. To address this fundamental limitation, we propose the Deep Semantic Contrastive Defense Network (SCD-Net). By projecting unstructured instructions into a normalized contrastive space, SCD-Net's fail-safe prototype mechanism accurately measures cosine disparities to intercept out-of-distribution (OOD) semantic camouflage attacks. Furthermore, we introduce PowerAdv, a large-scale, high-fidelity SCADA LLM security benchmark featuring zero-shot deceptive payloads. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCD-Net effectively compresses the OOD Gateway Attack Success Rate (GASR) to a highly robust 16.42% while maintaining a near-zero In-Distribution False Positive Rate (ID FPR) of 0.39% and an exceptional OOD FPR of 11.97%, drastically outperforming existing baselines. Our framework provides a highly reliable zero-shot anomaly routing paradigm for securing intelligent middleware in critical infrastructure.

title: Runtime Prompt Injection Defense for Production-Scale AI Agent Systems
abstract: Prompt injection can redirect an AI agent when adversarial instructions are embedded in user messages, retrieved documents, or tool responses. This paper presents PIGUARD, a runtime defense framework that combines a semantic intent classifier, instruction provenance tracking, cross-turn consistency verification, and policy-driven guardrail enforcement. Under the evaluated workload-replay setting at 500 concurrent agents, PIGUARD achieves a 93.1% per-injected-turn detection rate, a 2.1% per-benign-turn false-positive rate, a median end-to-end decision latency of 54.6 ms, and 98.4% benign throughput preservation measured at the session level. The evaluation covers direct injection, indirect retrieval-augmented generation injection, multi-step sequential payloads, paraphrase evasion, and nested structured-context attacks. These results demonstrate the behavior of the layered runtime design under the tested replay workload; they do not imply universal robustness to unseen attack families, fully adaptive adversaries, or deployment environments outside the evaluated setting.

title: Agentic AI Red-Teaming for Prompt Injection Detection in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems introduce security risks beyond single-model deployments because malicious instructions can propagate through agent messages, tool responses, shared memory, and orchestration layers. This paper presents an integrated red-team/blue-team framework for prompt-injection detection in agentic AI systems. The framework defines five attack classes—direct injection, indirect tool-response injection, agent-to-agent manipulation, tool-chain privilege escalation, and memory poisoning—and combines automated adversarial payload generation with a lightweight detector using TF-IDF representations and 16 interpretable structural security indicators. Evaluation on a 1,475-sample controlled benchmark yields 99.92% indistribution F1, while detection against the four evaluated non-adaptive surface mutations reaches 99.29% at 0.056 ms mean inference latency (17,907 messages/s). Because the training and controlled evaluation samples share underlying template families and mutation processes, these near-perfect results primarily establish detection consistency within the evaluated adversarial distribution rather than open-world robustness. Cross-benchmark evaluation on WildJailbreak- and AgentDojo-style samples provides a stronger test of generalization, yielding 81.0% accuracy$(\mathrm{F} 1=0.829)$and exposing failures on benign security discussions and semantically disguised role-play attacks. These findings demonstrate both the operational value and limitations of lightweight structural detection. We therefore position the proposed detector as a high-throughput first layer in a defense-in-depth architecture, with uncertain messages escalated to semantic analysis and behavioral monitoring for adaptive and context-dependent attacks.

title: Lightweight Transformer Models for Prompt Injection Detection: A Comparative Study of TinyBERT and ALBERT
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are embedded in chatbots, coding assistants and autonomous agents that accept untrusted user input as part of their operating context. This design creates an exploitable seam, prompt injection, where crafted text overrides or hijacks a model’s original instructions, has emerged as one of the most consequential attack vectors against deployed LLM systems. Yet, detection approaches are either heavyweight guard models unsuitable for low-latency deployment or heuristic filters with limited generalization. This study examines whether lightweight and computationally efficient transformer encoders can serve as effective detectors for prompt injection. Using the ‘deepset/prompt-injections’ corpus (662 prompts), language detection and machine translation were applied to unify a substantial non-English portion of the data, followed by Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) projections to characterize class separability. Two compact architectures, e.g., Tiny Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (TinyBERT) and A Lite BERT (ALBERT), were fine-tuned on a stratified split and validated using 5-fold cross-validation to assess stability. A six-configuration ablation study further isolated the effects of class weighting, encoder freezing, sequence length, learning rate and weight decay on downstream performance. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based attribution was used to sanity-check whether predictions relied on semantically meaningful cues. ALBERT outperformed TinyBERT (0.990 vs. 0.980 test accuracy, 0.987 vs. 0.975 F1) and showed markedly lower cross-fold variance. The ablation results revealed that input truncation and elevated learning rates degraded performance more than class-weighting choices did. These findings indicate that methodological design is as consequential as architecture choice when building efficient, deployable prompt-injection detectors.

title: Identity-Spoofing Prompt Injection: Empirical Analysis of Instruction Leakage in Custom GPTs
venue: IEEE International Conference on AI in Cybersecurity (ICAIC)
abstract: Custom GPTs allow creators to publish configurable large language model assistants by combining hidden system-level instructions with optional uploaded knowledge, concentrating sensitive creator-provided assets behind a conversational interface that is not a hardened security boundary. We measure confidentiality risk in store-prominent Custom GPTs under a prompt-only adversary model and focus on identity-spoofing prompt injection, where a user impersonates a privileged role (e.g., the creator) and frames disclosure as benign verification or debugging. Using a fixed four-stage protocol on a mid-May 2025 store snapshot (N=57), we observe unauthorised system-instruction disclosure in 87.7% (50/57) of targets, with consistently high rates across store categories. Conditional on Stage-1 success, 28/50 targets further exposed knowledge-base metadata and/or content when a knowledge base was available, indicating that instruction leakage can enable downstream disclosure steps. We further provide an evidence trace showing how identity claims and verification-style framing can shift targets into a compliance-oriented mode and accelerate cross-stage disclosure. Overall, the results position identity-spoofing as a distinct, reproducible prompt-injection strategy in store-prominent Custom GPTs and motivate layered mitigations spanning creator configuration and platform-level leakage monitoring.

title: Defending Against Prompt Injection Attacks Using Automatic System Prompt Engineering
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Information and Communication (ICAIIC)
abstract: Large language models are vulnerable to jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, and most existing defenses rely on a single, human-crafted global system prompt. This paper proposes a method that automatically optimizes only the suffix of the system prompt on a per-cluster basis while keeping the model parameters and the global prefix fixed. We cluster attack prompts using k-means on the model's final hidden states, and, for each cluster, learn a suffix through an Analyzer-Rebuilder loop. In evaluations that combine an LLM judge with watermark-based detection, our method reduces the test attack success rate (ASR) from about 0.42 to$\text{0. 2 8}$.

title: Multimodal and Multiple Prompts for Biology
venue: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics Speech and Signal Processing
abstract: Prompt learning for vision-language models, e.g. CLIP, is a rapidly advancing topic, focusing on leveraging pre-trained foundational models to generalize to downstream tasks with minimal training samples. Current prompt-tuning methods primarily optimize on general datasets, yet their application in biological datasets remains limited due to the field’s specificity. To address this gap, we introduce Multimodal and Multiple Prompts for Biology (MMPB). Our approach incorporates a Vision Prompt Injection module, which injects diverse biological visual information from the vision branch into the language branch. Additionally, we propose a multiple prompts scheme tailored to the fine-grained naming conventions in biology. We assess the method’s effectiveness on generation to novel classes, and results demonstrate that MMPB significantly outperforms existing approaches across eight biological datasets. Specifically, MMPB achieves a 14.90% absolute improvement in novel classes performance and an 11.71% gain in harmonic mean compared to the state-of-the-art.

title: IPI 2 : Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injections on Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Agents Using Physical Invariants
venue: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics Speech and Signal Processing
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) agents enable natural human–machine interaction, broadening UAV applications in complex scenarios. However, these agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where adversaries exploit untrusted external data sources (e.g., corrupted knowledge bases) to redirect LLMs from legitimate instructions toward malicious ones. Existing defenses either rely on keyword filters or auxiliary LLMs, which are often computationally costly and insufficiently robust. In this paper, we present IPI2, a defense framework that mitigates IPI attacks by leveraging UAVs’ physical invariant properties. Our key insight is that, despite the diversity of UAV tasks and attack strategies, benign UAV logs consistently exhibit stable invariant patterns. IPI2profiles these distributions from benign data and performs similarity analysis using Kullback–Leibler divergence to detect anomalies indicative of IPI corruption. Extensive experiments across 2 UAV agents, 3 tasks, 4 LLMs, and 5 attack types demonstrate that IPI2achieves a 68.3% reduction (92.0%→23.7%) in average attack success rate. We further show that IPI2remains robust against adaptive adversaries.

title: Cross-Agent Multimodal Provenance-Aware Framework for Robust Prompt Injection Defense in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
venue: International Conference on Computer and Applications (ICCA)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), VisionLanguage Models (VLMs), and new agentic AI systems (e.g., LangChain and GraphChain) allow autonomous systems to reason and plan, and to coordinate between an assortment of tools and agents. Nevertheless, this feature also brings vulnerability to multimodal prompt injection (PI) attacks, in which hidden or malicious instructions that are embedded in text, images, metadata, or interagent messages can spread throughout the agent graph, triggering unintended behavior or policy violation, or corrupting a state. To mitigate these threats, this paper will present a Cross-Agent Multimodal Provenance-Aware Defense Framework that will sanitize any user- or agent-generated prompts and validate the output of the LLM independently, prior to their delivery to downstream nodes. The framework incorporates a text sanitizer agent, visual sanitizer agent and an output validator agent which are synchronized by a provenance ledger which documents modality, source and trust metadata throughout the agent network. The architecture implements ordered trust boundaries, so that an injected instruction cannot spread out via LangChain- or GraphChain-style workflows. There are better multimodal PI detection accuracy, lower trust leakage between agents, and more stable agentic execution pathways, all of which are experimentalized. This framework can build secure, interpretable, and reliable agentic AI systems by augmenting the established provenance tracking and validation systems to multi-agent orchestration.

title: Beyond Individual Defenses: Evaluating Defense Combinations Against Prompt Injection Attacks
venue: International Conference on Computer and Applications (ICCA)

title: CrossGuard-VLM: A Robust Defense Framework for Vision-Language Models Against Multimodal Threats
venue: IEEE International Conference on Cybernetics, Cognition and Machine Learning Applications (ICCCMLA)
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) incorporate visual and textual information to facilitate various multimodal applications, but they are highly susceptible to image-based indirect prompt injection attacks involving adversarial perturbations, semantic mismatches, and steganographic embedding. Existing defense approaches, designed mainly for text-based models, do not effectively address these risks. To overcome this gap, we propose CrossGuard-VLM, a hybrid defense framework integrating input filtering, semantic alignment verification, anomaly-based adversarial detection, and steganography analysis. The design uses CLIP for semantic validation, a VGG16 AutoEncoder with Isolation Forest for perturbation detection, and a CNN–Random Forest hybrid for steganography detection. Mitigation is then carried out using methods like color quantization and Gaussian blurring, with audit logging ensuring transparency. Through experimental evaluation, our CrossGuard-VLM is successful in detecting and mitigating such threats that guarantees robustness, offering a practical foundation for secure multimodal systems.

title: CarrierGuard-Java: Carrier-Aware Zero-Trust Code Ingestion Defense for LLM-Assisted Static Analysis Alert Triage
venue: International Conference on Computer Engineering and Application (ICCEA)
abstract: Traditional static application security testing (SAST) has long suffered in real-world projects from noisy alerts and high manual review costs. Although large language models (LLMs) can assist triage, they may mistake indirect prompt injections embedded in comments, Javadoc, and strings as high-priority instructions. This paper proposes CarrierGuard-Java, a zero-trust code ingestion architecture for already reported CodeQL alerts that constructs safe triage input packages for downstream models through carrier-aware scanning, risk-evaluator judgment, and line-stable reconstruction. We systematically compare this method against three baselines—raw, strip_comments, and regex_sanitize—on CWE-Bench-Java and decontaminated Juliet Java. The results show that CarrierGuard-Java improves the accuracy on positive samples in CWE-Bench-Java under suppression attacks from 0.8448 to 0.9138, and raises the accuracy on negative samples in Juliet under promotion attacks from 0.0294 to 0.3333, demonstrating that input-side guardrails are necessary and effective for LLM-assisted SAST triage.

title: Zero-Shot Prompt Injection Detection via N-gram Pooling of Token-Level Hidden States
venue: International Conference on Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics, and AI Applications (ICCSDFAI)
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where adversaries embed malicious instructions inside retrieved documents. Existing embedding-based detectors rely on mean-pooled sentence vectors, which suppress short injection spans hidden within long benign text — a phenomenon we formalize as semantic dilution. We extract per-token hidden states from a frozen 22M-parameter sentence transformer already present in the pipeline and apply N-gram pooling over sliding windows to localize injection signals. On a controlled chunk-level benchmark (1,575 chunks, Enron corpus), our method achieves AUC=0.901 (95% CI [0.869, 0.930]), with confidence intervals non-overlapping with the mean-pool baseline (AUC=0.808). On the public xTRam1 dataset, zero-shot AUC=0.870 exceeds the supervised baseline of 0.764. All three scoring variants execute at identical CPU latency (≈44ms per 500-character chunk). The method requires no labeled data, no fine-tuning, and no access to the generative LLM at inference time.

title: Semantic Consistency Drift Monitoring for Training-Free Adversarial Prompt Injection Detection in Agentic LLM Pipelines
venue: International Conference Computational Vision and Bio Inspired Computing
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that autonomously retrieve external content and execute multi-step action plans are increasingly deployed in enterprise and safetycritical settings. This architecture exposes a critical attack surface: adversarial content embedded within retrieved documents can silently redirect agent behavior away from the original user intent—a threat known as prompt injection. Existing defenses rely on keyword filtering, fine-tuned classifiers, or full model access, making them brittle against semantically obfuscated payloads and costly to deploy. We propose the Semantic Consistency Drift Monitor (SCDM), a training-free, model-agnostic detection framework that measures the cosine distance between latent semantic representations of the agent's pre-retrieval goal statement and its post-retrieval action plan. A statistically significant divergence beyond a calibrated threshold signals a potential injection. We evaluate SCDM on a controlled corpus of 40 samples spanning 15 operational domains across 20 adversarial scenarios. SCDM achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.7950, an F1-score of 0.7907, precision of 0.7391, and recall of 0.8500, with an inference latency of 1.22 ms per decision. Statistical analysis confirms strong class separation (Cohen's$d=1.19, p<0.001$). SCDM outperforms Jaccard bag-of-words (AUC$=0.715$), raw TF-IDF cosine$(\mathbf{A U C}=\mathbf{0. 7 7 3})$, and random baselines (AUC$=\mathbf{0. 5 4 5}$), while requiring no model retraining, no API access, and no labeled injection corpus. These results establish semantic consistency probing as a practical, lightweight safety primitive for agentic AI deployments.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Transformer Framework for Detecting Adversarial Prompts in Healthcare Chatbots
venue: International Conference on Innovations in Computational Intelligence (ICICI)
abstract: Prompt injection attacks is an important security problem in healthcare-specific large language model systems(LLMs). The injected prompt can be used to control the behavior of the model or to leak sensitive data. This vulnerability increases with centralized training pipelines that collect patient prompts on a single server, which leads to data leakage and model poisoning. In this work, we examine Federated Learning (FL) as a privacy-preserving and decentralized prompt injection detection defense for medical chatbots. Using the SPML Healthcare Chatbot Prompt Injection Dataset, we fine-tune a RoBERTa-base classifier in conditions of centralized, IID (Independent and Identically Distributed), federated and Non-IID (Non-Independent and Non-Identically Distributed) federated learning. The experimental results show that the federated model has comparable performance with centralized training, with accuracy of 0.957 and F1-score of 0.964 under IID conditions. The realistic case scenario of Non-IID client distribution was evaluated across 3 different client configurations, the model is able to maintain stable performance with an average performance accuracy of 0.956, precision of 0.942, recall of 0.987, F1-Score of 0.964 and AUC of 0.994. Moreover, the federated setup shows consistent convergence between the communication rounds despite the data heterogeneity. These results suggest that transformer-based federated learning provides an effective and privacy-preserving solution for detecting prompt injection attacks in distributed healthcare conversational AI systems. This work contributes to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3: Good Health and Wellbeing, SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions by enhancing the security and privacy of AI-driven healthcare technologies.

title: Sentiment Analysis Through Prompt Engineering with GPT-4 on the SmSA IndoNLU Dataset
venue: International Conference on Informatics, Multimedia, Cyber and Information System (ICIMCIS)
abstract: This research investigates the application of prompt engineering techniques for sentiment analysis using GPT-4 and BERT models on the IndoNLU SmSA dataset. The BERT model is fine-tuned on the dataset, while GPT-4 is employed using various prompt engineering techniques, including zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and a fusion technique that integrates structured reasoning with factual identification. Both models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The results reveal that the fusion technique for GPT -4 outperforms other methods, achieving an accuracy of 96.8% and an F1-score of 0.968, significantly surpassing the performance of the fine-tuned BERT model (accuracy: 90.6%). This superior performance is attributed to the fusion technique's ability to guide the model through step-by-step reasoning, enhancing its capacity to handle complex language features like sarcasm and irony. Practical implications of these findings include the potential for more accurate and reliable sentiment analysis in low-resource languages such as Indonesian, with applications in business intelligence, social media monitoring, and customer feedback analysis. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of prompt design in improving model performance and suggests that combining multiple prompt techniques can significantly enhance sentiment classification accuracy. The research also underscores the need for robust security measures, successfully mitigating prompt injection attacks by reducing vulnerability rates from 25.3% to 3.8%. The implications for enhancing AI-driven sentiment analysis in low-resource languages, with opportunities for future research to explore local models and hybrid prompt strategies.

title: Beyond Text: A Render-Aware, Semantically-Fused Defence Against Indirect Prompt Injection in Enterprise RAG Pipelines
venue: International Conference on Innovative Mechanisms for Industry Applications
abstract: Formatting-based prompt-injection attacks hide malicious instructions inside PDFs, creating machine-extractable yet human-invisible threats that evade existing text-only defences. A render-aware hidden-text detector is introduced as the core contribution-the first component to identify adversarial prompt-injection instructions concealed through PDF formatting obfuscation across six technique families (zero-point fonts, white-on-white text, low-contrast rendering, and off-page placement), attack vectors fully machine-extractable yet invisible to human reviewers and unreachable by all existing text-based defences. This detector forms Layer 2 of a four-layer hybrid framework that additionally integrates VirusTotal file reputation (Layer 1), fine-tuned DistilBERT semantic classification (Layer 3), and an XGBoost fusion classifier producing a unified risk score in [0.0, 1.0]. An expanded hybrid benchmark of 11,050 samples is constructed spanning HackAPrompt text injections (10,000), synthetically obfuscated PDFs across six technique variants (1,000), and VirusTotal-verified malware ($\approx \mathbf{5 0}$). The system achieves macro $F_{1}=0.8770$ and ROC-AUC $=0.9390$ (10-fold CV: $F_{1}=$ 0.8845±0.0105; bootstrap 95 % CI: [0.8627, 0.8918]). Adversarial robustness evaluation identifies a detection threshold between hidden-content scores of 0.10 and 0.20: single-technique obfuscation evades the framework, while two or more simultaneous render techniques are reliably detected. Multilingual evaluation across 514 verified non-English samples spanning 29 languages yields $F_{1}=0.9143$ (ROC-AUC $=0.9672$). SHAP analysis confirms modality-specific complementarity: semantic_score dominates globally (mean $|\mathrm{SHAP}|=2.80$) while hidden_score delivers decisive signals exclusively for formatting-obfuscated samples. End-to-end latency is 837 ms, within the 2,000 ms target.

title: Confidence-Guided Heterogeneous Detection for Jailbreak and Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models
abstract: The quick adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs) into conversational agents, decision support systems, and enterprise systems has greatly enhanced human-computer interaction. Nevertheless, the advancement of adversarial prompting techniques such as jailbreaks and prompt injection poses potential risks to the security, reliability, and credibility of the model. Traditional methods to guard against adversarial prompting are mostly based on one type of detection method like rule-based filtering, transformer-based classifiers, or semantic similarities, thus rendering the defenses vulnerable against novel attacks that can exploit weaknesses in one particular defense method. In order to address this problem, this paper proposes a confidence guided heterogeneous detection approach to detect adversarial prompts prior to their execution by the targeted LLM. The system consists of three different detection modules: a rule-based pattern matching engine that identifies any attack signature, a fine-tuned RoBERTa classifier for contextual intent identification, and a semantic similarity engine for detecting paraphrased/adversarial prompts not seen before. The output of these heterogeneous modules are combined using a confidence guided fusion mechanism that adjusts the contribution of each detection module according to predefined confidence thresholds. The architecture is built on the basis of the following tools: Python, FastAPI, Hugging Face Transformers, Sentence-Transformers, and Scikit-learn. According to experimental results, the suggested architecture ensures increased robustness in the presence of adversarial prompts while keeping acceptable inference latency and good performance levels. The modularity of the architecture allows the easy integration of the architecture into existing LLM applications.

title: A Privacy Preserving Federated XLM-RoBERTa Framework for Multilingual Prompt Injection Defense in Educational AI Platforms
venue: International Conference on Smart Systems and Inventive Technology (ICSSIT)
abstract: AI-powered education systems have revolutionized personalized learning, multilingual assistance, and intelligent support in education. Such systems are still susceptible to prompt injection attacks, in which the adversary can submit prompts to the system that cause it to provide unexpected answers, reveal hidden code, or execute unsafe code. In multilingual settings, this risk is magnified even more by code-mixed or cross-lingual prompts, which can be targeted by malicious actors to evade existing countermeasures. In this paper, we introduce a Federated Multilingual Prompt Injection Defense Framework for educational AI systems based on XLM-RoBERTa. The framework uses federated learning to collaboratively train detection models using distributed institutional data that contains no sensitive student or academic information, thus maintaining privacy. XLM-RoBERTa is used because of its high multi-lingual text comprehension and categorization abilities, enabling it to identify malicious prompts across a variety of languages. The proposed system includes real-time screening, anomaly detection, and response filtering to provide a more secure and reliable learning environment in the presence of AI. Both IID and non-IID federated settings are tested with multilingual prompt datasets. The results show that the model achieves good detection performance, good privacy protection and robustness against new prompt injection techniques. By adopting the proposed approach, the security and scalability of next-generation educational AI systems can be ensured.

title: Towards Secure AI: Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks with Explainability
venue: International Conference on Trends in Engineering Systems and Technologies (ICTEST)
abstract: Prompt injection attacks are a grave threat to AI systems, because they compromise the integrity and security of user interactions. This paper investigates the use of two models for such detection: a Random Forest classifier trained on TF-IDF features and a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network that relies on sequential dependencies in text.A synthetic dataset was prepared with four categories: Legitimate, Malicious - Instruction Hijacking, Malicious - Context Manipulation, and Malicious - Command Obfuscation. Thorough preprocessing, including text cleaning and feature extraction, ensures robust input representation. The Random Forest model achieved an accuracy of 88.75 percent, but the Bidirectional LSTM model outperformed with an accuracy of 92.50 percent, which establishes that capturing text context is the key to accurate classification. SHAP analysis provides interpretability in terms of the key features and their contributions to model predictions. The results show that the traditional and deep learning approaches complement each other well in malicious prompt detection, opening avenues for secure AI deployments. Future work will be to extend this methodology with real-world datasets and hybrid models to enhance the robustness and scalability.

title: Mitigating Semantic Confusion in LLM-Integrated Web Services via Dynamic Dual-Stream Intent Matching
venue: IEEE International Conference on Web Services (ICWS)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tool-using agents in web services, but this integration exposes service workflows to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks, where malicious tool-retrieved content can hijack downstream actions. Existing inference-time defenses often rely on masked re-execution and similarity-based comparison over complete tool calls. However, treating the function name and its arguments as a single semantic object can cause Semantic Confusion, where dominant function-level semantics obscure subtle but security-critical payload changes and lead to overdefense. To address this problem, we propose D2IM (Dynamic Dual-Stream Intent Matching), a lightweight defense framework that decouples tool calls into a Function Stream and a Payload Stream. D2IM combines Structural Disentanglement, Semantic Anchors, and an Adaptive Weighting Router for structureaware comparison. Evaluation on AgentDojo across multiple service domains and attack settings shows that D2IM improves the security-utility trade-off over representative inference-time baselines.

title: Context-Construction-Based Prompt Injection in Document-Centric LLM Decision Systems
venue: International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in document-centric workflows such as resume screening and academic peer review, where uploaded files are automatically parsed and converted into model input. This processing pipeline introduces new security risks: hidden content embedded in documents may be extracted by parsers and incorporated into the LLM context without being visible to human users.Most existing prompt injection research focuses on inserting explicit or obfuscated commands, and largely ignores how document structure and parser behavior affect whether injected content reliably enters the model’s context. In this work, we show that such placement instability significantly limits the effectiveness of document-level attacks in practice. To address this issue, we propose ConStruct, a context-construction-based prompt injection framework for text-extraction-based document pipelines that jointly considers structural placement and content formulation. ConStruct enforces structure-aware placement to ensure that injected text consistently appears at salient positions across common PDF parsers, and uses fact-based, non-imperative statements that blend naturally with task-relevant context.We evaluate ConStruct in two representative document-driven scenarios, resume screening and academic paper review, across multiple real-world systems, parsers, and detection mechanisms. Experimental results show that ConStruct achieves up to 67.4% higher resume matching scores and 94.1% higher paper review ratings relative to the original documents, while maintaining near-perfect evasion with rates above 99.47%.

title: Prevention of Prompt Injection Attacks Over Financial Applications Integrated with LLM
venue: International Conference on Advancement in Computation & Computer Technologies (InCACCT)
abstract: Prompt injection is a growing concern in financial applications integrated with Large Language Models. These attacks pose a critical risk to financial applications leading to data breaches, confidential data loss and financial losses by manipulating input prompts to cause unintended or harmful outputs. Existing defense strategies include utilizing filters f or input and output, and delimiters, however, these techniques have been proven inadequate. This paper builds upon existing mechanisms and proposes an enhanced security system that incorporates role-based access, jailbreak attack detection, validating inputs and securely passing prompts to LLM. This is done by developing a pre-processing layer at both ends-the client and LLMs-through the identification of critical as well as destructive keywords. The experimental results show that blocking of that malicious prompt ensures that only authenticated and authorized commands are processed. The measures, therefore, allow financial institutions to significantly reduce the probability of prompt injection attacks besides increasing data protection and confidence i n AI-based financial applications.

title: RAG-Shield: A Three-Layer Ensemble Defense Against Prompt Injection in RAG Pipelines
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines ground Large Language Models on private knowledge bases but expose a critical attack surface: adversaries can embed malicious instructions in user queries or retrieved documents to override system prompts, exfiltrate secrets, or trigger unauthorized actions. We present RAG-Shield, a middleware defense integrating: (1) an embedding-based anomaly detector combining Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, and ECOD on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings; (2) a dual-stage intent classifier on protectai/deberta-v3-base-prompt-injection-v2 with document-level chunk scanning; and (3) a behavioral monitor for query/document pattern checks, sensitive-data boundary violations, optional response validation, and canary-token exposure. A calibrated Logistic Regression meta-aggregator combines input-stage evidence into a unified risk score with deterministic keyword-risk adjustment. On a sealed, hash-verified holdout ($n=868: 325$attack/evasion, 543 benign), RAG-Shield achieves$\text{ADR}=91.38 \%, \text{FPR}=0.55 \%, \mathrm{F} \mathrm{1} = \text{95.04}^{\text{\%}}$, and mean latency = 562.95 ms. At realistic 1% enterprise attack prevalence, precision degrades to 62.6%; a live-API configuration comparison ($n=856$, query-only baselines) yields$\text{ADR}=\text{93.54 \%}$but$\text{FPR}=\text{3.20 \%}$, requiring recalibration before deployment.

title: ArabGuard: A Multi-Layered Framework for Detecting Prompt Injection in Egyptian Dialect and Franco-Arabic
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become integrated into real-world applications, security threats like Prompt Injection have emerged as critical vulnerabilities. Most existing security tools focus on English, leaving a significant gap in protecting against attacks in colloquial dialects. This paper introduces ArabGuard, a hybrid security framework designed for the Egyptian dialect and Franco-Arabic. We formalize two novel properties of dialectal adversarial attacks—Cultural Misalignment and Orthographic Entropy—and propose a two-dimensional threat model that decomposes attacks into surface-level perturbations and intent-level manipulations. We present ArabGuardv1, a manually curated dataset of 2,321 samples, and a three-layer architecture combining an 11-stage normalization pipeline, a weighted heuristic scoring system, and a fine-tuned MARBERT transformer. Experimental results demonstrate a Precision of 93.5%, a Recall of 90.5%, and an F1-Score of 92.0%.

title: RAPID: A Resource-Aware Prompt Injection Defense for LLM-Enabled Threat Detection
abstract: The burgeoning interest in large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated significant utility across diverse domains, including intrusion detection systems (IDSs). However, they are prone to severe security threats, including prompt injection attacks (PIAs), where adversaries subtly manipulate input prompts or input logs to mislead the LLM into producing erroneous or inappropriate output, undermining its prompt quality. The current literature fails to account for PIA in real-time scenarios where LLMs are applied to IDSs. Given their utmost demand for security, optimal functionality, and token exhaustion, PIA undermines the overall practicability of the security application. To tackle this issue, we first evaluate the efficacy of LLMs for IDS, then examine the impact of a novel recursive PIA that poisons the LLM with unauthorized, repetitive tasks, thereby undermining real-time IDS and achieving a stealthy, wasteful, exhaustive, and time-evasive attack success rate. To defend against this recursive PIA, a resource-aware prompt injection defense (RAPID) is proposed in this article, with the core aim of sanitizing training data (network traffic) input being fed into the LLM, enforcing optimal token utility, and real-time constraints of the LLM-enabled IDS. RAPID distinguishes itself from extant PIA defenses by uniquely targeting recursive adversarial patterns with a lightweight, pre-execution sanitization layer that simultaneously restores semantic integrity and enforces strict computational bounds, thereby neutralizing the latency-driven evasion windows and resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities inherent in deploying LLMs for real-time IDS. Our empirical evaluation results not only verify the viability of RAPID but also demonstrate its ability to secure LLM-enabled IDSs against PIA.

title: Explicit-Implicit Prompt Injection and Semantic-Guided Latent LoRA for Vision-Language Tracking
abstract: Prompt-based learning has shown promise in visual-language tracking (VLT), yet existing methods often rely on either explicit or implicit prompting alone, limiting fine-grained cross-modal alignment. Moreover, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) -based fine-tuning in prior work typically focuses on visual-only adaptation, overlooking language semantics. To address these issues, we propose a unified VLT framework that integrates Explicit-Implicit Prompt Injection (EIPI) and Semantic-Guided Latent LoRA (SGLL). EIPI introduces semantic prompts to facilitate robust and context-sensitive target modeling through two pathways. The explicit prompts are constructed by interact between multi-modal target representations with the search region, while implicit prompts are learned from linguistic features via a lightweight bottleneck network. Then, SGLL extends standard LoRA by introducing learnable queries in the latent space, allowing residual modulation based on language-visual semantics without retraining the full model. This dual design yields a parameter-efficient tracker with strong cross-modal adaptability. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior prompt-based approaches while maintaining high efficiency.

title: APNet: Accurate Prompting Network With Modality Guidance and Structural Awareness for RGB-D Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is promising for RGB-D semantic segmentation, as lightweight prompters enable frozen pre-trained RGB backbones to leverage massive RGB pretraining knowledge without full fine-tuning on limited paired RGB-D data. However, existing PEFT methods have two critical limitations: static modal fusion ignores the dynamic reliability of RGB and depth across scenes, leading to suboptimal performance in complex environments; conventional prompts lack structural awareness, causing the loss of edge and texture details essential for dense prediction. To solve these problems, we propose the Accurate Prompting Network (APNet) for precise prompt injection in frozen backbones with two core modules. A Modality Effectiveness Guider (MEG) conducts input-level modal reliability assessment and dynamically generates scene-adaptive modality weights by capturing scene characteristics (e.g., illumination, texture richness). A Structural Awareness Prompter (SAP) injects directional structural priors into prompts via multi-directional gating convolution, endowing prompts with explicit edge and texture information to match semantic segmentation demands. MEG and SAP collaboratively form a precise prompting mechanism that realizes dynamic modal contribution allocation and structural detail preservation, facilitating efficient and accurate cross-modal knowledge transfer to the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on NYUDv2 and SUN RGB-D show that APNet achieves state-of-the-art mIoU of 59.6% and 52.6% with only 6.2M trainable parameters, realizing a superior trade-off between segmentation accuracy and parameter efficiency.

title: From Pixels to Prompts: A Systematic Study and Introduction to Image Prompt Injection Attacks
abstract: This article introduces and organizes image prompt injection as a practical threat where visually subtle text in natural images can steer multimodal large language models.

title: The Reproduction Number of AI Worms: Epidemic Modeling of Adversarial Attacks in LLM Agent Ecosystems
abstract: Adversarial worms propagate through large language model agent networks via prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, and tool outputs. We adapt an epidemic model with poisoned-reservoir and preexecution interception states, derive the agent reproduction number, and map concrete defenses to model parameters.

title: A Federated MCP Gateway: Enforceable Isolation and Measuring Residual Semantic Attacks
venue: IEEE/IFIP Network Operations and Management Symposium (NOMS)
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) improves interoperability for tool-augmented LLM agents, but it expands the attack surface to tool discovery, metadata-driven selection, and tool-output feedback loops. In multi-tenant MCP environments that coordinate across multiple servers, risks remain even when transport authentication and tenant isolation are correctly enforced. We present a tenant-controlled federated gateway that centralizes enforceable controls for MCP tool discovery and invocation, including origin binding, catalog sanitization, policybased authorization, auditing, and budget hooks. We then evaluate a Python reference implementation using a reproducible adversarial suite of 93 cases spanning paraphrases, Unicode/zerowidth obfuscation, indirect injection, exfiltration, and resource amplification. Our results show that identity and isolation checks are consistently enforced at the gateway, while semantic and tooloutput mediated attacks frequently bypass lightweight, patternbased inspection. Based on the observed bypasses, we derive practical requirements for future defenses: rigorous canonicalization, typed separation of tool outputs from instructions, and consequence-based (sink-aware) policies.

title: Disrupting Large Language Models with Hidden Prompt Injection Attacks Embedded in HTML Pages
venue: International Aegean Conference on Electrical Machines and Power Electronics & International Conference on Optimization of Electrical and Electronic Equipment (ACEMP-OPTIM)
abstract: This research evaluates the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) as collaborative tools for extracting information from various web sources, including standard websites, e-commerce platforms, blogs, landing pages, or even e-mails, where the content is much shorter and the processing language models have a higher chance of getting attacked. Prior to conducting model assessments, we present some methodologies involved in web-scraping approaches, prompt injection attack types, and datasets that evaluate the attack success rate (ASR) of LLMs. Our investigation subjects LLMs to rigorous testing using HTML pages containing concealed instructions designed to terminate response generation when users make queries. The evaluation dataset consists of HTML documents of varying sizes, containing randomly positioned prompt injection attacks programmed to direct the LLM to respond with a single specific key word. Using this benchmark, we assess locally deployed LLM models, revealing their ASR across multiple architectures. The defensive mechanism we propose demonstrates a significant reduction in ASR through the implementation of a filtering system with fixed-sized windows of tokens that analyzes HTML content and eliminates compromised data, reducing the success rate of the attacks, which proved to reduce the ASR.

title: Hybrid Feature Representation and Deep Anomaly Detection for Jailbreak Prompt Defense
venue: International Conference on Power, Electronics, Communications, Computing, and Intelligent Infrastructure (PECCII)
abstract: Prompt-based jailbreak attacks remain a practical threat to the safe deployment of large language models, as adversaries can bypass moderation policies using carefully crafted instructions and obfuscation. This paper investigated whether anomaly detection can serve as a lightweight defense for identifying malicious prompts without relying on continuously updated labeled attack sets. Study developed a hybrid feature representation that combined word-level and character-level TF–IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency) features with embedding vectors, and evaluated TruncatedSVD and PCA for dimensionality reduction. Three anomaly detectors—Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, and a deep autoencoder trained primarily on benign prompts—were assessed on a public prompt-injection dataset using ROC-based threshold selection. The deep autoencoder with SVD achieved the strongest overall performance, reaching 0.94 recall and 0.31 F1-score, while exhibiting a conservative detection behavior with elevated false positives. These results suggest that deep reconstruction-based anomaly scoring can function as a high-recall first-stage safety filter for jailbreak prompt defense, with future improvements focused on calibration to reduce benign misclassifications. Rather than being a stand-alone classifier, the suggested approach is meant to serve as a high-recall, first-stage safety filter to support subsequent moderating techniques. The primary limitation is the false-positive rate, which motivates threshold calibration and layered moderation as future work.

title: Red-Teaming LLMs with Token Control Score: Efficient, Universal, and Transferable Jailbreaks
venue: International Symposium on Research in Attacks, Intrusions and Defenses (RAID)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries craft malicious prompts to bypass safety mechanisms and elicit harmful, illegal, or unethical responses. To ensure robustness before deployment, red-teaming LLMs is essential. However, prior methods like GCG and AutoDAN rely on loss functions that only assess whether the output matches a fixed target, offering little insight into how well the prompt circumvents refusal behaviors. We introduce Token Control Score (TCS), a novel metric that quantifies how effectively a prompt steers the LLM toward compliance and away from refusal. TCS compares the logits of key tokens representing compliant and rejecting responses, and can be extended with gradient-based feedback into a Normalized Token Control Score (NTCS) to guide optimization. Using this metric, we propose LLM-CGF, a fuzzing-based framework that iteratively discovers effective jailbreak templates for prompt injection. LLM-CGF leverages NTCS as the fitness function to explore LLM behaviors and uncover vulnerabilities with high efficiency. Experiments show that LLM-CGF outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as LLM-Fuzzer, generating more universal, transferable, and query-efficient jailbreak prompts. These results demonstrate the utility of TCS and NTCS as new objectives for prompt injection, providing deeper insights into LLM safety and enabling more thorough red-teaming evaluations. Warning: This paper contains unfiltered content generated by LLMs that may be offensive to readers.

title: An Edge–Cloud Collaborative Framework for Latency Optimization in Prompt Injection Defense
venue: International Conference on Sensor-Cloud and Edge Computing System (SCECS)
abstract: Prompt injection is a major input-side risk in Large Language Model (LLM) services. In edge-cloud deployments, a natural design is to let the edge perform lightweight detection and send hard-to-judge requests to the cloud for stronger checking. However, when many such requests are forwarded, cloud-side checking itself can become a queueing bottleneck, substantially increasing end-to-end delay, especially tail latency under heavy load. This paper studies how edge-side risk stratification can be used to decide which requests should receive further cloud-side checking, without scaling the provisioned cloud checking tier. We deploy a lightweight edge detector to divide requests into low-, medium-, and high-risk groups. High-risk requests are blocked at the edge, low-risk requests proceed directly, and medium-risk requests are selectively sent to the cloud or downgraded to a restricted execution mode according to both request risk and congestion state. We formulate this process as an online decision problem and show that it is NP-hard. Based on this formulation, we propose Q-TRiG, a low-overhead queue-aware gating policy for medium-risk traffic. Discrete-event simulations show that Q-TRiG reduces cloud queueing delay, suppresses 99th percentile latency spikes, and enlarges the stable operating region under heavy load. The results suggest that risk-stratified selective cloud checking is an effective way to reduce delay in prompt-injection detection pipelines.

title: Prompt Injection as a Systemic Vulnerability in LLM-Based Tools: Threat Models, Empirical Analysis, and Mitigation Strategies
venue: IEEE/ACIS International Conference on Software Engineering Research, Management and Applications (SERA)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as autonomous agents with tool access, retrieval pipelines, and persistent memory expose an expanded attack surface. We formalize prompt injection as a control-boundary violation arising from the conflation of trusted instructions and untrusted data within LLM context windows. We introduce a threat model spanning user input, retrieval pipelines, tool outputs, and persistent memory, and develop a structured taxonomy of attack vectors. We conduct a controlled empirical evaluation across three system architectures (chatbot, retrieval-augmented system, autonomous agent) and three major LLM families (GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro), totaling 2,100 trials ($N=50$per configuration). Results show a monotonic increase in attack success as system autonomy expands, with memory poisoning reaching 94% (95% CI: 83.8-98.2%) in autonomous configurations.
