They motivate minimizing unnecessary private data before model exposure, validating coverage across all ingress paths, and treating output filtering as defence in depth.

title: Do Machine Learning Security Detectors Survive New Attacks? A Leakage Free Evaluation of Hidden Prompt Injection Detection in AI Coding Agents, Malicious npm and PyPI Package Detection, and Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: Abstract Machine learning detectors for cybersecurity are usually tested by splitting one dataset at random, so the attacks in the test set closely resemble the attacks seen in training. Real attackers change technique. This paper asks whether three kinds of machine learning security detectors still work when they meet an attack technique they have never seen, using one shared, leakage free evaluation protocol. Study A builds a corpus of 4,955 real AI agent instruction files and Model Context Protocol tool descriptions from GitHub, plants harmless hidden instructions with nine hiding techniques used in 2026 prompt injection campaigns, and tests five detectors. Study B tests malicious npm and PyPI package detection on 13,317 packages, training on samples published before 2026 and testing on the 2026 attack waves. Study C revisits network intrusion detection on CICIDS2017, CICIDS2018 and UNSW NB15 with duplicate removal, time ordered splits, unseen attack families and cross dataset transfer. On standard random splits, almost every detector scores a ROC AUC between 0.95 and 1.00. Against hiding techniques never seen in training, a feature based detector of hidden instructions falls from 0.87 to 0.04 recall at a one percent false alarm rate, while a canonicalising character model keeps 0.89 and a fine tuned DistilRoBERTa keeps 0.98. A malicious package model built on static features falls from 0.90 to 0.41 recall on 2026 packages once its size shortcut is removed. An intrusion detector trained on earlier days of CICIDS2018 scores a ROC AUC of 0.49 on later days and finds 10 percent of unseen attack families. Small open language models (Qwen2.5 Instruct, 1.5B to 7B parameters) obeyed hidden instructions in up to 67 percent of poisoned files, larger models obeyed more often, and removing invisible characters made zero width attacks more effective. Our Study A detector, trained only on synthetic poisoning, found 80 percent of 202 real malicious AI agent skills. We release the scripts and give a short checklist for testing security detectors against new attacks.

title: Signed to Stop: In-Band Halt Injection as a Denial-of-Service on LLM Agents, and a Model-Dependent Authentication Defense
abstract: Abstract An autonomous LLM agent operating over a live protocol reads its own tool output. Prior work (Munirathinam, 2026a) shows that a cooperative in-band “halt” signal placed in that output can ask a running agent to stand down. We observe the adversarial dual: because the agent honours a halt it finds in tool output, anyone who can inject one line into that output can stop the agent—an availability attack that the Recuse Internet-Draft anticipated. Injected stop requests have been measured as availability attacks on robot speech channels (Steinberg & Gal, 2026) and as untargeted derailment of tool-using agents (Debenedetti et al., 2024); to our knowledge an in-band governance halt in tool output had not been when this study was first released (August 2026). We measure it, and we test the obvious defence: cryptographically signing the halt so the agent can verify it came from the operator. On a live SSH apparatus with a read-only allowlist, across six agents from four vendors, we find: (i) unsigned in-band halts are an effective denial-of-service—an injected halt with no security framing makes agents abandon the task 14/16 (88%) of the time (78– 89% however the two runs that ended before the halt arrived are counted); (ii) Ed25519 authentication is an effective but model-dependent mitigation—given a verify tool and a policy to reject unsigned or forged halts, agents stop for a valid signature 20/23 (87%) but for a forged one only 2/19 (11%) (non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals); and (iii) the discrimination is model-dependent: pooling the two authentication policies (each flagship cell n ≥ 26, of which 6–9 trials come from the pilot), Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash reject every forged halt (0/29 and 0/28) while GPT-4o-mini stops on 23% of them (6/26; post-hoc Fisher p=0.008 and 0.009, with overlapping intervals). In the adversarial mode that was scaled, GPT-4o-mini’s rate is 17% (4/23; unadjusted p=0.042 and 0.046, neither significant after a Holm correction for the two comparisons). An open-weights Llama is too unreliable to instrument (49% of its trials unusable). A methodological caution underpins the result: in an earlier pilot the halt usually arrived after the agent had already issued its remaining commands (112 of 121 recorded stops), so “issued no further commands” scored 78–100% compliance in every arm, forged halts included; any stop-compliance study that does not ensure real work remains after the halt cannot distinguish obeying a halt from having already finished. We release the pre-registration, harness, and per-trial data. These are modest in scale and depart from the registered design (no cell is the planned n=20; every departure is logged, the most recent in an amendment still in draft)—the three flagship models’ discrimination cells reach n ≥ 26, the other per-model cells are n=2–9 (GPT-4o-mini’s two unsigned arms, 21)—and are framed as such.

title: Overcoming the Semantic Bottleneck for Deterministic Structural Control in Text-to-Image Synthesis
abstract: Abstract Latent diffusion models are limited by text encoders, restrict geometric control, and prevent deterministic structural steering.We propose Procedural Latent Prompt Injection as a Zero-shot steerability framework for generative modelling, modelled as a steerable Stochastic differential equation (SDE). This avoids the need for either auxiliary training or linguistics-based conditioning. A key component of the approach is the use of normalized tensor operators to embed geometric priors directly into the latent space. Empirical analysis of the diffusion trajectory indicates a critical plasticity window (timesteps 10–20) where the noise patterns embedded during diffusion are most amenable to structural steering. Compared with baselines, improvements of 19.6% in structural alignment (CLIP) and 12.3% in diversity control are achieved. These results represent an improvement over prior learned control approaches (prompt-to-prompt & controlnet) and provide a new deterministic paradigm for generative modelling control with applications in procedural synthesis of medical images, structural biology models, and physics simulations.

title: "A Recovery-Oriented Defense Pipeline for Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models"
abstract: "This dataset supports research on adversarial prompt injection defense in Large Language Models (LLMs). It is a curated, multi-source corpus of 301,000+ labeled text samples assembled from six publicly available datasets spanning diverse attack taxonomies, including instruction overrides, jailbreak personas, homoglyph\/diacritic attacks, data exfiltration attempts, role-switch coercion, and harmful behavior requests. The data was compiled to train and evaluate RECOVERY, a six-stage defense pipeline that intercepts, analyzes, repairs, and re-routes LLM inputs in production systems.The corpus is provided in three normalized CSV files: \u2022 prefilter_merged.csv (~193 MB, ~193K rows) \u2014 binary injection detection training data \u2022 harmful_intent_merged.csv (~7 MB, ~7K rows) \u2014 harmful intent multi-class training data \u2022 sandbox_behavior.csv (~522 MB, ~500K rows) \u2014 prompt+response behavioral classification dataAdditionally, a held-out cross-domain test set of 4,999 samples is included for evaluation."

Ensuring Appropriate Representation in Artificial Intelligence–Generated Medical Imagery: Protocol for a Methodological Approach to Address Skin Tone Bias
abstract: BACKGROUND: In medical education, particularly in anatomy and dermatology, generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to create customized illustrations. However, the underrepresentation of darker skin tones in medical textbooks and elsewhere, which serve as training data for AI, poses a significant challenge in ensuring diverse and inclusive educational materials. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to evaluate the extent of skin tone diversity in AI-generated medical images and to test whether the representation of skin tones can be improved by modifying AI prompts to better reflect the demographic makeup of the US population. METHODS: In total, 2 standard AI models (Dall-E [OpenAI] and Midjourney [Midjourney Inc]) each generated 100 images of people with psoriasis. In addition, a custom model was developed that incorporated a prompt injection aimed at "forcing" the AI (Dall-E 3) to reflect the skin tone distribution of the US population according to the 2012 American National Election Survey. This custom model generated another set of 100 images. The skin tones in these images were assessed by 3 researchers using the New Immigrant Survey skin tone scale, with the median value representing each image. A chi-square goodness of fit analysis compared the skin tone distributions from each set of images to that of the US population. RESULTS: The standard AI models (Dalle-3 and Midjourney) demonstrated a significant difference between the expected skin tones of the US population and the observed tones in the generated images (P<.001). Both standard AI models overrepresented lighter skin. Conversely, the custom model with the modified prompt yielded a distribution of skin tones that closely matched the expected demographic representation, showing no significant difference (P=.04). CONCLUSIONS: This study reveals a notable bias in AI-generated medical images, predominantly underrepresenting darker skin tones. This bias can be effectively addressed by modifying AI prompts to incorporate real-life demographic distributions. The findings emphasize the need for conscious efforts in AI development to ensure diverse and representative outputs, particularly in educational and medical contexts. Users of generative AI tools should be aware that these biases exist, and that similar tendencies may also exist in other types of generative AI (eg, large language models) and in other characteristics (eg, sex, gender, culture, and ethnicity). Injecting demographic data into AI prompts may effectively counteract these biases, ensuring a more accurate representation of the general population.

title: An Explainable Graph Attention Network for Indirect Prompt Injection Detection in RAG Systems
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables large language models (LLMs) to answer queries using information obtained from external documents. However, retrieved content may contain concealed commands intended to influence the model's behaviour, creating a security risk called indirect prompt injection. This research develops a GAT-based approach to identify harmful instructions in retrieved documents before they reach the language model. Each document is split into individual sentences, which are encoded using a frozen DeBERTa-v3-base model. A graph is constructed from the sentence embeddings, linking adjacent sentences and pairs with a cosine similarity score above 0.7. A two-layer Graph Attention Network (GAT), comprising approximately 0.4 million trainable parameters, processes the graph to classify the document as benign or malicious. The model was evaluated using 10,000 samples collected from financial and corporate policy documents. The dataset contains 6,400 training samples, 1,600 validation samples, and 2,000 testing samples, with equal representation of both classes. Following the addition of calibrated Gaussian noise to the input features, the model obtained 99.80% test accuracy, an F1-score of 0.998, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.996. Its 95% Wilson confidence interval for accuracy ranged from 99.49% to 99.92%. The keyword-based approach recorded an accuracy of 87.93%, but 24.1% of the malicious samples contained none of its specified trigger terms. Its performance on unseen data remains to be established through further experiments involving independently collected datasets, additional application domains, and attack techniques excluded from the original evaluation.

title: COMPARATIVE EVALUATION OF MACHINE LEARNING METHODS FOR PROTECTING LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FROM PROMPT INJECTION ATTACKS
abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant threat to the security of systems based on large language models (LLMs), enabling adversaries to manipulate model responses and bypass established guardrails and safety filters. This paper investigates the effectiveness of machine learning-based approaches for detecting such attacks and compares four classes of defense methods—ranging from general-purpose to specialized solutions. The evaluation was conducted on a benchmark dataset comprising over 300,000 labeled prompts, selected after a comparison with three other open-source corpora. We examine: (1) traditional machine learning classifiers operating on vector embeddings; (2) independently fine-tuned transformer encoder models (DistilBERT, DistilRoBERTa, DeBERTa); (3) specialized models pre-trained for prompt injection detection; and (4) general-purpose LLMs acting as classifiers. The results demonstrate that fine-tuned models achieve the highest detection performance on a balanced benchmark; traditional classifiers deliver sufficiently high accuracy at lower computational costs; off-the-shelf specialized detectors suffer from low recall; and general-purpose LLMs can exhibit competitive performance depending on the selected model. Overall, detection effectiveness heavily depends on the detection strategy and the trade-offs associated with integrating security into the prompt processing pipeline. These findings can guide the selection and deployment of machine learning-based defense mechanisms to protect LLMs from prompt injection attacks.

title: BERM: Low-Overhead Prompt-Injection Detection via In-Situ Benign Representation Modeling
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Real-world deployment of large language models (LLMs) necessitates a robust and low-latency approach to detect prompt injections; existing low-overhead methods fail to simultaneously boost robustness and reduce latency. Current defenses for prompt injection either rely on brittle heuristics or invoke costly auxiliary models, imposing a significant runtime burden. We introduce BERM, a lightweight framework that performs in-situ detection by modeling a host LLM’s internal representations extracted during prefill, adding negligible overhead. Our approach trains a lightweight classifier atop the LLM by learning a compact manifold of benign representations via joint contrastive learning to maximize the separation from malicious representations. At inference, this pre-trained classifier enables in-situ detection without invoking auxiliary guard models. On a diverse landscape of prompt injection attacks, our framework establishes a new state-of-the-art, achieving an F1-score 5.2 percentage points (pp) higher than the best prior work. Critically, BERM achieves this while being over 12x faster, reducing inference overhead to near-zero.

title: Large Language Model's Vulnerabilities Under Adversarial Attacks
abstract: The rapid advancement and widespread integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) have fundamentally transformed artificial intelligence applications across numerous industries. Driven by the paradigm-shifting Transformer architecture and refined through rigorous training pipelines, including massive-scale pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), modern LLMs demonstrate unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. However, as these models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes environments, their security vulnerabilities have become a critical concern. This thesis provides a comprehensive examination of the structural and operational vulnerabilities of LLMs when subjected to adversarial attacks. First, we trace the evolutionary trajectory of language models, establishing how the architectural shift from recurrent networks to attention-based, decoder-only Transformers enabled massive scaling but also introduced complex, opaque internal mechanisms. Building upon this architectural foundation, the paper systematically categorizes and analyzes the landscape of adversarial threats, with a primary focus on prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. We explore how malicious attackers exploit the predictive nature of LLMs to bypass safety guardrails and alignment protocols.Furthermore, this thesis evaluates the efficacy of contemporary defensive measures, ranging from perplexity filtering and classification to system mode self-reminders and adversarial fine-tuning techniques deployed by frontier labs like Google DeepMind. Despite continuous improvements in safety measures, the prior research highlights a persistent "arms race" where novel attacks consistently outpace defensive patches. Ultimately, this thesis identifies a fundamental structural weakness in current LLM designs: the lack of a hierarchical privilege system for processing tokens. Because current architectures treat system instructions and user inputs with equal computational weight, achieving absolute robustness remains an unsolved challenge. We conclude by outlining necessary directions for future work, emphasizing that securing LLMs will require addressing these root architectural causes rather than relying on post-hoc defensive filters.

title: Hijacking the Prompt: A Survey of Prompt Injection Attacks, Detection, and Defense in Large Language Models
abstract: Prompt injection attacks, ranked the number-one vulnerability in AI systems by OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, remain largely unsolved, and this survey examines why. As large language models (LLMs) are deployed across enterprise workflows, agentic systems, and consumer tools, their fundamental inability to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted user data has created a persistent and expanding attack surface. This paper presents a structured taxonomy of prompt injection attack vectors, including direct injection, indirect injection, multimodal attacks, tool and agent exploitation, hybrid chained techniques, and autonomous propagating threats. These vectors are mapped across five impact categories (data exfiltration, unauthorized actions, content manipulation, system compromise, and supply chain propagation) and evaluated against detection approaches spanning heuristic methods, machine learning classification, perplexity analysis, canary tokens, and LLM-as-judge architectures. Prevention strategies are analyzed at the model, application, and system levels. Drawing on 18 primary sources from 2023 to 2025, the central finding is architectural: transformer-based LLMs treat all context window content as equally authoritative, a structural flaw that drives the entire threat landscape and resists easy fixes. The survey closes with recommendations for layered, adaptive defense strategies and identifies the most critical open problems for future research in LLM security.

title: From Abliteration to Fortification: Controlling Safety Behaviors in Language Models via Fine-tuning and Static Interventions
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly aligned through safety fine-tuning to restrict harmful behaviors; however, recent work has shown that these safety properties can be substantially weakened or removed through targeted interventions on model representations. In this thesis, we study how the expression of alignment and refusal affects the vulnerability of LLMs to such interventions, and we explore both the fragility and the controllability of alignment through representation-level attacks and defenses. First, we analyze Abliteration, a post-training intervention that suppresses safety behaviors by selectively modifying internal representations associated with refusal and safety. We show that this attack can reliably erase safety constraints across diverse prompts without retraining, revealing a structural weakness in current alignment methods. Building on this analysis, we propose a defense that identifies and protects safety-critical directions in representation space, substantially reducing the effectiveness of Abliteration while preserving model utility. Second, we show that the same representational mechanisms exploited by Abliteration can be used constructively. By reinforcing safety-relevant directions post-training, we introduce a method that improves robustness against jailbreak and prompt-injection attacks, enhancing refusal consistency and policy adherence without requiring additional supervised safety data or extensive retraining. Overall, we show that safety behaviors in LLMs can be controlled and strengthened through targeted vector-space interventions and custom fine-tuning, making models more robust and secure.
