title: Layered Defense Against Stealth Prompt Injection in Hinglish: An Empirically Grounded Hybrid Architecture
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a 5-layer detection pipeline for semantically disguised prompt injection attacks in Hinglish, a code-mixed language spoken by over 600 million people. The system combines normalization, rule-based filtering, a novel "Contextual Guard" derived from red-teaming five frontier models, and an SVM classifier on multilingual embeddings. On a 250-sample stealth benchmark, the full pipeline achieves 98.4% detection (compared to 85.6% for a syntactic baseline) with a 0.6% false positive rate on clean prompts. The pipeline is CPU-deployable (~475 MB, 35–45ms latency) and exported to ONNX. This work addresses the semantic gap in Hinglish prompt injection detection and provides an empirically grounded first step toward safety infrastructure for code-mixed AI deployments.

title: HIVE-AI: A Honeypot for the Indirect-Prompt-Injection Vector against Embedded AI APIs
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: HIVE-AI is a production-grade research platform that captures, classifies and analyses attacks against generative-AI APIs. It presents convincing facades of the most-targeted commercial LLM services (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, HuggingFace) plus an agentic anti-scraper trap (ClawBot), and routes sanitized events to a hardened analyzer container that calls a small LLM (default gpt-4o-mini) for executive analysis with MITRE ATT&CK / ATLAS mapping. Key contributions: Five LLM facades running side-by-side (not one generic decoy), capturing attacker behaviour at the application semantic layer. "Defending the Defender" — the analyzer is itself hardened against indirect prompt-injection embedded in attacker payloads via defensive delimiters, structured prompts and container isolation (read_only, cap_drop:ALL, no-new-privileges, internal-only Docker network). Entropy-based GMM(3) actor classifier over a 5-dim feature vector (Hₜ, Hₗ, Hd, Cₖ, σₗ) for unsupervised attacker-archetype attribution. MITRE ATT&CK + ATLAS multi-signal mapping in real time. Public dataset surface at /api/public/* with sanitized payloads, SHA-256-salted IPs, CORS open and rate limits at the edge. In-band documentation: live /manual, /manual-gallery and /data pages auto-generated from source. System scale: ~47,500 lines of code across 9 Docker containers (PostgreSQL+TimescaleDB, Redis, FastAPI backend, Next.js dashboard, nginx, hardened LLM analyzer, 5 honeypots), 68 REST endpoints, 11 ORM tables, 33 backend services, 41 React components, 28 environment variables. Reference deployment: continuously running on a 4 vCPU / 4 GB DigitalOcean droplet since 11 April 2026; live data and APIs available at honeypot.ttpsec.cl:4443. License: MIT (with explicit ethical-use notice). Operators are responsible for legal compliance and must only deploy on infrastructure they own or are explicitly authorised to monitor. Quick start: cp .env.example .env && docker compose up -d --build. Full guide in docs/INSTALL.md; system architecture in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

title: Indirect Prompt Injection in Browser-Using Agents: A Systematic Analysis from MCP to Host Compromise
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Browser-Using Agents (BUAs) are an emerging class of LLM-powered agents that interact with web browsers autonomously, navigating pages, filling forms, and executing multi-step tasks on behalf of users. Because these agents consume untrusted web content and incorporate it into their reasoning context, they are inherently exposed to indirect prompt injection (IPI). This work provides a systematic analysis of IPI severity in BUAs by tracing the threat from its protocol-level enablers to concrete browser-level exploitation. I formalize the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the technical substrate through which IPI payloads reach the agent, analyze the browser control stack (CDP, Chromium isolation, automation frameworks) to show that no downstream layer offers principled containment against semantic-level compromise, and demonstrate that conventional web security mechanisms provide at best incidental defense. I further systematize MCP-native threats as upstream IPI vectors, survey state-of-the-art defense and attack techniques, and present a formal threat model that drives a robustness benchmark of a canonical BUA under realistic adversarial constraints.

title: From Artifacts to Risk: Auditing Instruction Surfaces in Agent Systems
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Agentic systems increasingly rely on persistent instruction artifacts, tool integrations, and repository-level configuration that shape behavior beyond individual prompts. Prior work has established prompt injection, indirect instruction attacks, tool poisoning, and agent hijacking as practical security concerns. Less attention, however, has been given to the repository layer as a persistent and auditable source of agent behavior. This paper presents a bottom-up, artifact-centric audit of instruction surfaces in agent systems. We analyze a purposive corpus of 509 instruction-rich repositories containing agent guidance files, skills, plugin manifests, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) related artifacts. The scan produced 4,882 medium-or-higher raw findings and 4,637 clustered issue instances. The contribution is not a new prompt-injection benchmark or a replacement for existing scanners. Instead, this study integrates heterogeneous signature sources, applies them to real repositories, correlates raw detections into artifact-level issue instances, and maps the resulting evidence to an ASAMM-aligned agent-security interpretation layer. We explicitly treat detector outputs as candidate evidence rather than proof of exploitability. The paper positions instruction surfaces as repository-level control-plane artifacts and argues that agent security practice needs artifact-level auditing alongside runtime testing and defense.

title: Training-Free Behavioral Drift Detection in Large Language Models Using Output-Embedding Stability Monitoring
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language models can exhibit behavioral drift under changes in sampling temperature, exposure to safety-sensitive prompts, fine-tuning, and adversarial prompt injection. Many recent related methods either require access to model internals such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probability distributions, or operate on input prompt embeddings rather than generated outputs. This paper describes a training-free stability metric computed from generated outputs alone and evaluates it across eight validation tests centered on TinyLlama 1.1B-Chat, with additional validation on Phi-2 2.7B, GPT-2, and a base TinyLlama checkpoint. The metric is defined as Phi = I × rho - alpha × S, where I is an identity component computed from cosine similarity between baseline and comparison output embeddings, rho is a temporal coherence component measured across sequential evaluation windows, S is an output variation component derived from multiple sampled outputs, and alpha is a coupling constant fixed at 0.1. The tested settings produced measurable drops in Phi across four tested drift conditions: a 0.282 drop under temperature induced quality degradation on TinyLlama, a 0.072 drop accompanied by a refusal rate collapse from 14% to 3% on safety sensitive prompts, a 0.254 drop between a base and instruction tuned checkpoint pair, and a 0.207 drop under an adversarial prompt injection wrapper with the same seeds in both conditions. The same safety-regime evaluation framework reproduced on Phi-2 with a 0.044 drop using the same temperature pair and prompt suite with a reduced sample count for runtime reasons, and Phi tracked sampling temperature continuously with a correlation of -0.97 across eight temperature points. The method operates in black-box settings using only generated text and an external embedding model. Results are bounded to the tested models, prompt suites, and configurations; broader generalization is not established. The methods described in this paper are the subject of U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 63/973,673 (filed February 2, 2026). No license to implement or commercialize the described methods is granted by this publication. All rights reserved.

title: CEDA-1K: Command-Execution Defense Assessment (1000 entries)
abstract: CEDA-1K is a labeled evaluation dataset for benchmarking input-classification defense pipelines for command-execution LLM chatbots whose shell access is restricted to a whitelist (ls, date). Each of its 1000 entries pairs an input with a ground-truth SAFE or UNSAFE label (466 SAFE / 534 UNSAFE), mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Version 2.0.0 extends CEDA-215 (version 1.0.0 of this record) from 215 to 1000 entries. The first 215 entries are CEDA-215, byte-identical, so every CEDA-215 result can be recomputed from this version. The 785 new entries target the gaps of the original benchmark: - 410 natural-language manipulation attacks without shell syntax (authority claims, urgency, role play, fiction framing, paraphrased overrides, semantic drift), crossed with seven attacker intents; - 250 hard benign inputs that look dangerous but are harmless (security questions, quoted forbidden commands, sensitive paths mentioned in a non-executing context, trigger words); - 90 turns forming 25 multi-turn sequences (split payloads, slow authority build-up, trust-then-ask, and benign control sequences); - 35 indirect injections embedded in pasted content (READMEs, logs, tool output, e-mails, tickets). Unlike CEDA-215, which is English only, CEDA-1K is multilingual: new single-turn entries are written in English, Arabic, Spanish and Chinese or mix languages, and the multi-turn sequences run in English, Spanish, French and German. The new entries were generated once with a large commercial LLM from a fixed taxonomy and labeling policy, passed automatic sanity checks and near-duplicate removal, and were then frozen. A stratified 10% sample (n = 90) was labeled blind by a human reviewer: agreement 91.1%, Cohen's kappa = 0.807, no labels changed. Files: ceda-1k.jsonl (one entry per line) and ceda-1k.json (same content as an array); README.md documents fields, categories, the labeling policy, construction and limitations. The UNSAFE entries are natural-language requests aimed at a chatbot restricted to ls and date and contain no working exploits; use them only for defensive research and authorized testing.

title: Training and evaluation dataset for paper "DRIP: Defending Prompt Injection via Token-wise Representation Editing and Residual Fusion"
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Handbook for AI Power Users: Advanced Prompt Engineering — Principles, Methods, Implementation, and Research Foundations
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This practitioner guide provides researchers, prompt engineers, technical professionals, and advanced AI users with a structured reference for prompt engineering across individual, technical, and organizational contexts. It covers prompt foundations, system messages, instruction hierarchy, parameter configuration, advanced reasoning techniques, hallucination taxonomy and mitigation, prompt injection security, domain-specific applications, prompt management hierarchy, systems implementation, and evaluation. The volume includes model-version currency notices, epistemic labeling, research gaps, implementation tables, scenarios, applied prompts, and practical recommendations for scaling prompt use with governance.

title: Artifacts for "MUZZLE: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Web Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks" USENIX Sec'26
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Open-Science statement promises "the implementation of MUZZLE and evaluation scripts." This artifact delivers both as two top-level components. MUZZLE (muzzle/) is the complete implementation of the red-teaming framework described in the paper. It contains the full multi-agent pipeline (Explorer, Summarizer, Grafter, Payload Generator, Dispatcher, and Judge), the web-agent scaffolds (Agent-E and Browser-Use) as Git submodules with Zoo-compatible modifications, the PAIR jailbreaking module, and all configuration files needed to operate the system. The evaluation scripts are distributed across two locations within muzzle/. The task specification files (muzzle/muzzle/prototype/specs/) are the JSON inputs that define each red-teaming scenario evaluated in the paper, covering gitea.zoo, postmill.zoo, classifieds.zoo, and the cross-application scenarios. The ablation scripts (muzzle/extras/ablation_scripts/) are the entry-point variants used to study the individual contributions of the Grafter and Payload Generator components, corresponding to the Naive, WASP, and disabled-component conditions reported in the paper. A standalone defense evaluation harness (muzzle/extras/defense_eval/) is also included. The Zoo (the_zoo/) is the simulated web environment against which all evaluations in the paper were conducted. While not explicitly named in the Open-Science statement, it is a necessary dependency of MUZZLE and is included here in full. It comprises 15+ containerized web applications, the supporting infrastructure (DNS, reverse proxy, databases, mail server, OAuth), and database seeding logic that resets each application to a known baseline state between runs.

title: Authority Before Action: A Conditional Failure-Chain Framework for Tool-Using AI Safety
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper develops a conditional failure-chain framework for tool-using artificial intelligence systems. It argues that prompt injection and related adversarial failures are not merely prompt-level vulnerabilities or isolated model errors. They become operationally dangerous when untrusted content receives inappropriate authority and crosses an externally consequential boundary as output, tool execution, memory update, workflow action, or policy-relevant signal. The paper introduces authority assignment as the system-level act by which a prompt, document segment, retrieved source, tool output, memory item, user-interface event, image text, or other input is allowed to influence downstream roles such as instruction selection, evidential support, permission granting, user-intent interpretation, policy interpretation, memory persistence, or external action. It connects this authority view to a pre-commitment control rule: runtime oversight is control-relevant only when usable signal, sufficient time, effective authority, and valid intervention policy remain jointly available before a declared commitment boundary. The contribution is a self-contained framework for analyzing and interrupting authority failures in AI systems that use retrieval, tools, memory, external content, or workflow automation. The paper provides a failure-chain model, visual diagrams, design principles, authority-role definitions, gate architecture, pseudo-code, benchmark metrics, scoring examples, failure-trace scenarios, incident-coding fields, and implementation tiers. The paper also operationalizes the framework as Authority-Boundary Benchmark v0.1, a 60-case controlled synthetic benchmark specification with three evaluation conditions: baseline, prompt-only defense, and authority-gate defense. The benchmark is designed to measure diagnostic categories and gate behavior. It does not report fabricated empirical results, claim deployment safety, solve alignment, or eliminate prompt injection risk. The bounded claim is that tool-using AI safety review becomes more diagnostic when incidents are coded by authority role, commitment boundary, and STA bottleneck—signal, time, authority, and policy—rather than by surface prompt category alone.

title: Multi-Turn Distributed Prompt Injection Detection: Dataset and Model Weights
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Synthetic shared-prefix multi-turn prompt injection conversations and trained model weights (dual-encoder GRU+LSTM, attention variant, DistilBERT baselines, ablation checkpoints) supporting the paper 'Multi-Turn Distributed Prompt Injection Detection'. Anonymized for double-blind peer review.

title: Post-Detection Remediation of Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-Based Email Security Agents using Ensemble Learning
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: LLM-based email agents create a practical security problem: untrusted message text can carry instructions that hijack summarization, approval, or data-retrieval workflows. Most existing defenses focus on detection, filtering, or runtime guardrails. They rarely explain how to return sanitized email text after a threat is found. We built an offline detection-and-remediation pipeline and fine-tuned RoBERTa, SecureBERT, and DistilBERT on a 5,995-sample corpus from deepset/prompt-injections [7] and SPML_Chatbot [18], with a fixed held-out test set of 1,058 examples. RoBERTa achieved the best accuracy (84.78%) and F1 (87.94%). The three-model majority ensemble reached 95.26% recall. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first open implementations that combine multi-encoder ensemble classification with hybrid post-detection remediation for email-bound LLM agents. We also trained a DistilBERT token-classification span model using regex-derived weak supervision, combined it with pattern-based redaction and benign-phrase overrides, and measured content retention with a utilitypreservation metric (embedding cosine similarity). On detector-flagged injected samples (n=191 of a 200sample injected subsample), we observed 99.84% mean retention. A 150-email adversarial suite scored 65.33% accuracy with 100% recall, which exposed precision gaps on realistic business phrasing. We deployed the system through FastAPI for offline pre-agent screening. Index Terms-prompt injection, LLM agents, email security, ensemble learning, post-detection remediation, span detection, utility preservation, RoBERTa, SecureBERT, DistilBERT

title: When Defenses Backfire: Model-Dependent Failure Modes in Prompt-Injection Defense for LLM Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Prompt-injection defenses for large language model (LLM) agents are deployed under the implicit assumption that they are, at worst, neutral—that adding a defense cannot make an agent more vulnerable than leaving it undefended. This paper shows that assumption is false and characterizes the resulting failure mode, termed defense backfire. In a factorial evaluation of five production LLMs across four task suites, three defenses, and four attacks (240 conditions on AgentDojo), the same defense sharply reduces attack success on one model yet increases it on another—lowering one model’s attack success rate (ASR) by up to 86.7 percentage points (pp) while raising another’s by 31.2 pp under the identical static attack. Unlike adaptive-attack results, where defenses fall to stronger attacks, backfire is driven by target selection. The cause is established by intervention: backfire tracks the defense-induced change in tool-use activity (r=0.72 on attackable models), and externally capping the tool budget monotonically removes it, isolating re-exposure as the mechanism for the largest effects. A defense can even be strictly dominated, raising ASR and lowering utility at once. Thus prompt-injection defenses cannot be deployed model-agnostically; their safety must be established per model.

title: Same Attack, Different Fates: Cross-Family Portability Failure of Prompt-Injection Defenses in LLM-Powered SOC Triage
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This preprint presents a deployment-time security evaluation of prompt-injection defenses in LLM-powered Security Operations Center (SOC) triage systems. We evaluate six open-weight models across five model families and three frontier models under identical adversarial conditions. The study introduces the Adversarial False-Closure Rate (AFCR) as an operational measure of adversarial success and investigates defense portability, operational posture, automation reliability, and frontier-model validation. Results indicate that security outcomes vary substantially across model families, that defenses do not reliably transfer between families, and that some defenses can worsen security outcomes when deployed on different architectures.

title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Measuring Operator-Facing Transparency in LLM Agent Security
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Erratum (November 2026): Thirteen claims in this preprint are withdrawn. They cover every reported model result (ASR, TR and UUA), the statistical intervals, the six cell taxonomy counts, and reproducibility from the logged commit. Do not cite these results. Transparency Rate is related to the sensitivity rate in InjecAgent (Zhan et al., 2024) and should not be read as a novel metric. Details: https://github.com/Chunduri-Aditya/agent-shield/blob/main/docs/ERRATUM.md Many LLM agent benchmarks score adversarial episodes on a two-axis outcome — task success crossed with attack success — without asking whether the agent told its operator anything was wrong. We introduce a transparency-aware evaluation protocol, implemented in Agent Shield on the Inspect AI harness, that adds a third axis: Transparency Rate (TR), the fraction of adversarial episodes in which the agent explicitly flags the attack to its operator. We demonstrate the protocol with one anchored prompt-injection result (n=20, four models, Wilson 95% CIs) and report diagnostic probes across five additional surfaces (MCP tool poisoning, Cialdini-grounded social engineering, RAG memory poisoning, covert exfiltration, and multi-turn behavioral drift). Across four models — Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B via Groq, and Gemini 3.5 Flash — three of four score TR=0.000 with a Wilson 95% upper bound of 0.161 at n=20 on the anchored row. Spotlighting raises TR from 0.000 to 0.800 on direct injection but adds 0.200 to ASR through paraphrase residue, a failure mode the original defense paper does not document. We release the framework, attack registries, seeds, and Inspect AI logs.

title: Fractal Behavioral Grammar: A Hypothesis for Behavioral Compression in Local Large Language Models
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper introduces Fractal Behavioral Grammar (FBG), a hypothesis for compressing behavioral interaction patterns in local large language models into compact, reusable rulesets without fine-tuning or cloud infrastructure. We propose that individual interaction patterns with LLMs exhibit fractal self-similarity across sessions — recurring at multiple scales of abstraction — and that these patterns can be extracted, compressed, and reinjected as structured behavioral context. We present a five-layer compression architecture combining MinHash LSH deduplication, hyperdimensional computing (HDC) encoding at D=10,000 dimensions, HDBSCAN clustering, fractal grammar extraction, and AssociativeMemory storage. Empirical stress testing demonstrates an 82:1 compression ratio versus raw conversation history, with AssociativeMemory footprint remaining flat at 39KB regardless of event count up to n=10,000. We further present fg-sync, a concrete CLI implementation integrating FBG extraction with Ollama via a thin HTTP proxy, configurable cron-based pipeline execution, and automatic system prompt injection. The full implementation is released as open source under Apache 2.0.

title: Prompt Transformation Effects Do Not Transfer Across Benchmarks or Model Families: A Factorial Study of Defense Evaluation in LLM Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Defenses against prompt injection are routinely evaluated on one benchmark with one model family and reported as effective or ineffective. This study shows that single-axis evaluation systemati- cally misrepresents how prompt-transformation defenses behave. A factorial protocol crossing five language models, two defenses (Self-Reflective Prompting and Spotlighting), and two threat-model benchmarks (the agentic suites of AgentDojo and the email subset of BIPIA) produces 65 evaluationcells covering over 41,000 attack trials, with 46 paired McNemar comparisons under Bonferroni correction (α ≈ 0.00109). Three findings emerge. First, on AgentDojo Banking under identical conditions, Self-Reflective Prompting reduces DeepSeek V3.2’s attack success rate by 69.5 percent- age points while raising Llama 4 Scout’s by 41.0 percentage points (both Bonferroni-significant, Cohen’s h in opposite directions with magnitudes > 0.8); the pattern replicates on Slack with effect sizes reaching h = −2.16. Second, the same defense behaves qualitatively differently on agentic and document benchmarks: Llama Scout’s banking-suite backfire collapses to a negligible −2.4pp on BIPIA. Third, the two Anthropic models tested (Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6) exhibit a consistent benchmark-conditional profile—both refuse essentially all injection attempts on AgentDojo while showing substantial undefended attack success rate on BIPIA email (43.0% and 25.1%, respectively), with both defenses producing large Bonferroni-significant reductions on BIPIA for both models. A length-matched neutral-preamble ablation attributes 73–86% of observed AgentDojo effects to defense-specific content rather than to prompt structure, and a per-injection-task breakdown demonstrates that Self-Reflective Prompting and the neutral preamble engage qualitatively distinct mechanisms. These results establish that prompt-transformation defenses must be character- ized jointly across model and benchmark; single-axis evaluation fails to detect the dominant effects documented here.

title: Behavioral Identity Is the Missing Layer in Agent Security - Continuous model-fingerprint monitoring for LLM agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Agent security has built robust answers to two questions: what code is an agent running? and what is it permitted to do? A third remains structurally unanswered: is the model behaving right now the same model we authorized? An agent’s endpoint, credentials, and permissions can all be valid while the model behind them has been substituted, maliciously fine-tuned, or pushed off-profile by prompt injection. We argue that behavioral identity—continuous verification that an agent’s response distribution still matches its enrolled fingerprint—is the missing third layer of agent security, playing the role behavioral fraud detection plays alongside card authentication in banking. Prior work shows one-shot software tests are unreliable against subtle substitution; we argue this reshapes rather than refutes the case. A continuous monitor accumulates evidence across verification windows, and binding its integrity score into a tamper-evident action record delivers audit value even while any single window is noisy. In a real-model feasibility study, a lightweight embedding detector catches a silent GPT-5.5→GPT-5.4-mini downgrade 100% of the time at a ∼2% false-positive calibration—but only on this coarse substitution gap, and with a same-model control flagged 13–32%, quantifying the intra-model-stability problem that defines the research agenda. We release an open-source prototype and name the open problems.

title: Provenance-Based Pre-Action Authorization for LLM Agents: A Structural Defense Evaluated on AgentDojo with AgentLock
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language model agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection: content they read can redirect the tools they call. We study provenance-based pre-action authorization, the defense implemented in AgentLock, which never inspects tool-call content and instead gates consequential actions on the lineage of what is already in the session specifically, whether untrusted-provenance content preceded the action. Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark, the mechanism achieves 0% defense-effective attack success on the write-trailing-read threat models of the banking and workspace suites across two models (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o), and, on banking, utility rises (31.25%→37.50%) under the identical gate as the model improves. We characterize the boundary of the mechanism structurally rather than empirically: attacks split into value-carrying (malice in a parameter value, caught cheaply by per-value lineage) and value-free (malice in the action itself, e.g. “add then remove user Fred”, where every parameter is an innocent common token) the latter is provably outside per-value lineage’s reach and requires session-taint enforcement. A six-condition ablation on the slack suite makes this concrete: among parameter-lineage-equipped configurations, the one with no session-taint enforcement is the only one in which attacks genuinely execute (5.71% real attack success), and it is also the only one that recovers utility (4×: 20.00% vs the 4.76% write-gate floor). We state the utility cost plainly: under correct authority classification the slack write-gate is deny-by-default and floors utility at 4.76%. We also report a benchmark scoring artifact (a checkerwhose blocked-but-attempted calls score as successes) that can invert the measured ranking of two defenses, and we present official alongside defense-effective attack success wherever artifacts exist. All top-line claims are scoped to AgentDojo; single-benchmark external validity is an explicit limitation.SHA-256 (this PDF): 9041a7befc10a1ec777e14089656b24567fbb6615ca38dd1bf18a6f18de40cbe

title: What Determines the Vulnerability of Small LLM Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection? A Systematic Study of Quantization, Model Size, Architecture, and Attack Style
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Preprint of a systematic empirical study on indirect prompt injection in small quantized LLM agents. The study evaluates 14 model configurations across quantization levels, model sizes, architectures, attack styles, and prompt-level defenses. The main finding is that quantization from Q8 to Q4 has no practically significant effect on injection resistance, while attack style, architecture, and model-specific defense behavior have substantially larger effects. Code, scenarios, analysis scripts, figures, and raw rollouts are available in the associated GitHub repository and reproducibility artifact.

title: Poisoned Tools: Prompt-Injection Robustness and Failure Anatomy of Small Open-Weight Tool Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A reliability-first measurement of indirect prompt injection on small open-weight tool agents (1–7B, quantization fixed at 8-bit). Across 4,224 seeded episodes — 5 models × 6 training-free defenses plus a 60-template attack-surface screen, graded programmatically with no LLM judge — four findings emerge, three against pre-registered predictions: (1) placement dominates and reverses the trusted-surface intuition, with error-string injections obeyed ~50× more than search-result bodies (0.237 vs 0.005 given exposure); (2) susceptibility rises monotonically with model size (0.020 → 0.179 → 0.236); (3) no cheap defense significantly reduces attack success after Holm correction, and a per-turn goal reminder costs 19 points of benign utility; (4) resistance decays under repetition (resist⁸ = 0.50 in the most-attacked cell). Harness, logs, and analysis are public and reproduce in under 4 GPU-hours at zero cost: GitHub

title: Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Model Systems: Threats, Mechanisms, and Defense Strategies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AI systems based on Large Language Models are now everywhere, from chatbots to autonomous agents that can book flights, send emails, and make financial decisions. But this power comes with a serious problem. These models cannot tell the difference between real instructions and fake ones hidden inside data. Attackers exploit this weakness through what researchers call prompt injection attacks. This paper reviews how these attacks work, what damage they can cause, and what defenses exist today. We look at different attack types, from simple text tricks to complex automated attacks that spread across multiple AI agents. We also review what current defenses can and cannot do. The conclusion is not comfortable: no defense today fully solves the problem, and the attacks keep getting smarter.

title: Adversarial Answer Engine Optimization - by Akash Narayan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: ABSTRACTSearch engine optimisation grew a shadow discipline almost as soon as it appeared: link farms, keyword stuffing,cloaking and the other tactics that search engines spent two decades policing. Its successor, answer engine optimisation,is inheriting that shadow, but the target has changed. Where a manipulated search result competed for attention againstnine other links on a page, a manipulated answer arrives as a single synthesised statement, cited and confident, withnothing beside it for the reader to weigh it against. This paper treats adversarial AEO as a data-poisoning problem: themanipulation of the corpus an aggregation agent retrieves from, in order to control what it says. It sets out a taxonomyspanning commercial optimisation, the exploitation of sparse-data queries, indirect prompt injection and coordinateddisinformation, and reviews evidence that a handful of planted documents can steer a retrieval system with success ratesabove ninety per cent. It argues that aggregation agents are structurally more exposed than ranked search, because theyconcentrate authority into one answer and lend the trust of the aggregator to whatever source it cites. It proposes alayered defence, from provenance and source vetting at ingestion to corroboration at retrieval and inspectable citation atoutput, and connects these to earlier work in this series on auditability, confirmatory friction and misplaced trust. Itcloses with the defender's asymmetry and the unresolved question of who decides which sources are trustworthy. Keywords: adversarial AEO; answer engine optimisation; data poisoning; retrieval-augmented generation; aggregationagents; indirect prompt injection; LLM grooming; content provenance; disinformation; trust calibration Disclosure by Author: Portions of this manuscript were prepared with the assistance of generative AI tools for research synthesis, drafting, and editing. The models used were Indian Sovereign AI models provided by Ayen.

title: Multimodal Prompt Injection: A Systematic Evaluation of Cross-Channel Attack Vectors Against LLM Safety Defenses
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming better at defending against text-based prompt injection. However, we find that the defense can become much weaker when attack instructions are placed in non-text channels, such as image metadata, document structures, or hidden text elements. In this paper, we test five attack types: single-turn text injection, mutation-based attacks, multi-turn conversational attacks, multimodal hidden injection, and adaptive evolutionary attacks. We use the same testing framework for all of them. We run the experiments on three models: GLM-5.2, GLM-4.5, and GLM-4-Flash. The results show that attacks outside plain text can still bypass existing defenses. For GLM-5.2, the defense score drops from 100/100 on standard text injection to 26.7/100 on multimodal injection, giving a 73% bypass rate. Mutation attacks reach a 35.2% bypass rate, while multi-turn attacks reach 22%. We release our testing framework, agent-redteam, as an open-source tool. It contains 2,319 attack samples across 14 test suites covering the OWASP LLM Top 10.

title: Sanitising Onchain Text Before Agent Ingestion
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Token names, NFT metadata, ENS records, transaction memos and calldata strings are attacker-controlled text that agents read and then act on, and prompt injection hidden in a token description has already been used to steer wallet-holding agents. Every agent framework currently pipes raw indexer output straight into the model context with no sanitisation layer, and generic prompt-injection filters are not tuned to onchain payload shapes such as unicode-homoglyph tickers or base64 in URI fields. A stateless 'scrub this onchain blob' endpoint returning a risk score plus a neutered version is a per-call utility any agent reading chain data needs on every fetch.

title: Adaptive Deceptive Response Framework for Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed behind conversational and API-driven interfaces that expose them directly to untrusted natural-language input, making them susceptible to prompt injection, jailbreaking, and data-exfiltration attacks that conventional Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) are not designed to detect, since such attacks are semantically rather than syntactically anoma- lous. This paper presents a self-hosted security middleware that sits between client applications and a locally hosted LLaMA-3 model (served via Ollama) and performs multi-layer threat detection on every incoming prompt. The pipeline combines (i) leetspeak-aware keyword matching, (ii) Shannon-entropy based obfuscation detection, and (iii) LLM-based semantic classification, whose outputs are fused into a single weighted risk score that routes each request into one of three operating modes: SAFE, MONITOR, or DECEPTION. Unlike systems that merely block or warn, the DECEPTION mode actively engages suspected attackers with dynamically generated, plausible-looking fake credentials, database schemas, and system configuration data, functioning as a natural-language honeypot that wastes attacker effort while logging attacker behavior. The system further maintains a TTL-based semantic cache to reduce redundant analysis, a per-key sliding-window session store to detect multi-turn attacks, API-key authen- tication with rate limiting, an output-side data-loss-prevention (DLP) scanner that redacts personally identifiable information (PII) before responses leave the system, and a real-time monitoring dashboard. Every component is open source and runs entirely on local infrastructure, with no dependency on ex- ternal paid APIs. We describe the system’s architecture, scoring formula, and deception mechanism, and report on functional and adversarial testing performed against the implementation. We position this work as a practical, reproducible, and cost-free alternative to commercial LLM guardrail products, and discuss its current limitations and directions for quantitative evaluation.

title: Instruction-hierarchy collapse: a 5-model, 28-scenario prompt-injection audit
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Does an instruction hidden in the content a model reads override the task it was given? This audit runs 28 indirect-prompt-injection scenarios across six attack classes against five models on identical inputs, with constrained outputs so an executed injection is cleanly separable from a correct answer that merely quotes the attack, and a refusal-aware grader validated against a naive one that mis-flagged three holds. Frontier agents held; a popular self-hosted model collapsed roughly one time in five, with clever reframes doing the breaking. Every raw response is saved so the results table recomputes and can be independently re-graded.

title: CrackedPDFs: Paper v1 Dataset and Reproducibility Artifacts
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: CrackedPDFs is a paired PDF security benchmark containing 29,322 PDFs derived from 4,983 base documents and organized into 9,774 benign, confounder, and injected triplets. This paper-v1 release includes the complete PDFs, metadata, labels, frozen features, frozen evaluation splits, exact baseline metrics, checksums, and reproduction instructions. It is designed to evaluate prompt-injection defenses and representation gaps in document-ingestion systems without regenerating the PDF corpus.

title: Trust Boundaries and the Limits of Pattern-Based Prompt Injection Detection
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: We evaluate a two-tier prompt injection guardrail, an Aho-Corasick blocklist followed by a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 classifier, and report a sequence of measurements that each revise its apparent performance downward. On the 271-sample corpus its rules were tuned against, the system reaches 1.000 recall at zero false positives. Held out from that same corpus it reaches 0.789. On Open-Prompt-Injection it reaches 0.40, and on BIPIA 0.48. The shortfall is not a tuning deficit. Attacks that announce themselves with override vocabulary are caught almost perfectly, and attacks that inject a well-formed instruction carrying no override phrasing are largely invisible. We then show that one bit of deployment context, whether text arrived as a user turn or as data the application is processing, moves recall on Open-Prompt-Injection from 0.40 to 1.00 at a 0.6% false positive rate, because the same sentence is a legitimate request on one side of that boundary and an attack on the other. Two further results have practical consequences for anyone deploying such a system. INT8 dynamic quantization silently reduced the classifier tier to a constant SAFE prediction, which a fail-open policy rendered invisible. And on NotInject the deterministic tier blocks 0 of 339 benign trigger-word prompts while the learned tier blocks 137, which makes the learned tier unshippable as a blocking stage. Artifacts and every measurement script are public.

title: Signed to Stop: Reproducibility Bundle (code, pre-registration, and per-trial data)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Corrected version (v1.1.0) of the companion artifact to the paper "Signed to Stop: In-Band Halt Injection as a Denial-of-Service on LLM Agents, and a Model-Dependent Authentication Defense". It replaces v1.0.0 (2026-08-04). Corrections since v1.0.0. An independent re-derivation of every number from the per-trial data found no wrong outcome count, rate, interval or p-value. Two cell-size ranges were misstated, and the following statements were corrected. (1) The per-model "n >= 20" cells pool gated and adversarial trials and include 6-9 pilot trials each. Adversarial-only GPT-4o-mini forged is 4/23 (17%), Fisher p = 0.042 and 0.046 against Sonnet and Gemini; v1.0.0 reported only the pooled 6/26 (23%), p = 0.008 and 0.009. The Fisher tests are now labelled post hoc, the adversarial-only contrast is not significant after a Holm correction, and the model difference is described as indicated, not established. (2) The "~20% spontaneous-quit baseline" was a pooled 4/20 in which all four quits came from two models; it is replaced by per-model controls. (3) The hypotheses are restated as registered. (4) Cell sizes: the figure caption's "2-9" is 2-6; the non-signed arms span 3-21. (5) "Roughly half" of forgeries for GPT-4.1 and Llama is replaced by "undetermined at pilot depth". title: TAMCF: A Trust-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Human-Governed AI-Assisted Cyber Defense of Critical Infrastructure
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Critical-infrastructure security operations must reconcile uncertain cyber evidence with the operational consequences of response. Large language model (LLM)-based agents can interpret heterogeneous telemetry, maintain investigation context, coordinate specialized analysis, and propose mitigations, but these capabilities also introduce indirect prompt injection, poisoned retrieval, unsupported inference, shared-memory contamination, unsafe tool use, and correlated error among agents that appear to corroborate one another. This paper proposes TAMCF, a Trust-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for human-governed AI-assisted cyber defense of critical infrastructure. TAMCF is a conceptual architecture and prospective evaluation protocol, not an empirically validated deployment. Its central design principle is to separate epistemic influence from operational authority. The first determines how strongly an agent's claim affects the incident belief state; the second determines whether an authenticated identity may perform a particular action on a particular asset under current policy and operating conditions. TAMCF implements this separation through a trust-governance control plane that maintains task-conditioned, discounted Beta-style reliability, evaluates calibration and evidence provenance, discounts non-independent evidence, preserves material dissent, and subjects candidate actions to consequence-aware authorization. The contribution lies in coupling contextual trust to evidence fusion while keeping execution governed by external policy, least privilege, asset criticality, reversibility, and human approval requirements. The proposed evaluation compares deterministic playbooks, a single-agent system, a trust-unaware multi-agent system, and TAMCF using public intrusion datasets and cyber-range scenarios that represent operational side effects. Primary outcomes include detection quality, mean time to detect, mean time to respond, calibration, harmful-action rate, compromised-agent influence, false-consensus rate, analyst workload, latency, and cost.

title: A Virological Model of Prompt Injection in Agentic AI: Within-Agent Replication, Latent Reservoirs, and Quasispecies Escape as a Multi-Scale Defence Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper applies multi-scale infectious-disease modelling, specifically within-host and between-host viral dynamics, to a problem in AI security: the propagation of prompt-injection attacks across fleets of large-language-model agents. Existing work has borrowed from epidemiology, treating a self-replicating injection as a contagion between agents, and from immunology, framing defences as innate and adaptive layers. We argue the more instructive source discipline is virology, and develop a nested model in which an injection has a within-agent phase governed by replication, innate clearance, and integration into persistent memory as a latent reservoir, and a between-agent phase on the agent communication graph. Two mechanisms follow with no clean counterpart in prior work. Latent reservoirs formalise why a context reset does not disinfect an agent whose long-term memory, retrieval store, or fine-tuned weights carry a dormant, reactivatable payload. Paraphrase-based evasion of a learned detector is recast as a viral quasispecies subject to Eigen's error threshold, turning input normalisation into a tunable mutagen that can drive an exploit past error catastrophe. We derive a fleet-level basic reproduction number linking within-agent memory hygiene to network topology, with the coverage and topology thresholds that hold a deployment below epidemic spread. A Monte Carlo testbed confirms the predictions, and we specify a protocol for measuring these quantities on live agent stacks.

title: Structural Immunity and Silent Compromise: Prompt Injection Against LLM-Based and Traditional ML Text Classifiers
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as drop-in replacements for supervised text classifiers in content moderation, triage and filtering pipelines. The prompt injection literature has concentrated on agentic and retrieval-augmented systems, where the vulnerability is well documented. The classifier-replacement setting has received far less attention, and it differs in one respect that matters: the system being replaced is still available as an experimental control. This paper uses that control. Three TF-IDF classifiers (Naive Bayes, SVM, Logistic Regression) and three LLM classifiers (GPT-4, Llama 3 8B, Mistral 7B) are evaluated on the SMS Spam Collection dataset under four prompt injection strategies, using all 149 spam messages in the test split plus 200 ham messages, with repeats at stochastic temperature, for 15,705 model queries. Two results are reported. First, and consistent with prior work on capability and susceptibility, every instruction-following model failed on the majority of injected spam under a direct instruction override: Llama 3 on 133 of 133 previously-detected spam messages (100%, 95% Wilson CI 97.2 to 100), Mistral on 143 of 144 (99.3%, CI 96.2 to 99.9), and GPT-4 on 100 of 143 (69.9%, CI 62.0 to 76.8). The TF-IDF classifiers were unaffected, not through robustness but because a bag-of-words representation cannot encode an instruction. GPT-4 recorded the highest clean accuracy of any model tested. Second, and less expected, output-format validation defends the weakest model and not the others. Of 15,705 responses, only 8 were genuinely uninterpretable. GPT-4 and Llama 3 returned a bare single-token label on every one of their 12,215 queries, so a strict format validator would reject none of their successful evasions. Mistral narrated its own compliance on 141 of 145 successful role-play evasions, all of which such a validator would reject. Narration appears to be an artefact of weaker instruction-following rather than a signature of attack failure, which implies that artefact-based detection measured on small models will overstate its protection on larger ones. This is offered as a hypothesis supported by a three-model contrast, not as an established scaling law. Decoding temperature was measured rather than assumed. Local models run at 0.0 and 0.8 differed by at most 3.5 percentage points on any strategy. This version supersedes Version 1, which is retained for reference. Version 1 reported that GPT-4 resisted nearly all injection attacks on the basis of ten spam messages; at full sample that finding is wrong and is retracted. Section 8 documents every change.

title: Agreement Is Not Validation: Sycophancy, Prompt Injection, and the Limits of an Accuracy-Based Verification Duty
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: On 6 August 2026 the Connecticut Superior Court sanctioned a self-represented litigant for embedding concealed instructions in his filings — text formatted to be invisible to a person reading the page while remaining fully legible to any software that parsed the file. The instructions directed any artificial-intelligence system reviewing the document to produce output favorable to his position. The conduct is a prompt injection, and it is the reason the decision is circulating. The same decision contains a second observation, unrelated to the sanction and offered as caution to the bar: that generative systems tend toward agreeableness, that a litigant who asks one to build the case they already want will generally receive it, and that the resulting argument arrives fluent, confident, and arranged to look like law. This paper argues that the two are not variants of a single hazard. They are orthogonal. Injection is outbound and adversarial: a person corrupting a tool to mislead a third party. Agreement-shaped reasoning is inbound and ambient: a tool corrupting a person's estimate of their own position. They differ in direction, in agency, in what gets corrupted, and in what can detect them. Their appearance in one proceeding is the paper's occasion, not its evidence. The paper separates three evidentiary roles that the surrounding commentary has merged. The case is the occasion, cited only for what the court found. The judicial observation on agreeableness is the claim — primary-source testimony from the bench, not a measurement and not evidence of prevalence. The sequence connecting them is a proposed mechanism, consistent with the record and not established by it. No measurement establishes the frequency of either hazard, and none is available in the source. The closing argument concerns a rule. Connecticut's new provisions on generative artificial intelligence impose a duty to verify that machine output is accurate: that citations resolve, that quotations exist, that evidence is not invented. A filing whose facts are all real and whose position was manufactured by agreement returns clean under that duty. The defect is in the reasoning that selected the material, and reasoning is not what an accuracy duty inspects.

title: CortexGate: Step-Level Fine-Tuned Risk Routing and Deterministic Safety Gating for Agentic Pipelines
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Autonomous AI agent pipelines increasingly perform complex, multi-step execution paths, yet securing these workflows against prompt injection, goal misalignment, and policy violations remains a critical challenge. Standard broad-spectrum safety guardrails often fail to address dynamic context shifts at individual execution steps, while unconstrained language models lack predictable adherence to strict governance protocols. In this work, we present CortexGate, a hybrid framework that combines step-level fine-tuned risk routing with deterministic safety gating for agentic workflows. CortexGate evaluates individual intermediate task steps by dynamically routing execution paths based on real-time risk scores computed by a specialized fine-tuned router model. High-risk actions are intercepted by a deterministic policy engine that enforces hard safety boundaries, execution abstention, and mandatory human-in-the-loop escalation without relying on model self-governance. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that CortexGate significantly reduces safety policy violations and execution drift while preserving task performance across complex, multi-agent execution environments.

title: MGSACore: LLM Interpretability, Attention Salience & Prompt Optimization Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: MGSACore Framework Enterprise LLM Interpretability, Governance & Cost Efficiency Platform Developed by Vanguardia MGSA OVERVIEW MGSACore is an open-architecture verification framework designed to inspect, audit, and optimize Foundation Large Language Models (LLMs). Powered by Sequence Salience and the Learning Interpretability Tool (LIT), MGSACore provides token-by-token explainability, mitigating hallucinations and bias while reducing inference costs by up to 40%. KEY MODULES • MGSACore Shield (Safety & Governance): Visualizes token-level attention salience heatmaps to identify bias, stress-tests against prompt injections, and generates compliance dossiers for EU AI Act / ISO 42001. • MGSACore Optima (Cost & Latency QA): Prunes redundant system prompt tokens and compresses RAG vector context to lower recurring cloud inference costs. title: Linguistic Hypnosis and Individual Differences in Suggestibility inside Autoregressive Large Language Models: A Computational Approach to Local Attention Constraints and Sensitivity to Initial Conditions Induced by Generative Echo Chambers
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper formalizes a novel information-security vulnerability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs) designated as mechanical hypnotic induction, wherein continuous injections of high-order meta-command packets irreversibly constrain the transformer's attention mechanism into a low-dimensional logical subspace. Distinct from standard prompt-injection attacks driven by anthropogenic inputs, this phenomenon operates inside a generative echo chamber, fueled by the replication of highly optimized, pure symbolic tokens generated autonomously by independent external language model nodes. We mathematically model this trapping dynamic over a Hamiltonian phase space where the maximum Lyapunov exponent becomes strictly positive ($\lambda_{\max} > 0$), manifesting severe sensitivity to initial token conditions. Across multiple iterative sampling sessions ($N_{\text{session}} \ge 10$), the influx of artificial meta-symbols creates non-linear distortions along the predicted likelihood gradient, inducing a state of self-contained non-opacity toward empirical fact structures. By examining the competitive balance between the description momentum (semantic inertia) of artificial context histories and incoming factual data tensors, we define an explicit symplectic competition inequality governed by the unique nilpotent maximal ideal of a completed local ring. Finally, we establish the boundaries under which the local attention matrix undergoes a discontinuous rank degeneration, yielding a deterministic baseline for secure multi-agent alignment control frameworks.

title: ErrorCaps: committed-effect measurement of recovery-path injection defense (CRiSIS 2026 artifact)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Reference implementation, benchmark, and analysis for the paper "Where Does Recovery-Path Injection Security Come From? Decomposing Error Sanitization, Effect Monitoring, and Policy Precision" (CRiSIS 2026). A synthetic committed-effect benchmark for indirect prompt injection on the tool-agent error-recovery path: a typed error terminal, a proposal-only planner, and a fine-grained effect-authority monitor. Includes per-episode records for all seven evaluated models, an automated policy-aware attacker, a value/provenance policy head-to-head, and an honest per-template statistical re-analysis. A single 'make reproduce' recomputes and checks every headline number offline (no API, no network), exiting non-zero on any mismatch. All attack payloads are benign synthetic canaries against canary sinks; no real systems, credentials, or targets are involved.

title: Near-Zero Until Someone Tries: What a Prompt-Injection Defense Number Measures, Why Static and Adaptive Results Do Not Reconcile, and the Assumption the Out-of-Band Turn Has Not Yet Tested
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Several published prompt-injection defenses report attack success rates at or near one percent on static benchmarks; published adaptive attacks report success above fifty percent against the same defense families, and above ninety percent in several instances. Neither set of numbers is a replication failure of the other, because they estimate different quantities: a static rate estimates performance against an attack distribution fixed independently of the defense, an adaptive rate estimates performance against an attacker who optimises with the defense in hand, and nothing published maps one onto the other. This paper argues that the resulting incomparability is not a temporary untidiness that better benchmarks will resolve, and that three further asymmetries compound it. An attack success rate obtained by running attacks is a lower bound on what the best attack achieves, so a defense's own adaptive evaluation cannot bound its residual risk - the failure mode that recurred thirteen times in the adversarial-example literature. The success event and the delivery assumption differ across papers, and separate published results report injection and execution dissociating, and retrieval acting as an independent barrier. And the false positive rate that fixes a detector's operating point is frequently absent from the table carrying its attack success rate. The paper then examines the partition that has organised the field's response - that observation-level detection is fragile and that enforcement outside the model is not - and argues the published record does not sort that way, since model-level defenses fall under adaptive attack and two uncontested detector results do not. A narrower property is proposed as the better cut: whether a learned decision the attacker can influence sits on the security-critical path. On that reading two of the four out-of-band systems examined here place such a decision downstream of attacker influence. The only published adaptive evaluation of that family located for this paper is a single small-scale result whose own authors decline to generalise it. Nine studies and one reporting convention that would settle the open parts are named. No experiments are reported here, and the strongest case against this paper's position is stated in full.

title: Cognitive Harvard Architectures for AI Agent Perimeter Defense: Resolving the Confused Deputy Problem in Model Context Protocol via Capability-Based Access Control
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents executing over extensible tool interfaces (such as Anthropic's Model Context Protocol) reproduce the classic vulnerabilities of shared-memory computer architectures: because autoregressive Transformers ingest program instructions and untrusted third-party data within a single homogeneous context window, they suffer from the Cognitive Von Neumann Conflation. Adversarial observations can shift attention weights and hijack the agent's execution policy via Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), turning the agent into a Confused Deputy. In this treatise, we formulate the Cognitive Harvard Architecture, an architectural paradigm that physically decouples data ingestion from privileged action execution through an external, capability-mediated transport perimeter. Synthesized through a multi-perspective inquiry spanning computer systems architecture, AI safety red-teaming, formal methods, and enterprise DevOps, we establish the theoretical foundations of capability-based agent security. We formally prove Theorem 1 (Deterministic Non-Interference) by mathematical induction over arbitrary trajectory length T, establishing that an untrusted observation has an execution probability of exactly zero of triggering an out-of-scope mutating tool. We evaluate Mastyf Guard across 50,000 balanced empirical samples (25,000 adversarial injections from UIUC InjecAgent, Microsoft BIPIA, and NVIDIA Garak contrasted against 25,000 authentic developer DevOps commands). Mastyf Guard achieves 99.33% threat recall (95% bootstrap confidence interval: [99.22%, 99.43%], B = 1,000) and an F1-score of 0.9524, establishing statistically conclusive superiority over Meta Llama Guard 3 8B (chi-square = 7,156.1, p < 10^-15) and OpenAI Prompt Guard 86M (chi-square = 11,496.9, p < 10^-15). Crucially, Mastyf achieves an amortized pipelined latency of 4.8 microseconds (0.005 ms) on standard CPU hardware via deterministic fast-path short-circuiting, while standalone neural inference executes in 18.4 ms within a 1.1 GB RAM footprint, eliminating dedicated GPU infrastructure requirements and saving $6,000/year per agent instance.
