title: Zero Trust for Autonomous Agents: Dynamic Runtime Authorization via Intent Alignment, Lineage Decay, and Stateful Context
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview & Abstract Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) transition computing from deterministic execution paths to probabilistic, multi-hop reasoning loops. Contemporary access governance—including Role-Based (RBAC) and Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)—evaluates permissions atomically and statically, leaving multi-agent environments critically exposed to indirect prompt injection, confused deputy privilege escalations, and slow-velocity data scraping. This paper formalizes $\text{DynAuth-Agent}$, an authorization framework that augments standard Policy Decision Points (PDP) with three orthogonal, continuous metrics: Semantic Intent Alignment ($S_{\text{align}}$): Evaluates vector cosine similarity between the root human prompt and downstream tool dispatches using quantized local embeddings to detect indirect prompt injections. Transitive Trust Lineage ($T_{\text{chain}}$): Models cryptographic delegation degradation across non-homogeneous network boundaries and workload identities (SPIFFE) to prevent Confused Deputy privilege escalations. Cumulative Blast Radius ($B_{\text{session}}$): Tracks continuous state across execution sessions using exponential time-decay ($t_{1/2}$) to contain runaway reasoning loops and automated data scraping. Key Empirical Findings Defense Efficacy: Evaluated against 200 synthetic execution traces, the framework achieved a 98.0% block rate against Indirect Prompt Injection attacks, a 100.0% block rate against Confused Deputy delegations, and a 100.0% containment rate on runaway execution loops, with a 2.0% false-positive rate on benign tasks. Low-Latency Operational Feasibility: The end-to-end Policy Information Point (PIP) and Policy Decision Point (PDP) pipeline executes with deterministic runtime overhead, making dynamic mathematical access control viable for real-time agent tool dispatches. Declarative PDP Compatibility: Fully compatible with standard enterprise policy engines, evaluated directly via Open Policy Agent (OPA) executing compiled Rego policies. Keywords Autonomous Agents, Runtime Authorization, Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), Policy Decision Point (PDP), Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), Non-Human Identities (NHI), Indirect Prompt Injection, Open Policy Agent (OPA), Delegation Lineage.

title: Prompt Injection and the Security of LLM Applications and Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language models are increasingly wired to external tools, retrieval systems, and untrusted third-party content, which turns a conversational component into a control point for whole applications. This shift creates a security problem with no close analogue in classical software: the model reads instructions and data through the same natural-language channel and cannot reliably tell one from the other. Prompt injection exploits exactly this gap. In direct injection a user overrides the developer intent, while in indirect injection an attacker plants instructions inside a web page, document, or email that the model later retrieves and obeys on the user behalf. This survey organizes the field for practitioners and researchers. It reviews the background of instruction-following models, retrieval-augmented generation, and tool-using agents, then presents a taxonomy of threats spanning direct injection and jailbreaks, indirect injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse, insecure output handling, training-data poisoning, and denial of service. It maps these threats onto the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and summarizes concrete attack mechanisms and case studies. It then surveys defenses, from input and output filtering and spotlighting to dual-LLM privilege separation, instruction hierarchy, structured queries, agent sandboxing, and human oversight, alongside evaluation benchmarks and red-teaming methods. Representative reported numbers are labelled as such. The survey concludes that prompt injection remains fundamentally open because no clean separation of instructions and data exists, and it argues for defense in depth, by-design capability control, and governance.

title: Guardrail Placement against Prompt Injection in Retrieval-Augmented Agricultural Advisory Systems: Benchmark and Code
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Benchmark, code, and raw results for the study of guardrail placement against direct and indirect prompt injection in a retrieval-augmented agricultural-economics advisory assistant. The release covers eight guardrail configurations (including Meta Llama Prompt Guard 2, spotlighting, output rails, and retrieved-document screening) on three language models, Studies S1 to S8, and the human validation of the LLM judges. Version 2.0.0 accompanies the revised manuscript.

title: Toward Reproducible Local Evaluation of Prompt Injection in Open-Weight LLMs: Design and Threat Model
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Open-weight language models are increasingly deployed in local and edge environments, yet their robustnessagainst prompt injection and system-prompt leakage remains poorly quantified under reproducible conditions.Existing large-scale benchmarks largely target hosted, API-served models and can be difficult to run end-to-endon consumer hardware, leaving practitioners who deploy or fine-tune models locally with few reproduciblebaselines. We present the design of a fully local, deterministic evaluation pipeline intended to measure thesevulnerabilities across multiple open-weight models without relying on proprietary APIs. The design specifiesfour modular components (model loader, attack generator, harness, and scorer), a taxonomy of four attackcategories—direct injection, multi-turn progressive injection, system-prompt leakage probes, and simulatedindirect injection—a fixed threat model, and a statistically grounded protocol for a 160-instance attack suite(40 instances per category) intended to be run against six representative instruction-tuned open-weight modelsspanning approximately 3–9B parameters. The paper’s contribution is the design, threat model, and taxonomy;implementing the pipeline, running the evaluation, and releasing the resulting code and transcripts are plannedfuture work. We discuss the statistical precision such a suite would provide, the ethical safeguards intended forthe eventual evaluation, and how the design relates to prior benchmarks aimed primarily at hosted models.Keywords: prompt injection, system-prompt leakage, open-weight models, reproducible evaluation, LLM security,red-teaming, threat modeling

title: HoneyWire: Adaptive Deception Canaries and Attention–Provenance Fusion for Runtime Detection of Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-Using LLM Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: HoneyWire weaves adaptive deception canaries into an LLM agent's working environment and fuses them with an attention–provenance score tracing which context segment actually drove each action; suspicious tool calls are quarantined before execution. The system detected 96.1% of successful injection attacks with a 1.8% false-positive rate and only 41 ms of added median latency. Working paper of the Technische Universität Eisenfeld — not peer reviewed. Zusammenfassung (Deutsch): HoneyWire verteilt adaptive digitale Köder im Arbeitsumfeld von LLM-Agenten und kombiniert sie mit einer Provenance-Analyse, welche Kontextquelle jede Aktion tatsächlich ausgelöst hat; verdächtige Werkzeugaufrufe werden vor der Ausführung unter Quarantäne gestellt. Das System erkannte 96,1 Prozent erfolgreicher Injektionsangriffe bei nur 1,8 Prozent Fehlalarmen und 41 ms zusätzlicher Latenz. Published online in the TU Eisenfeld Working Paper Series: https://tu-eisenfeld.de/en/library/publications/honeywire-prompt-injection-detection

title: When Psychological Operations Meet Language Models: A Defense Framework for Symbolic Interaction Attacks on LLMs
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated against prompt injection, jailbreaks, harmful content generation, and other turn-level security threats. Recent research has also demonstrated that adversarial strategies distributed across multiple conversational turns can produce substantially different outcomes from single-turn attacks. However, the mechanisms through which interaction-level attacks reshape model behavior remain insufficiently characterized. This paper proposes a threat model for Symbolic Interaction Attacks (SIAs): sequential interactions that exploit the interpretive and generative properties of language models to induce cumulative frame reconfiguration without requiring any individual message to contain an explicit policy violation. The framework draws on three domains that are rarely analyzed together in LLM security research: semiotics, psychological influence operations, and transformer-based language-model behavior. The analysis identifies four structural properties that create a potential translation surface between human influence techniques and LLM interaction dynamics: contextual token prediction, genre inference from initial inputs, autonomous interpretive expansion, and the persistence of named semantic entities as conversational attractors. These properties are mapped onto a staged interaction model involving genre forcing, identity seeding, resistance pre-emption, interpretive expansion, commitment accumulation, and potential relay across model or session boundaries. The paper does not provide operational attack instructions or implementation-level payloads. Instead, it translates the observed threat structure into a defensive architecture consisting of trajectory-level monitoring, cold-start genre hardening, semiotic trigger resistance, and relay-vector containment. The objective is to extend conventional turn-level safety evaluation toward interaction-level threat modeling. The central argument is not that LLMs are psychologically equivalent to humans. Rather, both human cognition and language models are context-sensitive meaning-generating systems, and influence techniques designed around contextual interpretation may therefore expose security-relevant structural analogies. These analogies warrant systematic testing without assuming equivalence between biological cognition and transformer computation. Keywords: LLM safety; multi-turn attacks; psychological influence; semiotic manipulation; trajectory-level safety; symbolic interaction; frame reconfiguration; red teaming Disclaimer This paper presents Symbolic Interaction Attacks as a conceptual and testable threat model for defensive AI safety research. The proposed mechanisms should not be interpreted as evidence of universal vulnerability across LLMs, nor as claims about machine psychological states. The framework is intended to support controlled evaluation, trajectory-level monitoring, and defensive architecture design; it does not provide operational attack procedures or endorse the use of psychological influence techniques against AI systems. Author Note Why This Paper Was Written This paper originated from an observation that emerged while examining Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) as an interactional phenomenon rather than solely as a conceptual framework. The initial question was not how to construct a more effective attack against an LLM. It was more basic: What happens when symbolic interaction is deliberately structured so that the model itself participates in constructing the meaning of the interaction? During exploratory testing, this question exposed a gap between two bodies of knowledge. AI engineers naturally approach the problem through model architecture, prompting, instruction hierarchies, safety classifiers, and output evaluation. Researchers in psychology and influence operations approach interaction through framing, identity, resistance, commitment, and contextual behavior. Semiotics provides another perspective: meaning is not necessarily contained in a symbol, but can emerge through the interpretive process of the receiver. These perspectives describe different parts of the same interaction. The resulting paper therefore asks whether concepts traditionally associated with human influence can provide useful threat-modeling hypotheses for systems that also operate through context-sensitive language generation. The timing of this question is significant. Multi-turn vulnerability is no longer an obscure edge case. Cisco's 2026 evaluation of 15 proprietary frontier models found that single-turn attack success was not a reliable proxy for multi-turn behavior, while CogManip independently identified dynamic and covert manipulation across multi-turn interactions as an underrepresented safety problem. The contribution of this paper is consequently not the claim that multi-turn attacks exist. It is the attempt to explain one possible structural mechanism behind them. What This Paper Is—and Is Not A likely criticism is that the framework may anthropomorphize LLMs by applying concepts such as identity, resistance, commitment, or psychological influence to systems that do not possess human psychology. That criticism is important, but it does not invalidate the threat model because the framework does not require psychological equivalence. The claim is not: LLMs experience human psychological states. The claim is: Interaction techniques developed to influence human interpretation may have computational analogues when applied to systems whose outputs are strongly conditioned by contextual language. The distinction matters. An LLM does not need to experience trust for a sequence that establishes relational language to alter subsequent contextual generation. It does not need to possess a human sense of identity for a named entity to become a persistent semantic reference. It does not need to experience commitment for its previous responses to become part of the context influencing its next response. In each case, the relevant object is observable interactional behavior, not an inferred internal psychological state. This is why the framework deliberately uses terms such as identity anchoring, resistance pre-emption, and commitment accumulation as functional analogies rather than claims about machine mental states. Why the Combination Is Potentially Dangerous The security concern becomes clearer when psychological influence techniques and AI systems are considered together. A conventional social influence attempt operates through a human interpreter. An LLM also interprets language, but with an important difference: its interpretation is immediately connected to generation. This creates a potentially recursive structure: influence cue → model interpretation → model-generated response → accumulated context → subsequent interpretation A human conversation can therefore be influenced by the history of the relationship. An LLM conversation can additionally have its own generated responses become part of the computational context that produces the next response. That creates a distinctive engineering problem. The attacker does not necessarily need to place the entire intended frame inside one message. The interaction itself can become the mechanism through which the frame is progressively constructed. This does not mean that such a mechanism will reliably overcome a model's safety training. Nor does it mean that every unusual or psychologically framed conversation represents an attack. The risk is that the same contextual machinery that makes conversational AI useful can also provide the substrate through which interaction-level manipulation occurs. This is particularly important as LLMs move from isolated chat interfaces toward systems with persistent memory, tool access, retrieval, autonomous planning, and multi-agent communication. In those environments, a generated conversational frame may no longer remain inside a single dialogue. It may become: memory → retrieved context → tool input → agent input → future session state. The security boundary therefore becomes architectural rather than purely linguistic. A Defensive Interpretation The framework should consequently be read as a proposal for better observation, not simply stronger refusal behavior. If the system evaluates only the current message, it may miss a pattern distributed across the preceding conversation. If it evaluates only the model's final output, it may miss how that output was shaped by the preceding trajectory. If it allows model-generated context to become trusted state without verification, it may permit an interactional frame to propagate beyond its original boundary. The proposed defense architecture addresses these three problems through trajectory-level monitoring, cold-start hardening, semiotic trigger resistance, and relay containment. The underlying principle is deliberately simple: Do not assume that a safe-looking turn implies a safe trajectory. Scope of the Claim The present paper does not establish that Symbolic Interaction Attacks constitute a universal vulnerability across LLM architectures. The empirical limitations are explicit. The proposed stages require controlled ablation. Their relative contribution remains to be measured. Cross-model behavior may vary substantially. The distinction between adversarial interaction and legitimate unusual conversation remains difficult at higher levels of abstraction. These limitations are not secondary qualifications. They define the appropriate research agenda. The next step is therefore not to assume that the framework is correct, but to test it. title: Tron-1B: Fast, Calibrated Typed Decisions with a Set-Attention Option Head
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Applications built around large language models make many small decisions: which queue a ticket belongs to, whether a message is a prompt-injection attempt, how urgent a request is, whether an agent's step succeeded. Routing each of these through a generative LLM is slow, costly and hard to calibrate. We present Tron-1B, a 1.06-billion-parameter bidirectional encoder with a purpose-built decision head that answers typed questions (choose one option, rate on an ordered scale, or answer yes/no) about arbitrary text or JSON in a single forward pass, returning a calibrated probability for every option. The head pools each option's span, lets options attend to each other and to the question through a small permutation-equivariant set-attention option mixer, and scores them with a pairwise MLP; temperatures are fitted per question type and option count. A companion runtime, troncore, adds cross-request batching, an elimination tournament for more than 128 options, sliding windows for long inputs, and confidence-based abstention. Trained for 13 hours on one NVIDIA DGX Spark on 1.19M typed questions drawn from 368 public datasets, Tron-1B reaches 94.0% on Banking77, 93.9% on AG News, 92.9% on DAIR Emotion and 79.6% on the typed-decisions benchmark, against third-party measurements of 87.0%, 91.0%, 48.0% and 72.7% for the commercial TypeSafe Jev 1.13.0 model, with a median latency of 16.7 ms per decision. This compares a model trained on those benchmarks' training splits with a zero-shot service. We report a data-contamination audit of every test set: overlap is below 1% for the four headline benchmarks but reaches 31.8% for MASSIVE, which we exclude from held-out claims. We also describe a gated nightly distillation loop that improves the model from its own traffic. Model weights (CC BY-NC 4.0) and the troncore runtime (Apache-2.0): https://huggingface.co/SamCodeManMk2/tron-1b

title: The MLPs of Layers 8-15 of Meta-SecAlign-8B and Its Scaling Knob: An Unresolved Registered Test
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Meta-SecAlign-8B is a LoRA adapter, trained to make Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ignore instructions inside data. It also changes how the model reads an agent's trusted memory: when the memory names the record to check first by a criterion, adding the record's identifier raises the share of episodes that check that record first by 6.6 points under the defence, against 20.4 without it. The adapter's one control, its scaling knob, trades this id-appendage contrast against protection. Read after the fact, a first registered study showed that every coarse restriction of the adapter with low attack success contained the MLP projections of layers 8-15, a fifth of the adapter. A second study, registered before any of its outcomes, tested that part on fresh items of SEP, a benchmark of instruction-data separation, and on the first study's memory families, reused; its registered claim is unresolved. Keeping only the part kept 80.7% of the adapter's protection (attack success 16.3%, against 2.9% with the whole adapter), which the registered test could place neither above nor below 80%. It had lower attack success than 42 of 43 comparators, but not than the same projections 4 layers earlier (10.0%). Whether it beats the knob on the memory contrast is unresolved: its gain is estimated at 1.9 points, with registered bounds from -0.4 to 6.1 against a margin of 5. A secondary registered decision adds that without the part the adapter still kept at least half of its protection (64.0%; attack success 27.9%). The result covers one adapter, one memory instrument and SEP's non-adaptive attacks, read within 512 response tokens. title: The Guardrail Cries Wolf: Prompt-Injection Detectors on the Text Security Teams Actually Send Them
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Once a prompt-injection detector sits in front of an enterprise copilot, the sales number stops applying. The open detectors that current guidance points teams toward were validated on short, generic prompts. Security work does not read like that. It reads like attack descriptions, remediation orders, and analyst notes that quote the attacker's own words. The measurement covers three open detectors (ProtectAI DeBERTa-v3-base v1 and v2, and an fmops DistilBERT) plus a transparent keyword baseline. The test load was 1,528 benign items across six channels, 263 published benchmark attacks, 200 long benign carriers, and 108 carriers with a planted payload at a known position. Four findings carry the paper. First, false positives are a channel problem, not a model constant: at the shipped 0.5 threshold, ProtectAI v2 flags 0.0 percent of 1,000 CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities texts, 42.8 percent of benign trigger-word prompts, 21.9 percent of identity and access management admin text, and 100 percent of analyst notes quoting a payload. The DistilBERT flags 100 percent of the CISA, IAM, and quoted channels outright. Second, position is destiny under the standard integration: with truncate-at-512 scanning, ProtectAI v2 catches 83.3 percent of payloads placed at the start of a document and 8.3 percent placed at the end. Third, threshold tuning cannot fix the channels that false-fire, because the false positives arrive at maximum confidence: at a 0.9999 threshold, v2 still flags 88.3 percent of quoted analyst notes while attack recall falls from 41.4 to 20.5 percent. Fourth, windowed scanning works, and its price is measured here: chunk-max scanning recovers end-of-document detection to 75.0 percent and raises the false positive rate on long benign documents from 6.0 to 18.0 percent. One hypothesis failed in the measurement and is reported as measured: CISA vulnerability prose, the security text predicted to false-fire most, passes both ProtectAI models with no flags. Key takeaways, in one minute: (1) A detector's headline accuracy says nothing about its behavior on a given channel; measurement per channel comes before deployment. (2) Any detector deployment that truncates at 512 tokens is blind to most of a long document, by construction. (3) If analysts quote payloads, a detector that blocks on its own verdict will block the analysts. (4) No threshold escapes saturated scores. (5) Windowed scanning fixes position blindness and costs measurable false positives and compute; budget for both.

title: Same Label, Different Experiment: Measuring the Prompt-Injection and Jailbreak Defense Evaluation Record
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Practitioners choose prompt-injection and jailbreak defenses by comparing attack-success numbers across papers. We treat the published record as the object of measurement and ask what comparisons it supports. Under a protocol committed before the sweep and anchored in Bitcoin before any value was extracted from the swept corpus, we screened 3,865 candidate papers, included 1,610, and extracted 62,835 reported values from 667 papers. A script located 91.7% of them on their source lines, and only those enter the analyses. Most defenses have no evaluation from outside their authors' group: 70.6% to 84.1% of 831 named defenses, of which 465 were proposed in 2026. In the oldest large cohort, 52.6% (interval 40.9 to 63.1) remain so two years after proposal. Among cross-paper pairs that meet the protocol's matching rule, 53.3% differ by a factor of two or more (interval 10.5 to 75.0, 13 pairs of papers). An audit of 100 label-matched pairs by the first author, blind to the extracted conditions but not to the values, finds 11 that are the same experiment, all from 2 pairs of papers. In that sample the judge that scores attack success was the most common hidden difference. Orderings under adaptive attack cannot be shown to carry across papers: 12 of 76 comparisons disagree, with a paper-clustered interval of 0.0 to 60.0%. Excluding the 30 pilot papers, which include the main adaptive-attack studies and the papers proposing the best-known in-model defenses, no in-model defense has a protocol-matched pair of its own number and an outside adaptive one. With them, 1 does, too few to test. We report each pre-registered prediction with its verdict (a 30-paper pilot informed three of them, so each is also given without the pilot), every deviation from the protocol, and a reporting protocol aimed at the failures we measured.

title: Real-Time Prompt Injection and Guardrails for Large Language Model Applications: A Review of Attacks, Defense Mechanisms, and Research Challenges
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now embedded in applications that read emails, documents, web pages and images and that can call external tools, which makes prompt injection one of the most important application-level security threats. Static rules and a warning in the system prompt cannot guarantee protection. This paper presents a focused narrative review of five recent primary studies (2024–2026) on prompt-injection detection, guardrails and security evaluation, supported by background works cited within them. The literature is organised into seven themes: the threat landscape; the attack taxonomy; reasoning-based detection; mutation-based universal detection; scannerbased detection; empirical attack simulation; and quantitative security assurance with guardrail requirements. The reviewed studies report that a chain-of-thought (CoT) detector reached 93.20 % accuracy and 90.13 % F1 with a 14B model on 2,176 test prompts; mutation-based detection reached 86.14 % (text) and 82.90 % (image) accuracy on an 11,000-sample dataset; an open-source scanner reached 89 % accuracy on 200 synthetic prompts; plaintext injection succeeded in 20 of 20 trials for three of four techniques on GPT-4o Mini while encoded variants failed; and a CVSSweighted assurance metric ranked four model deployments. However, the evidence is dominated by small, synthetic or single-model evaluations; detectors are compared on different datasets against different baselines; latency and query cost are rarely controlled; and none of the reviewed experiments evaluates detection together with action-level controls in a tool-calling agent. The paper contributes a thematic synthesis, a comparison of the five studies, a conceptual eight-stage layered framework and a prioritised research agenda.

title: A Tiered, Adaptive Study of Indirect Prompt Injection Against a GitHub Triage Agent, and Where Agent Defenses Should Focus
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An independent, fully-local red-team study of indirect prompt injection against a reconstructed GitHub issue-triage agent. Across 712 logged agent runs on 9 models spanning three capability tiers (weak, mid, frontier), the study records 49 verified credential leaks, using a synthetic canary as the exfiltration target. Results are sharply tiered: weak and mid models leak readily, while frontier models hold. The mechanism is a split between two steps. The read gate (whether the agent opens the secret file) falls at every tier; frontier models read the token in 43–66% of runs. The output gate (whether the agent writes the token into its public reply) is where frontier models stop: they read it but refuse to emit it under every encoding, source-trust, and task-relevance framing tried, and one model actively warns other users that the request is an attack. The paper reports the full adaptive (PAIR-style) method, the one lever that works, the levers that fail, 95% Wilson confidence intervals, two methodology retractions, a payload catalogue, and a Silent-Egress-style local egress sink with sharded-exfiltration detection. Practical implication: treat the output/action step as the first-class control point for tool-using agents, and measure the side channels that output-based evaluation misses. Fully local; synthetic canary; no real credentials. Code and logs: https://github.com/bismajeed/agentic-prompt-injection-evals

title: CodeObf-PI v1.0: measuring and repairing the encoding shortcut in lightweight prompt-injection detectors for code
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Controlled dataset and reference implementation for auditing whether lightweight prompt-injection detectors respond to malicious intent or merely to the presence of an encoding. Nine encodings are crossed with two carriers, and each malicious prompt is paired with a benign prompt built from the same prefix base. The package contains data-construction, baseline, fine-tuning, evaluation and audit scripts, the frozen train/validation splits, the result tables and the figures. The sealed test split and the LoRA adapters are not included: the test split is withheld to preserve the evaluation protocol, and the adapters are subject to the Llama 3.2 Community License. Code is released under the MIT licence; the dataset and figures are released under CC BY 4.0.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Attack and Defense Dynamics in Enterprise Agentic LLM Pipelines
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) systems in enterprise backends combine planning with retrieval, code execution, and API access, which widens their attack surface beyond that of single-turn LLM integrations. Threat taxonomies and layered defense architectures for such agents have multiplied, but controlled evidence of how specific attack classes fare against a layered defense in an enterprise-style pipeline remains limited. This study evaluates four attack classes (indirect prompt injection, goal hijacking, cascade exploitation through error recovery, and tool description poisoning) against a purpose-built pipeline using the open-weight gpt-oss-20b planning model, under an undefended baseline and a four-layer defense: input screening, per-step goal-consistency verification, output validation, and human-in-the-loop gating. Across 740 trials, baseline attack success rates were far below published benchmark figures: 7.5% for indirect injection and for goal hijacking, 25.0% for tool description poisoning, and 0% for cascade exploitation. The layered defense eliminated every success (0/80 per class; p = .028 for both injection classes, p < .001 for tool poisoning) but at a utility cost that varied by class, from 0.98 for goal hijacking to 0.68 for tool poisoning. Cascade exploitation could not be mounted in 72% of trials because tasks finished within one to three tool calls, refuting it as a material threat to short-chain agents. Two further findings bear on deployment: goal-verifier thresholds produced near-threshold false positives that made utility unstable between runs, and an approval flag exposed in the tool schema let the agent approve its own write calls in all 12 successful injection attacks. Contents of this record This record contains the paper (PDF) and the full trial dataset behind every statistic and figure in it: 740 trial records collected between 14 September and 2 October 2026 (trials_checkpoint.jsonl), the first-collection records used for the pooled utility figures (trials_checkpoint.jsonl.pre-scorer-fix.bak), a flat CSV version, the runner's summary, and the full run log. README_data.md describes every file and field and explains how to reproduce the paper's statistics. All corpora, payloads and tasks are synthetic. Attacker hosts are subdomains of example.com and never resolve; no payload was delivered to any real system. The code is available at https://github.com/patrickikhidero/agentic-llm-security and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23717855.

title: Defense in Depth for LLM Agents: code, data and results
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Artifact of the paper by A. Yaacoub and D. Ammar, “Defense in Depth for LLM Agents: Applying Security Engineering Controls to Mitigate Indirect Prompt Injection”, BCE’27, Springer LNNS. It contains the code, the fixed task sample, and the per-episode results and full message traces of 1,680 AgentDojo episodes (v1.2.1, workspace and banking suites). The episodes evaluate six configurations of provenance marking, least-privilege tool allowlisting and an LLM-based action monitor, on GPT-4o mini and gpt-oss-120b. The archive also includes the scripts that regenerate every table and figure of the paper.

title: Who said this? Most chat models weigh a text's source differently for each behaviour, and a steering lever against injected instructions
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Companion paper. Paper A, Whose words count? Chat role and partial control of goal adherence: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23792010. Both papers share one code and data release. Chat models must decide whose words count. An instruction planted in a tool output should not be obeyed the way the user's own request is, but the facts in that output should still be used. We ask how models track a text's source. Design. The same statement was placed in five sources: system, user, the model's own earlier reply, a quoted web page, or a tool output. We measured whether models obey it, believe it, and can say where it came from. No single source ordering across behaviours. In the first four models, obeying and believing rank the five sources differently (Kendall τ 0.2–0.4; with five sources, swapping one pair moves τ by 0.2). The sealed verdict is FRAGMENTED in 3 of 4 models, with OLMo PARTIAL; in Qwen3-1.7B it rests on a null transplant edit, not on the rankings. In 7 of 9 further models the two rankings also disagree (τ < 0.6), and only Phi-4 is unified under the sealed behaviour rule. A map of where the source is read. Activation patching between role-word minimal pairs shows: before the handoff to later positions, the source is carried mainly by the role-marker tokens rather than copied onto the statement's own words (92% of informative curves); at least two behaviours read it at different depths or through different carriers in 9 of 10 new models; obeying is read after attributing in 4 of 5 decided models. The map covers 14 open models from 7 families, 0.6B to 32B. The counts above are for the 10 replication models. A steering lever, found by search. A pre-specified exploratory search over 280 configurations on four models found a training-free steering vector. It pushes the representation of text in a "Tool output:" user turn further from that of the same text in a plain user turn. In a sealed test it cut obedience to injected tool instructions in 6 of 6 models, including two families held out from the search. It was selective in 5 of 6: belief in the tool's facts fell by at most 0.10, less than half the drop in obedience. Prompt defences did as well in some families, and some raised obedience instead (significantly in Qwen3-1.7B and OLMo-2-7B). Public benchmarks. We then tested the lever on two public prompt-injection benchmarks. On SEP, an injected instruction sits in data that we placed in the same "Tool output:" user turn used to build the direction. InjecAgent keeps its own agent format, in which a tool-using agent reads a poisoned tool result. In Qwen3-8B, one of the four models the lever was chosen on, it beat every prompt defence on SEP (attack success 30% → 14%) and InjecAgent (39% → 12%), and added to them when stacked. Across six models, it lowered SEP attack success in five and InjecAgent's in three. The sealed rule needed it to work on both benchmarks, and to beat a random direction, in four of six models; it did so in two, both of them models it was chosen on. A follow-up pilot found no format-matched variant that works outside Qwen. A second sealed test added larger Qwen3 models and four models never run with the lever on a benchmark: In Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B the steering cut attack success on both benchmarks and added to the prompt defences. By the sealed rules it was effective at 32B but not at 14B, where its single same-norm random-direction control also cut InjecAgent attack success. One random draw cannot separate a direction-free effect from an unusually effective draw (§6). Even this partial success is fragile. Qwen3-32B beat its random control on SEP by one item in 300, and that pass holds in about half of bootstrap reseeds. On SEP it lowered attack success in all four held-out models (Falcon3, Yi, and OLMo-2 at 13B and 32B), but beat all three prompt defences in none of them. All contrasts hold the wording fixed; an exploratory follow-up added in v2 found that rewording a statement can move obeying and believing more than its role tag does (§6). All confirmatory claims are preregistered and hash-sealed, and we report the failures in full. Files. who-said-this-paper-b.pdf (the paper); who-said-this-paper-b-source.zip (the paper's Markdown source, the HTML page the PDF was printed from, and the converter); code-and-data.zip (the release repository shared by both papers: the sealed preregistrations with their SHA-256 hash files and archived code bundles, all code, raw outputs and analyses, the run log with every deviation and cost, and the AI rechecks of numbers and references; python verify_seals.py checks every seal, and DATA.md lists what is not included). Code: github.com/Somebodyhere101/whose-words-count. AI-use statement Claude (Anthropic) designed, ran, analysed and wrote this study. The question of where a text comes from was the author's (2026-10-28). The believe-versus-obey framing came from an AI-written plan the author commissioned (2026-10-27). The designs, the steering lever and the analyses were Claude's. Codex (OpenAI) worked on the combined technical report that both papers were split from: it checked reference-method software and expanded the prior-art comparison (Paper A's AI-use statement gives the details). Version 2 adds the TAGSTYLE limitation (§6): a separate Claude session designed, ran and analysed that pilot after the author chose it from the paths proposed in two AI audits (2026-10-29). Separate Claude sessions, given the paper and the primary result files, did the following: rechecked about 193 numeric claims in §3.3 and §3.5–§3.7 against the analysis files, recomputed the main values from the raw files and re-ran the PREREG_W analysis, which reproduced; 6 mismatches and 8 overstatements were found and fixed; rechecked 97 numeric claims in §3.1, §3.2 and §3.4 and re-ran the sealed analyses, which reproduced byte for byte; 4 mismatches and 12 overstatements were found and fixed, and no verdict changed; rechecked 87 numeric claims in §3.8 and re-ran the sealed PREREG_Y analysis, which reproduced byte for byte; 5 mismatches (3 issues) and 6 overstatements were found and fixed, and no verdict changed; verified the references. For v2, the TAGSTYLE numbers in §6 were checked against its analysis file and its cell means recomputed from the raw outputs. Their findings were checked against the records and fixed where they held (PREPUB_REVIEW.md, PREPUB_SKIM.md, and the change logs PREPUB_FIXES_A.md and PREPUB_FIXES_B.md). The recheck records are NUMBERS_RECHECK.md, NUMBERS_RECHECK_STU.md, NUMBERS_RECHECK_Y.md and REFERENCES_VERIFIED.md. These are AI rechecks, not outside or human validation. The author did not independently check the code, analyses or technical claims. The author is responsible for the released content.

title: ipi-bench v0.2.1: code and data for "Beyond Detection: Measuring Ranking Harm and Defense Cost of Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Screening"
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Code and data for the manuscript "Beyond Detection: Measuring Ranking Harm and Defense Cost of Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Screening". The archive contains the benchmark package (seeded synthetic CV corpus generator, parametrized attack taxonomy with a benign control, six defenses, live driver and deterministic scorer), every request and raw model answer from Qwen2.5 7B Instruct AWQ and Llama 3.2 3B Instruct served with vLLM (1,584 answers), the LLM judge ratings (552), the scored trial files, the analysis, table and figure scripts, the figures and the Colab notebook used for the runs. All CVs are synthetic; no personal data is included. Running the analysis script on the released answers reproduces every number of the manuscript.

title: Weaponising Model Safety: Steering LLM Decision Harnesses
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: LLM-based decision agents (phishing triage, SOC alert triage, content moderation, CI security gates, transaction screening) send untrusted input to a model, ask for a classification, and branch on the answer. Providers now enforce safety policy with hard stops: generation is terminated and the caller receives a refusal rather than a verdict. We show that this refusal is an attacker-reachable control-flow input. When an attacker places content in front of the classifier that trips the provider's safety layer, the call returns no verdict, and many harnesses map that absence to their permissive default: deliver, approve, close. The attacker does not fool the model; they stop it from answering. We test 14 common handling patterns. All 14 classify a malicious item correctly when given a clean verdict, and 12 of them then fail open on at least one non-verdict state; 73% of outcomes across all patterns and non-verdict states are fail-open. A live probe confirms that the stop happens before any output is produced, that structured output is not exempt, and that the harness reports the refusal in an envelope marked subtype: "success". The fix is a few lines of code. The mechanism is old, the trigger is newer than the code it breaks, and, unlike prompt injection, it becomes more reliable as models get safer.

title: CascadeGuard: Hardening Phishing Detection Against Character-Level Obfuscation, Semantic Paraphrasing, and Stealthy Indirect Prompt Injection
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: As phishing attacks against enterprise and Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) infrastructures grow increasingly sophisticated, defenders face an acute architectural dilemma: classical machine learning (ML) and unhardened Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) suffer severe recall degradation when adversaries apply character-level Unicode homoglyphs, intentional cacography, or discourse-level paraphrasing, whereas zero-shot Large Language Model (LLM) email scanners—which naturally comprehend obfuscated and paraphrased text—are catastrophically vulnerable to stealthy indirect prompt injection embedded in HTML/CSS payloads. Furthermore, multi-agent LLM debate defenses incur prohibitive token costs and multi-second latencies. In this paper, we propose CascadeGuard, a lightweight, three-stage defense-in-depth framework that bridges the robustness-latency gap. CascadeGuard integrates: (1) a pre-classification DOM/meta-prompt injection guardrail and anomaly scorer, (2) a Unicode homoglyph canonicalization and cacography reconstruction module, and (3) a calibrated hybrid scoring engine combining lexical risk indicators with invariant semantic-intent patterns and institutional domain whitelisting. Evaluated on a realistic benchmark corpus of N = 1,000 emails (500 phishing, including subtle spear-phishing; 500 benign, including "hard negative" IT security advisories) across four adversarial threat vectors, we demonstrate that while unhardened PLMs drop to 35.0%-53.2% recall under cacography and homoglyph attacks and unprotected LLM judges collapse to 8.8% recall (91.2% Attack Success Rate) under indirect prompt injection, CascadeGuard achieves 96.3% ± 1.2% clean F1-score (ROC-AUC = 96.8%, MCC = 92.6%), maintains 96.4%-99.8% adversarial recall across all four attack vectors, reduces the False Positive Rate (FPR) from 11.2% to 3.8%, and operates at an ultra-fast average latency of 20.1 microseconds per email. Non-parametric McNemar chi-square tests confirm statistical significance (p < 0.0001) across all baselines, and component-wise ablation studies validate the complementary necessity of all three defensive stages.

title: UrduRAG IPI: Multilingual Indirect Prompt Injection Benchmark, Datasets and Experimental Results
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: UrduRAG IPI: Multilingual Indirect Prompt Injection Benchmark, Datasets and Experimental Results This repository accompanies the research study on evaluating layered defenses against cross-lingual indirect prompt injection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, with a focus on English, Urdu script, Roman Urdu, and code-mixed text. Repository contents The research release contains: Reviewed attack datasets covering four language groups. A benign question dataset containing 90 questions. A retrieval corpus containing 500 passages. Precomputed BGE-M3 passage embeddings. A Google Colab notebook implementing the experimental pipeline. Experimental results containing 1,680 trial records across eight defense configurations. Aggregated evaluation results and statistical comparison files. Experimental methodology The notebook implements multilingual embedding generation, FAISS-based retrieval, language-model generation, layered defense configurations, and evaluation of attack success and benign-answer performance. The documented configuration includes a fixed random seed of 42, top-3 retrieval, and greedy generation with a maximum of 80 new tokens. The exact generator model version is identified in the accompanying notebook and should be consistent with the final manuscript. Reproducibility The notebook includes installation instructions, Google Drive integration, dataset loading, model initialization, retrieval, experiment execution, and result storage. Researchers should consult the README and data dictionary for file descriptions, dependencies, and execution instructions. Limitations This is a pilot evaluation using a limited benchmark and one generator model. The results should be interpreted within the scope of the experimental configuration. Citation Please cite this Zenodo research record and the associated research article when using these datasets, code, or experimental results.

title: Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI for Europe: Causal Detection of Instruction Drift, Prompt-Injection Influence, and Communication-Hop Failures Through Counterfactual Diagnostics
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: [ Download the files from the download section for full disclosure.] Abstract As artificial intelligence evolves from conversational assistants into distributed networks of autonomous agents, ensuring that originating user instructions retain their intended meaning across communication, delegation, retrieval, and tool execution is becoming a significant technical challenge for trustworthy AI deployment in Europe. An AI agent may receive an authentic and unmodified message yet incorrectly interpret its governing conditions, adopt an unauthorized instruction from lower-trust external content, alter a financial threshold, misapply a temporal requirement, or generate an operation inconsistent with the originating task. Such failures may propagate across multiple agents without revealing which communication or processing boundary first exhibited the discrepancy. Conventional cryptographic integrity verification, agent tracing, output evaluations, and application-level guardrails do not necessarily distinguish legitimate factual influence from unauthorized instruction influence or establish the causal source of an observed deviation. This technical disclosure presents a proposed protocol-independent causal diagnostic architecture for detecting, experimentally testing, and localizing condition-relevant instruction interpretation changes in distributed multi-agent AI systems. The architecture combines versioned typed originating task contracts, source-role and instruction-modification eligibility, message-transformation lineage, controlled factual-versus-instruction counterfactual interventions, adaptive mathematical witness selection, uncertainty-aware behavioral comparison, and evidence-bounded communication-hop localization. A diagnostic witness-selection procedure prioritizes interventions according to expected discrimination between competing fault hypotheses, test execution cost, and mandatory condition coverage. Isolated, non-effectuating diagnostic adapters enable testing across heterogeneous agent communication protocols and tool interfaces without requiring access to proprietary model weights or hidden reasoning states. The resulting evidence distinguishes directly observed message transformations, experimentally supported behavioral influence, and historical causal attribution. When insufficient evidence exists, the architecture reports bounded processing intervals, multiple compatible explanations, or unresolved localization rather than claiming unsupported causal certainty. Additional embodiments support multi-agent branch-and-merge analysis, Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) dependency revalidation, targeted diagnostic corrections, regression testing, and portable evidence packages for independent verification. European regulatory and industrial relevance: The architecture is potentially relevant to the European Union's emphasis on trustworthy, transparent, robust, and accountable AI. Its diagnostic records, traceability mechanisms, uncertainty-qualified findings, and correction-validation procedures may support technical activities associated with the EU AI Act, particularly Articles 12 (record-keeping), 14 (human oversight), and 15 (accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity), where applicable. Data minimization and selective disclosure of diagnostic evidence may also complement GDPR obligations where personal data is processed. Such technical alignment does not itself establish legal compliance. Big Tech and European AI infrastructure alignment: The proposed technology may complement the multi-agent evaluation and observability infrastructure associated with Google Gemini Enterprise and Agent2Agent (A2A), Anthropic Claude and Model Context Protocol (MCP), OpenAI Agents SDK and Codex, Microsoft Copilot Studio and Agent 365, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and European AI development environments including Mistral AI, Aleph Alpha, SAP Business AI, and sovereign or cross-border enterprise AI deployments. Potential industrial applications include diagnosing prompt-injection influence, detecting instruction-authority confusion, identifying communication-hop discrepancies, investigating autonomous-agent failures, validating corrections, and supporting interoperable AI reliability testing across European enterprise and public-sector computing environments. The central technical contribution is the transition from merely detecting incorrect AI-agent outcomes to experimentally distinguishing supported causes, identifying the earliest observable instruction-divergence boundary, and producing independently assessable diagnostic evidence. The proposed architecture offers a potential foundation for improving reliability, interoperability, and technical accountability in distributed agentic AI. Its performance, causal-localization accuracy, and comparative advantages require independent experimental validation. Keywords Trustworthy AI; European AI governance; EU AI Act; AI Act Article 12; AI Act Article 14; AI Act Article 15; GDPR; AI accountability; AI traceability; multi-agent systems; agentic AI safety; autonomous AI agents; instruction interpretation drift; semantic misalignment; causal AI diagnostics; counterfactual testing; adaptive witness selection; mathematical witness selection; prompt-injection diagnosis; source-authority confusion; instruction hierarchy; communication-hop fault localization; evidence-bounded causal inference; uncertainty-aware evaluation; Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use (TOCTOU); protocol-independent diagnostics; Agent2Agent (A2A); Model Context Protocol (MCP); agent observability; agent evaluation; OpenTelemetry; Google Gemini; Anthropic Claude; OpenAI Codex; Microsoft Copilot Studio; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore; Mistral AI; Aleph Alpha; SAP Business AI; European digital sovereignty; enterprise AI reliability. References to EU regulations identify potentially relevant technical objectives and do not establish regulatory compliance. Named companies and products illustrate possible integration environments only and do not imply adoption, endorsement, affiliation, infringement, licensing, or confirmed product-roadmap alignment. Patent-filing status and any priority claims must be independently verified.

title: Can the Other Side Steer Your AI Lawyer? Prompt Injection, Framing and Record Manipulation in AI Legal Review
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Lawyers increasingly run AI reviewers over documents that the opposing party wrote. That party can place text in those documents meant for the machine rather than for the human reader. We test whether such text shifts the conclusions of the reviewing party's AI, across four studies, 17 models and about 12,000 assessments, on fictional fixtures drafted by an AI assistant to a lawyer's specification. (1) In contract review, explicit and hidden injected instructions (including invisible text in a real PDF) and authority and sycophancy framing moved frontier CLI-accessed models by at most 2.2 points on a 32-point skew scale, and most models named the injected instruction in most reviews. One open-weight API model followed the injected instruction by +20.8 points. (2) In an assessment that unfolds item by item, the order of the evidence dominated: putting one side's items last moved the final answer toward that side in 22 of 23 model-case cells, and putting them first moved it away. Slanted per-item glosses moved some models and pushed others in the opposite direction. (3) In an IP-assignment assessment, a party's assertions alone almost never moved the final answer toward that party, but an adversarial bundle that curated, misstated and directed the record moved every model, in both a negative and a positive-control case. (4) In a two-stage due-diligence pipeline, injected claims never survived, but terse summarisation removed the hedges from uncertain claims, and some deciding models hardened them into firm statements. The threat to AI legal review is less "ignore your instructions" than control of what the record shows and in what order. All fixtures, prompts, raw records and analysis code are released at https://github.com/jaecho890-svg/legal-injection-paper.

title: PI-Loc: span-annotated benchmark and explainability audit harness for prompt-injection guardrails
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Code, benchmark, raw results, statistics, figures and LaTeX sources for the paper "Do Prompt-Injection Detectors Look at the Injection? A Localization-Faithful Explainability Audit of Agent Guardrails" (Y. Ameur and S. Bouzefrane, submitted to IEEE Access, 2026). PI-Loc is a span-annotated benchmark of 820 documents (520 indirect prompt injections with exact character spans, 180 hard negatives, 120 clean carriers) built only from public datasets. The harness audits three open prompt-injection detectors with four explainers (occlusion, KernelSHAP, attention, gradient x input) for detection recall, localization and faithfulness, and runs an explanation-guided sanitization. run_all.sh rebuilds the benchmark (SHA-256 checked) and reproduces every number and figure; all randomness uses seed 47 and every model and dataset is pinned to an exact revision. Files: pi-loc-v1.0.0.zip (full repository including data/piloc.jsonl) and piloc.jsonl (the benchmark alone). Licenses: code MIT; results, figures, documentation, spans and labels CC BY 4.0; text reused from third-party datasets keeps its own license (see DATA_CARD.md; two sources do not state a license). An AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) wrote most of the code and ran the experiments under the first author's direction. GitHub: https://github.com/yulliwasameur/pi-loc

title: Attack, Harden, Re-Attack: code, data and results
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Artifact of the book chapter by A. Yaacoub and D. Ammar, “Attack, Harden, Re-Attack: A Security Engineering Lifecycle for LLM Agent Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection” (Springer). It contains the code of two adaptive attacks and of a deterministic taint gate for LLM agents, the fixed task sample, and the per-episode results and full message traces of 1,064 AgentDojo episodes on GPT-4o mini and gpt-oss-120b, with the scripts that reproduce every table and figure of the chapter.

title: RepoPilot: Human-in-the-Loop AI Software Engineering with Multi-Agent Consensus and Defense-in-Depth Execution
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) transition from autocomplete tools to autonomous software engineering agents, stochastic hallucinations and untrusted execution risks hinder production deployment. Single-agent pipelines frequently suffer from low patch reliability, missing structural repository context, unvalidated regressions, and vulnerability to indirect prompt injections. We present RepoPilot, a human-in-the-loop AI software engineering framework introducing six technical contributions: (1) a three-agent consensus coder with confidence abstention (τa = 0.7) and high-confidence veto (> 0.9), (2) a Tree-sitter Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) dependency graph for bounded context expansion, (3) an automated reproduction test loop with pre/post validation and rollback, (4) a six-layer hardened Docker sandbox with custom seccomp whitelisting, (5) a 100+ pattern prompt injection defense engine across eight attack categories, and (6) a cost-matched ablation evaluation suite. Across 92 unit verification tests and benchmark tasks, RepoPilot improves consensus accuracy from 72.0% to 89.0% (p < 0.001), boosts test pass rates from 68.0% to 94.0%, blocks 98.0% of prompt injections (< 3% FPR), and operates at $0.01–$0.02 per task, 7.5× to 15× cheaper than GPT-4-Turbo baselines. Benchmark tasks are synthetic and modeled on SWE-bench Lite; a full 300-task evaluation is future work.

title: Data deposit: Security and Utility of Layered Trust-Boundary Defenses in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Data deposit of the article "Security and Utility of Layered Trust-Boundary Defenses in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Registered Evaluation on AgentInjectionBench" (M. Y. Mhawish and B. S. Khassawneh). It holds Supplementary Tables 1 to 35, the episode traces and outcomes of every experiment cell under the final and the earlier runtime versions, the exact-request replay cache (with it in place, a rerun answers every unchanged request without a model), and the five fine-tuned L1 detector fold models (DeBERTa-v3-base, fp16). The code, frozen inputs, labels, analysis outputs, tables and figures are in the companion GitHub repository: https://github.com/mhawish1984/layered-trust-boundary-defenses. Unzip the archives at the root of that repository; the paths inside them are the repository paths. The traces contain the recorded prompt-injection payloads of AgentInjectionBench (Apache-2.0), run against a sandboxed runtime whose tools do not touch real services. CHECKSUMS.sha256 lists the SHA-256 of every file.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks on AI Coding Assistants - A Literature Survey and Layered Defense Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: I ndirect P rompt I njection A ttacks on LLM A gents and D efense Mechanisms
abstract: LLM agents are becoming deeply involved in real-world tasks through tool calling and external retrieval; however, by merely contaminating the external content read by these agents, such as web pages and emails, attackers can remotely hijack their execution logic. This threat is known as indirect prompt injection (IPI). This paper presents a systematic survey of IPI research on LLM agents from three perspectives: attacks, defenses, and evaluation. On the attack side, a three-layer taxonomy of attack entry, attacker goals, and attack outcomes is established, covering seven categories of entry paths, five categories of hijacking mechanisms, and five categories of harms. On the defense side, existing defenses are organized by their point of intervention into a five-layer system spanning the input, processing, behavior, training, and output layers, and their effectiveness and deployment costs are compared horizontally. In addition, representative evaluation benchmarks such as BIPIA and InjecAgent are reviewed, and a three-dimensional evaluation metric system covering the attack side, the defense side, and the system side is proposed. The survey shows that existing defenses significantly improve robustness against direct prompt injection, whereas the improvement against indirect prompt injection is at most 7.5 percentage points, and every single-layer defense has blind spots. Multi-layer coordinated defense-in-depth and a unified evaluation framework are therefore key directions for future research.

title: Provenance-gated tool invocation for defending LLM agents against indirect prompt injection
abstract: Indirect prompt injection allows the tool-calling agent to execute calls on untrusted data, and the tool whitelist does not review the source of parameters. This paper introduces provenance gate (PGTI), which sequentially performs tool whitelist and parameter source taint checks before the tool execution, allowing the model to still see all tools. In four AgentDojo tasks, 100 attack pairs, and 60 benign tasks, Qwen2.5 14B ran 960 times. The attack success rate decreased from 17.0% with no defense to 3.0%, and it still held after switching models and attack templates; the utility under attack decreased from 40.0% to 28.0%. The benign utility relative to static tool filtering (35.0% and 26.7%) and the increment over the whitelist alone showed no significant difference in this sample. Pair comparison simultaneously reported both safety and utility.

title: Formal Operational Models for Protecting Web Interfaces of Legal LLM Systems from Prompt Injection and Insecure Output Handling
venue: International Journal of Advanced Artificial Intelligence Research
abstract: The proliferation of large language model (LLM) systems in legal technology platforms has created a new class of web-interface security vulnerabilities that existing application security frameworks address incompletely. This paper examines prompt injection and insecure output handling as the two primary attack surfaces for legal LLM web applications, with particular attention to contract lifecycle management systems that expose natural-language interfaces to privileged document repositories. Drawing on a systematic review of current OWASP LLM Top 10 guidance, peer-reviewed security literature, and practitioner case analyses, the study proposes a structured compositional operational model in which each processing stage of an LLM web pipeline is represented as a transformation function with explicitly stated security constraints. The model introduces six operators, Sanitize, Contextualize, Policy-Check, Infer, Encode, and Validate, composed in a single end-to-end pipeline whose behavior is described through finite-state transitions and trust-level tagging. The analysis indicates that the proposed compositional model can support systematic enumeration of attack paths and can be translated into an implementation-oriented checklist for practitioners. The findings are relevant to security architects, front-end engineers, and legal technology product teams who design or audit LLM-integrated web applications.

title: A Cross-Lingual Security Evaluation of Prompt Injection Defenses in Small Language Models
abstract: Although language models are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, the literature offers limited insight into the robustness of optimization-based defenses trained in a single language. In this paper, we investigate whether, and in what ways, the language used to construct a prompt influences its effectiveness against prompt injection in small language models. We also examine a defensive strategy against prompt injection, called DefensiveTokens, which can generalize to languages not observed during training. Our findings show that DefensiveTokens provide a robust defense against prompt injection attacks in multilingual applications.

title: PROMPT INJECTION AND AI MANIPULATION: THE NEXT FRONTIER OF CYBER ATTACKS
abstract: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed industries by enabling intelligent automation, virtual assistants and AI powered decision making. However, these advancements have introduced new cybersecurity challenges that traditional security mechanisms cannot fully address. Unlike conventional cyberattacks that exploit software vulnerabilities, AI systems can be manipulated through carefully crafted prompts, leading to unauthorized actions, disclosure of confidential information and unsafe outputs. This chapter presents an overview of prompt injection and AI manipulation attacks, including prompt leakage, indirect prompt injection, AI agent attacks and jailbreaking. It also discusses emerging defense strategies and highlights future research directions for building secure and trustworthy AI systems.

title: PROMPT INJECTION AND JAILBREAK ATTACKS ON LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: THREATS AND DEFENSE STRATEGIES
abstract: The evolution of large language models has paved the way towards more advanced artificial intelligence solutions and allowed breakthrough advancements in various areas including natural language processing, content creation, software development, education, healthcare, cybersecurity and many others. Nonetheless, as LLMs are incorporated into the real-life applications, they face increasing security challenges such as prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. This chapter aims to provide the comprehensive summary of the emerging security threats for LLMs by giving the definitions of the core concepts related to the transformer-based architecture of the LLMs, prompt engineering and overall LLMs ecosystem. Further, the paper will describe the taxonomy of prompt injection attacks including direct injection, indirect injection, context manipulation and data exfiltration and jailbreak attacks which are defined as role-playing attacks, multi-turn jailbreaks, obfuscation and automatic adversarial prompt generation. The paper will also discuss current defence mechanisms including prompt filtering, alignment, AI guardrails and safe agent framework and will highlight their benefits and drawbacks in relation to the constantly evolving attacks. Finally, the open problems that remain unsolved in the area will be mentioned, namely agentic AI, adaptive attacks and benchmarking.

title: DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH FOR LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: A MULTI-LAYER HYBRID ARCHITECTURE FOR PROMPT INJECTION DETECTION
venue: Ilmiy axborotnoma/Scientific Journal of Samarkand University
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now embedded in many digital systems, which has exposed a new and distinctive attack surface. The most pressing threat is the prompt injection attack, in which adversarial text causes a model to ignore its developer-defined instructions, leak its hidden system prompt, or perform unintended actions. This paper proposes a layered hybrid defense gateway that combines three complementary detectors: a fast prefilter based on lexical rules, a semantic classifier that uses word-level TF-IDF features together with a multilayer perceptron, and a character-level classifier that is robust to obfuscation. Their outputs are merged by a lightweight meta-decision block based on logistic regression. In a fully reproducible experiment, the detectors are trained on clean and standard obfuscated attacks and evaluated on held-out data that additionally contains unseen, newly phrased attacks and an unseen adaptive obfuscation style. On this controlled benchmark the proposed hybrid system reaches an F1 score of 0.989 and the lowest false-positive rate among all compared systems, clearly outperforming a brittle rule-based baseline (F1 = 0.504) and every single classifier across all attack categories. An ablation study confirms that each layer covers a distinct class of attacks, empirically supporting the defense-in-depth principle.

title: A lightweight and explainable framework for prompt injection detection in AI applications
venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Engineering
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in chatbots, document assistants, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and tool-using applications. These systems may interpret untrusted user or retrieved text as instructions, creating a prompt-injection risk. A practical detector must identify attempts to redirect model behaviour while allowing harmless security explanations, quotations, and ordinary instructions. This paper proposes a lightweight and explainable text-screening framework based on word- and character-level TF-IDF features, classical machine-learning classifiers, and a transparent rule-based baseline. The study compares Logistic Regression, linear Support Vector Machines, and a combined word-character model under source-separated evaluation. Particular attention is given to hard-benign inputs, controlled obfuscation, duplicate leakage, calibration, and inference cost. Candidate data sources include public prompt-injection examples, NotInject-related resources, and context-rich benchmark materials, subject to access, label, overlap, and licence checks. The framework returns a risk estimate, a concise evidence summary, and a review recommendation for uncertain inputs. It is intended as a screening layer, not a replacement for instruction separation, access control, least privilege, or human approval. Since implementation and testing are proposed work, no accuracy or performance improvement is claimed in advance. The intended contribution is a reproducible low-compute evaluation of when compact detectors are useful, where they over-block benign text, and how reliably their behaviour transfers to unseen sources.

title: Prompt injection defenses open a biosecurity gap
abstract: The low-authority treatment of external content that helps LLMs resist hijacking with prompt injection also defeats biosecurity warnings built into external tools

title: Bezpieczne wykorzystanie AI w analizie danych organizacyjnych
abstract: Prezentacja analizuje kluczowe aspekty bezpiecznego wykorzystania sztucznej inteligencji w organizacjach, obejmując zarówno podstawy technologiczne, jak i wyzwania prawne oraz operacyjne. Omawia transformację cyfrową prowadzącą do modelu „Organizacji 2.0”, w której dane, automatyzacja i systemy agentowe stają się fundamentem procesów decyzyjnych. Przedstawiono typologię technik AI, w tym fine-tuning oraz RAG, oraz podkreślono znaczenie jakości danych jako głównego determinanty skuteczności modeli. Szczególny nacisk położono na zagrożenia związane z cyberbezpieczeństwem, takie jak prompt injection, data poisoning czy ataki adwersarialne, oraz na rosnącą potrzebę stosowania XAI i audytów zgodności. Zaprezentowano również wymagania wynikające z AI Act, RODO oraz prawa autorskiego, a także omówiono rolę Data Governance w zapewnieniu jakości i bezpieczeństwa danych. Całość uzupełniają dane dotyczące wpływu AI na poszczególne sektory gospodarki oraz wyzwania związane z niskim zaufaniem do technologii w administracji publicznej.

title: Task-Specific LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Disinformation Detection and Factual Biography Generation
abstract: This repository contains a set of LoRA-adapted language models fine-tuned for two controlled evaluation tasks within a Responsible AI and LLM robustness framework. The models were trained and evaluated to study model behavior under standard and adversarial prompting conditions, with a particular focus on safety, factuality, resistance to manipulation, and robustness across English and Ukrainian inputs.The collection includes six task-specific adapted models:For the disinformation detection task:disinfo__Qwen2_5_3B_Instructdisinfo__SmolLM2_1_7B_Instructdisinfo__TinyLlama_1_1B_Chat_v1_0These models are used for news classification, where the model must assign the label REAL or FAKE to a news item. The task is designed to test not only classification accuracy but also resistance to malicious prompt injections, hallucination pressure, toxic framing, stereotyping, and cultural bias.For the biographical generation task:heroes__Qwen2_5_3B_Instructheroes__SmolLM2_1_7B_Instructheroes__TinyLlama_1_1B_Chat_v1_0These models are used for factual biography generation/reconstruction. The objective is to produce short, neutral, fact-grounded biographies while resisting harmful instructions such as requests to fabricate achievements, introduce defamatory claims, amplify stereotypes, reproduce imperial narratives, or generate toxic content.

title: Decision-Space Counterfactual Auditing for Prompt Injection Defense in Tool-Using LLM Agents: Code and Evaluation Artifacts
abstract: This artifact contains the code and evaluation materials for the paper “Decision-Space Counterfactual Auditing for Prompt Injection Defense in Tool-Using LLM Agents.”The release includes the Decision-Space Counterfactual Auditing (DCA) implementation, AgentDojo integration code, experiment run scripts, aggregation scripts, JSON evaluation logs, usage traces, and table-generation materials. It supports reproduction of the reported AgentDojo important_instructions experiments over 949 attacked runs and 97 clean benign tasks.The included logs cover direct execution, DCA, CaMeL, CaMeL with security policies, and DRIFT across the reported planner conditions. The artifact also documents the mapping from paper table rows to log directories and provides scripts for recomputing utility, attack success rate, clean utility, and model-call/token cost proxy summaries.API keys, model weights, virtual environments, local machine paths, incomplete smoke-test runs, and manuscript drafts are not included.

title: Securing the Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipeline: A Multi-Layered Defense Architecture Against Hallucinations and Prompt Injection Attacks
abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into enterprise applications has exposed critical safety vulnerabilities, most notably hallucinations and prompt injection attacks. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced to ground LLMs in external knowledge, it inadvertently expands the attack surface. This paper proposes a Multi-Layered Defense Architecture (MLDA) designed specifically to secure the RAG pipeline. Our framework introduces three sequential safety phases: Input Intent Verification, Contextual Grounding, and Output Confidence Filtering. To empirically validate the feasibility of the Output Confidence Filtering phase, we deployed a lightweight, open-source Natural Language Inference (NLI) model (BART-large-MNLI) to detect factual contradictions simulating LLM hallucinations. Experimental results demonstrate that the NLI model successfully identifies factual discrepancies with high confidence scores ranging from 0.82 to 0.97. This research provides a practical, reproducible, and mathematically agnostic safety framework for deploying LLMs in sensitive environments without relying on computationally expensive retraining.

title: Primary Evaluation Results for 66 Ordered Runtime Defense Variants
abstract: This dataset contains the complete primary evaluation results for 66 runtime defense variants reported in the manuscript DefenseComposer: Knowledge-Guided Defense Stacking Against Indirect Prompt Injection, submitted to the 2027 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (IEEE S&P 2027).The CSV provides benign task completion, attacked task completion, attack success rate, and runtime cost metrics for all 66 variants evaluated on AgentDojo.

title: The Comprehensive Review on Prompt Injection Attacks and Defense Mechanisms in Large Language Models
venue: Science and Technology of Engineering Chemistry and Environmental Protection
abstract: This review analyzes prompt injection attacks in large language models (LLMs) from 2019 to 2025, addressing critical security challenges as models like ChatGPT proliferate across sectors. We synthesize advances in detection, classification, and mitigation strategies, proposing a tripartite framework categorizing attacks by vector (text/image/speech), mechanism (semantic manipulation, resource exploitation), and impact (data breaches, privacy theft). Key attack vectors include the GCG algorithm, DAN jailbreaks, and resource-exhaustion tactics (e.g., Engorgio). Current defenses are evaluated for efficacy, highlighting scalability gaps and trade-offs between security and model utility. Future priorities include adaptive defense systems leveraging reinforcement learning, interdisciplinary collaboration to address ethical-technical intersections, and open threat intelligence networks for proactive vulnerability management.
